case_summary.text: EXICSE/ST/VAT : Once assessee cleared said goods on payment of duty, Cenvat credit cannot be denied on inputs/input services if subsequently it is found to be not amounting to manufactured and hence, not excisable.

CST & VAT : No input tax credit is allowable on raw materials used in manufacture of 'exempted goods'; but, where exemption is granted to 'person or class of persons' (say, 'manufacturers' of goods), raw materials used in manufacture of such goods is eliglble for input tax credit under Rajasthan VAT Act
Goods and services utilized for exports of inputs without using them in manufacturing weren’t eligible for credit

Excise & Customs : Where goods cleared from factory on payment of duty are received back in factory on account of being defective and are used in further manufacture, they are eligible for credit as 'input'
Input used in generation of dutiable waste are eligible for credit even if final product is exempted

EXCISE/ST/VA : Where appellant purchased certain goods, namely, Carbon Electrode Paste, Tamping Carbon Paste, Whytheat -A and Castable Refractory and goods had been used and consumed by appellant during manufacturing process, these were to be treated as inputs not capital goods, and therefore, appellant was entitled to take cenvat credit of 100 per cent of duty paid in procurement of said goods
Cenvat Credit : Welding Electrodes, plastic pallets and plastic crates used in relation to manufacture of final products, are eligible for credit as input
CST & VAT : Where 'raw wool' was exempt if used in manufacture of 'woollen yarn', said exemption was available even when raw wool was used in manufacture of 'woollen carpet yarn'
ST : Input services used in manufacture of exempted intermediate product is eligible for credit, if such intermediate product is used in manufacture of dutiable final product
ST : I. If assessee has not availed any credit of raw materials used for manufacture of exempted product, question of reversal of credit under rule 6 does not arise

EXCISE : Condition of non-availment of Cenvat credit prescribed in Condition No. 20 of Notification No. 6/2002-C.E. was not required to be fulfilled when assessee had imported inputs duty-free and it was not possible for assessee to avail credit of inputs
ST : If assessee has not availed any credit of raw materials used for manufacture of exempted product, question of reversal of credit under rule 6 does not arise
ST : Credit may be taken on capital goods used in manufacture of intermediate products cleared under Exemption Notification No. 214/86-CE, if duty is payable on final product
Credit denied as assessee couldn't prove use of input in manufacturing capital goods eventually used in factory
Cenvat Credit : Where, while issuing show-cause notice, claim of assessee that input services are being used in relation to manufacture of final products was not disputed, credit cannot be denied

IT : Where assessee was engaged in manufacture of polyurethane foam [PT foam] in different shapes of automobile seats and it claimed deduction under section 80-IB contending that PT foam was used by it as a raw material for manufacturing automobile seats and, therefore, end product was automobile seats, since assessee simply produced foam seats and did not undertake any further process to change its original character as PT foam, said item was covered by Entry No. 25 of Eleventh Schedule to Act

EXCISE/ST/VAT : Total Cenvat Credit" for purpose of formula under Rule 6(3A) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 is only total Cenvat credit of common input services and not Cenvat credit on input/input service exclusively used for manufacture of dutiable goods; Government had no intention to deny Cenvat credit on input/input service even though used in dutiable goods
ST : Input services used exclusively for manufacture of exempted goods are not eligible for credit, even if such goods are used by another unit of assessee for manufacture of dutiable goods

ST : Rule 6 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 doesn't apply if no cenvated input is used in manufacture of exempted goods; therefore, no payment under said rule is required on clearance of exempted Bio-composit fertilizers, manufactured out of wastes viz. press mud and spent wash

IT : Where assessee was engaged in manufacture of polyurethane foam [PT foam] in different shapes of automobile seats and it claimed deduction under section 80-IB contending that PT foam was used by it as a raw material for manufacturing automobile seats and, therefore, end product was automobile seats, since assessee simply produced foam seats and did not undertake any further process to change its original character as PT foam, said item was covered by Entry No. 25 of Eleventh Schedule to Act and, therefore, assessee was not entitled to deduction under section 80-IB

GST : In case of manufacturing utilising multiple inputs, refund of unutilised ITC cannot be denied on other inputs having higher tax rate than that of principal output merely on ground that tax rate of principal input is not more than principal output

Excise : Where, despite process not amounting to manufacture, by retrospective amendment of rule 16 of Central Excise Rules, 2002, wire drawing units were deemed to be assessee for certain period in respect of duty paid by them, said units were eligible for Cenvat credit as per CENVAT Credit Rules

Excise & Customs : Waste or Scrap is also a final product; therefore, in case of a manufacturer whose main final product is exempt, but, waste/scrap is liable to duty, he is entitled to credit of proportionate inputs which generated such waste/scrap in manufacturing process
Credit not allowable if inputs used in manufacture of exempted goods but are available if used by exempted persons

EXCISE/ST/VAT : Bulk drugs are consumed by appellant in manufacture of formulations and both are exempted vide Notification No. 6/2003-C.E. dated 01.03.2003; Bulk drugs exempted from payment of duty vide Notification No. 6/2003-C.E. not intermediate product but final product; therefore, payment of 10% of value of clearances of bulk drugs while clearing bulk drugs from bulk drugs division to formulation division proper under Rule 6(3)(b) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.

ST: Where assessee took credit of duty paid on Dumpers and their parts, which were used in factory in manufacture of final products, requirement of pre-deposit was to be dispensed with following precedents in favour of assessee

ST : Construction services used for construction of factory for expansion of production facilities were input services; security services used for both exempted as well as dutiable products were eligible for credit; and GTA and telephone services used for both exempted and dutiable products were ineligible for credit as separate records were not maintained for them

EXCISE : Exemption to packing materials procured duty free from DTA was not deniable when procedures for procurement were followed and imported duty free inputs under Advance License were used and finished goods were exported
ST : Cenvat Credit was not deniable on materials namely steel plates, steel sheets, angle, etc. as these were inputs used for repairing/maintaining vessels/barges used for providing output services
Cenvat Credit: Plastic flooring is not eligible for Cenvat credit since it is neither any aid of manufacture nor any inevitable necessity to carry out manufacture
Input services used exclusively for manufacture of exempted goods are not eligible for credit

GST: Where assessee manufacturing combed cotton yarn used certain inputs taxable at higher rates than output and claimed refund of accumulated ITC under inverted duty structure, rejection of refund on ground that principal input matched output rate was improper since statute allows refund if any input attracts higher GST, circular restricting such refund was unconstitutional and refund with interest was directed.

Cenvat Credit : Since no duty was paid/payable on final product (i.e., sugar plant) set up in a foreign country (i.e., Vietnam), therefore, no credit was allowable of duty paid on inputs/machineries/goods used in setting up of that sugar plant outside India

Excise & Customs: Where : (a) several suppliers are founded to be fake, bogus or non-existent, and (b) inputs used in manufacture of export goods are found to be non-duty-paid, assessee cannot be allowed rebate on inputs

GST : Waste/Scrap is a final product; hence, even if main final product is exempt, manufacturer is entitled to credit of proportionate inputs which generated such waste/scrap, if such waste/scrap is liable to duty

Cenvat Credit : Where final product, being garments, are liable to duty based on tariff value, such tariff value is deemed to be inclusive of all charges including packing and, therefore, cost of packing used therein is eligible for 'input' credit
IT : An assessee is entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I where process of twisting and texturising of partially oriented yarn amounted to manufacture in terms of section 80-IA
Twisting and texturising of partially oriented yarn to be deemed as manufacture; HC allows sec. 80-I relief

EXCISE/ST/VAT : Cenvat Credit not deniable on materials namely steel plates, steel sheets, angle, etc. as these are inputs used for repairing/maintaining vessels/barges used for providing output services

Excise & Customs : Where : (a) several suppliers are founded to be fake, bogus or non-existent, and (b) inputs used in manufacture of export goods are found to be non-duty-paid, assessee cannot be allowed rebate on inputs
Credit of packing material is available even if final product is liable to duty on tariff value basis

EXCISE/ST/VAT : Sine assessee debited entire Cenvat credit availed on account of service tax paid on input services utilized in manufacture of dutiable final products and not availed credit of duty paid on inputs used on exempted final product, question of recovery of 5% or 10% of value of exempted goods does not arise
'Raw wool' is also exempt from VAT if used in manufacturing of exempted 'Woollen Carpet Yarn': HC

Cenvat Credit : Expression 'used for providing output services' cannot, prima facie, be given wide import so as to cover raw materials used for construction of building; hence, construction materials are ineligible for credit
ST I : Services in relation to import of raw materials are input services, as they have nexus with manufacture of final product
Credit couldn't be denied if duty paid goods were returned and used in further manufacturing

GST : Reversal of proportionate input tax credit of common inputs/input services/capital goods is not warranted at hands of manufacturer contemplating to operate import and re-sale transaction from a Free Trade Warehousing Zone; in terms of amended section 17(3) of CGST Act, 2017, read with Explanation 3 of rule 43 of CGST Rules, 2017 even when activity/transaction is covered under paragraph 8(a) of Schedule III as long as it does not relate to supplies from ‘Duty Free Shops’ at arrival terminal in international airports to incoming passengers

Cenvat Credit : If inputs have been stored outside factory without seeking permission and without following procedure specified in Rules and there is no positive finding that inputs were used in manufacture and credit was taken only after receipt of inputs in factory, assessee cannot be allowed any credit on such inputs
Manufacturer of paper insulated wire got sec. 80-IC relief as it was different from its raw material ‘wire’

GST : Where Appellate Authority had denied refund of accumulated ITC on account of inverted tax structure by classifying spunbonded polypropylene bed sheets under Chapter Heading 5603 instead of Chapter Heading 6304 of Customs Tariff Act, 1975 without examining common parlance test and processes undertaken on non-woven fabrics, matter was remanded to it for fresh decision on issue of classification and refund claim

HEADNOTE: Section 5A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Exemption from duty of excise - Set-off - Proforma credit--Polyester fibre produced from ethylene glycol has to be given a set-off under notfn. 201/79-CE applicable to CETI: 68 goods even if some methanol, which is exempt, is produced during the chemical process. A Trade Notice explaining proforma credit is equally applicable to set-off under Notfn. 201/79-CE for CETI: 68 as the basic principles for grant of both are the same

FACT: The appellants manufacture man-made polyester fibre falling under CETI 18 using duty-paid ethylene glycol of CETI 68 and DMT in addition to other inputs. Set-off of duty paid on ethylene glycol claimed under Notfn. 201/79-CE was refused by the Asstt. Collr. for various reasons. After filing a new classification list, set-off was claimed under the amendment to the proviso which said that proforma credit could not be denied or varied on the grounds that part of the input was non-excisable waste. An appear was filed to the CCE contending that the duty-paid ethylene glycol was captively consumed in the manufacture of polyester fibre and even the waste is recycled and captively used in the manufacture of DMT. When the Asstt. Collr. held that proforma credit was applicable only for a limited amount, a second appeal was filed to the CCE, and a third appeal against the demand of duty. The CCE (Appeals) decided three appeals in favour of the appellants, but the Tribunal decided otherwise. This appeal was then filed.

HELD: Total set-off of duty paid on ethylene glycol used in the manufacture of polyester fibre must be allowed even if some part of it is contained in the methanol which is a by-product of the chemical reaction during manufacture. Since the formation of methanol cannot be prevented by using less ethylene glycol, it is obvious that the final product is polyester fibre, not methanol. ".....it is clear that the Tribunal should have held that even though a part of the ethylene glycol was contained in the by-product methanol, yet the credit of duty could not be reduced to the extent of the ethylene glycol contained in the methanol as ineligible. ......ethylene glycol was used in the manufacture of polyester fibre. It appears that methanol arises as a part and parcel of the chemical reaction during the process of manufacture when ethylene glycol interacts with DMT to produce polyester fibre. It is not possible to use a lesser quantum of the ethylene glycol to prevent methanol from arising for producing a certain quantity of polyester fibre. Thus, the quantity of ethylene glycol required to produce a certain quantum of polyester fibre is determined by the chemical reaction. It may be mentioned herein that it is not as if the appellants have used excess ethylene glycol wantonly to produce the methanol. It is clear that the appellants are not engaged in the production of methanol but in the production of polyester fibre. That position is undisputed. Therefore, it appears that the Tribunal erred when it held that the appellants were not entitled to a part of the credit of duty since ethylene glycol when it interacts with DMT also gives rise to methanol."

2. Set-off of duty paid on inputs can only be denied if the final product is totally exempt from duty. So credit of duty cannot be denied on non-excisable methanol which arose during the manufacture of dutiable polyester fibre. "....the only situation where the credit of the duty paid on the inputs could be denied was only where the final products were wholly exempt from the duty of excise or chargeable to nil rate of duty. In the present case, the excisable goods, namely, polyester fibre were not wholly exempt from duty nor chargeable to nil rate of duty. It cannot be read in the notification that the notification would not be available in case non-excisable good arise during the course of manufacture. In fact, the Tribunal seems to have erred in not bearing in mind that exemption notification was pressed in service in respect of polyester fibre which is excisable goods and not in respect of methanol which arises as a by-product as a part and parcel of chemical reaction."

HEADNOTE: Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Inputs - Manufacturer took Modvat credit on polyester fibre used as inputs for manufacture of yarn - Process loss being abnormal, manufacturers were denied credit on certain parts of inputs - Manufacturer contended that process loss was more than normal because of poor quality of input - Further, Board’s Letter, dated 15-1-1988 clarified that credit of duty on input cannot be denied on ground that parts of inputs is contained in wastes and scraps, which may even be exempted from customs duty - Whether in view of this clarification and fact that revenue had not conducted any experiment to determine range of normal loss during processing of goods and further in view of lack of evidence of any malpractice by manufacturer, demand on manufacturer could not be sustained - Held, yes Circulars and Notifications : Board’s Letter, dated 15-1-1988

FACT: The appellants manufactured polyester viscose blended yarn and cotton polyester yarn. They took Cenvat credit on the polyester fibre which was the input. The revenue proceeded against the appellants on ground that in use of polyester in production the normal process loss can be limited only to 2 to 3 per cent. However, the actual loss in case of the appellants was much more. Therefore, the duty was demanded from the appellants on certain quantity of polyester fibres on which Modvat credit was taken. Besides that penalty was also imposed on the appellant. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) set aside order of the original authority.

On appeal :

HELD: Revenue had not conducted any experiment to determine the range of normal loss, while processing the goods. Further in the Board’s Letter, dated 15-1-1988, it was clarified that credit to the duty on inputs cannot be denied on the ground that parts of the inputs is contained in the wastes and scraps, which may even be exempted from Customs duty. [Para 2]

No doubt, the loss of polyester fibre in this case was something more than the normal but the appellant attributes it to the poor quality of the fibre received. There was no evidence of any over malpractice by the respondents. In these circumstances, the order of the Commissioner appeared to be legal. Hence, the revenue’s appeal was to be dismissed. [Para 3]

U. Rajaram for the Appellant. M.V. Raman for the Respondent.

, polyester fibre were not wholly exempt from duty nor chargeable to nil rate of duty. It cannot be read in the notification that the notification would not be available in case non-excisable good arise during the course of manufacture. In fact, the Tribunal seems to have erred in not bearing in mind that exemption notification was pressed in service in respect of polyester fibre which is excisable goods and not in respect of methanol which arises as a by-product as a part and parcel of chemical reaction." 3. Trade notice clarifying rule 56A must be considered in interpreting exemption Notfn. 201/79-CE since it is applicable to both. "On an analysis and comparison of aforesaid, it is clear that the clarification in the form of trade notice issued by the Pune Collect prate in respect of rule 56A was as much applicable to that rule as to notification No. 201/79. .....exemption notifications are meant to be implemented and trade notices in these matters clarify the stand of the Government for the trade. It is clear, therefore, that the Tribunal failed to interpret the words of the exemption notification No. 201/79 properly and fully. .....it appears further on a comparison of the rule 56A and the notification No. 201/79 that these deal with the identical situation."

4. Methanol arising during the process of manufacture of polyester fibre through chemical reaction is a product which can be said to be used to its manufacture. "Just because methanol arises as a part and parcel of the chemical reaction during the process of manufacture, it cannot be said that methanol was not used in the manufacture of polyester fibre."

2002 Rules, exception clause contained in sub-rule (5) of rule 6 was applicable in case of only exempted goods, whereas exception clause contained in sub-rule (6) of rule 6 of 2004 Rules, applies both to exempted goods, as also goods subject to duty, because the term used in sub-rule (6) is ‘excisable goods’ and not ‘exempted goods’, as was the case in 2002 Rules. [Para 11] The scheme of the 2002 Rules as also the 2004 Rules shows that Cenvat credit/refund is allowed on the inputs of all manufactured goods which are not exempt from duty, as is clear from a combined reading of rule 3 and sub-rule (1) of rule 6 of 2002 Rules, as also the 2004 Rules, so as to avoid indirect double taxation on inputs. However, this rule is not absolute. It is subject to exception clause, contained in rule 6(5) of the 2002 Rules and rule 6(6) of the 2004 Rules, and one of the exceptions is in respect of excisable goods, which are cleared for export under bond in terms of the provisions of Central Excise Rules, 2002. [Para 16]

Sub-rule (5) of rule 6 of the 2002 Rules was applicable only in case of exempted goods. That meant that the exception was not applicable in case of dutiable goods. It appears that this led to anomalous situations. For example, if the goods were dutiable and were exported, credit for Cenvat could not be claimed in respect of input of those goods, at least under the aforesaid exception clause. To overcome this kind of anomalous situation, exception clause contained in sub-rule (6) of rule 6 of 2004 Rules has been made applicable to all excisable goods. [Para 17]

Thus, there was no merit in the submission of the revenue that term ‘excisable goods’ used in sub-rule (6) of rule 6 of 2004 Rules, meant only dutiable goods. [Para 18]

An assessee manufacturing goods chargeable to nil duty, is eligible to avail Cenvat credit of duty paid on the inputs under the exception clause to rule 6, as contained in rule 6(5) of the 2002 Rules and rule 6(6) of the 2004 Rules, used in the manufacture of such goods, if the goods are exported. [Para 20]

Further it is clear from a bare reading of rule 5 of the 2004 Rules that a manufacturer, who exports the final products which are exempt from duty, can claim refund of Cenvat credit. [Para 21]

HEADNOTE: Section 37 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Rule making powers of Central government - Drawback - average of duties paid on inputs is admissible as fixed. It is a composite figure comprising both customs and excise duties. Act does not envisage total refund either of customs or of excise paid on such inputs. Hence customs duty paid on DMT cannot be refunded in full

FACT: The appellants manufacture polyester fibre yarn. In 1975 they were awarded a contract by Imperial Chemical Industries, Singapore for manufacture of blended yarn to be exported to an ICI customer in Sri Lanka. ICI Singapore supplied free of cost one of the raw materials, dimethyl terephthalate (DMT) for manufacture of the polyester fibre yam which was to be blended with viscose staple fibre yarn for production of the blended yarn to be exported to Sri Lanka. The appellants obtained Customs Clearance Permits (CCPs) for the DMT so supplied. The conditions of the CCPs were that the polyester fibre would be manufactured from the imported DMT under Customs bond, the blending with viscose fibre would be carried out under excise supervision (manufacture in bond), and thereafter the blended yam would be exported to Sri Lanka. However, the Customs authorities were not in a position to permit manufacture of polyester fibre under bond and declined the appellants' request for such manufacture, as a result of which the appellants could only clear the DMT after paying the customs duty in force at the time. The DMT thus cleared on payment of duty was used for manufacture of polyester fibre, which in turn was blended with indigenous viscose fibre to produce blended yam which was duly exported. Subsequently, on 2.8.1976, a notification was issued which fully exempted imported DMT from customs duty, but as the import of DMT in their case was prior to that date, the appellants were not entitled to avail of that exemption. The appellants then filed a claim for drawback of the customs duty paid by them on the DMT, and the rejection of this claim at all levels up to the High Court has led to the present appeals to the Supreme Court. The plea of the appellants is that the drawback permissible was equal to the excise duty on the manufacture of blended yarn. As they had not paid any excise duty in view of manufacture under excise supervision, the question of drawback of excise duty did not arise. The fact that the drawback was equal to the excise duty payable indicated, according to them, that the customs duty element had not been considered while computing drawback.

HELD: Drawback--The drawback rules do not envisage refund of the entire amount of duty (customs + central excise) paid by an individual manufacturer in the production of export goods, but only of an 'average amount of duty paid on materials', taking into consideration the circumstances of the trade and other relevant factors. Merely fulfilling the conditions of section 75 of the Customs Act or section 37 of the Central Excises Act is not enough to entitle a manufacturer to drawback on the entire amount of duty paid. "......the assessees' arguments are based on a basic misapprehension that, under the Acts and rules, a manufacturer is automatically entitled to a drawback of the entire customs and excise duties paid by him if the terms and conditions of section 75 are fulfilled. Though section 75 of the Customs Act and section 37 of the Central Excises and Salt Act empower the Government to provide for the repayment of the customs and excise duties paid by individual manufacturers also, the rules as framed (rule 3 in particular) provides only for a refund of the "average amount of duty paid on materials" of any particular class or description of goods used for the manufacture of export goods of that class or description by manufacturers generally, except to the extent prescribed under rule 7......The rules do not envisage a refund of an amount arithmetically equal to the customs duty or central excise duty which may have been actually paid by an individual importer-cum-manufacturer.........section 75(2) requires the amount of drawback to be determined on a consideration of all the circumstances prevalent in a particular trade and the fact situation relevant in respect of each of various classes of goods imported and manufactured.......the drawback rules provide for a determination of the drawback after taking into account the "average" amount in respect of each of the various items specified in rule 3 in relation to each type of goods listed in Schedule II........the amount of drawback is not intended to be the amount of the duties that may have been paid by individual manufacturers; it is to be determined by considering the overall position prevalent in the country in respect of each of the categories of trade in the goods specified in Schedule II."

Further, that proviso (i)(b) indicated that when inputs fall under different tariff items the procedure could be made available to goods specifically sanction remission or adjustment of duty by the Central Government. Lastly, it was pointed out that there was no repugnancy between sub-rule (I) and sub-rule(2) of rule; which had to be read harmoniously with the proviso HELD: Wording of rule 56A(1) and (2) read with the proviso attached to sub-(2) clearly shows that specification of excisable goods means specification finished excisable goods for which the credit procedure laid down in sub-rule (sic) attracted. "In our view, the question has to be answered in the light of the express language of rule 56A (1) and (2) read with the proviso attached to sub-rule (2) as held the field at the relevant time ....in the context of the caption to rule 56A (1), it must held that specification of excisable goods would be specification of the finished excisable goods. Once that specification is made under sub-rule (1) of rule 5 procedure of sub-rule (2) would get attracted, as provided by sub-rule (1) of 56A itself Once that eventuality takes place, the entire machinery of sub-rule (2) of rule 56A will be made available for the specified excisable goods in question..... ....When the procedure laid down under sub-rule (2) gets attracted to the specified excisable goods, the entire sub-rule (2) would get attracted and not sub-rule dehors the proviso. On the express language of sub-rule (2) of rule 56A, it must be held that proviso which forms a part and parcel of sub-rule (2) also gets attracted case of special excisable goods, duly notified in the official gazette by the Central Government under sub-rule (1) of rule 56A.......it is sufficient to note that the specified finished excisable goods, procedure of sub-rule (2) alongwith the proviso gets attracted."

2. "No credit rule" applies to finished excisable goods in the manufacture which duty paid inputs mentioned in the later part of the proviso to sub-rule (2) 56A have been used. "Thus, the proviso contemplates no credit rule in connection with the finished excisable goods which are made up of material or component parts, as are dealt with in the later part of the proviso.....a conjoint reading of caption of rule 56A with sub-rule (1) clearly indicates that excisable goods that are to be specified under sub-rule (1) will be those excisable goods which are finished excisable goods and which utilise duty paid material or component parts in their manufacturing process."

3. Proforma credit scheme is a composite, well-knit scheme for the workability of which both inputs and outputs have to be considered comprehensively together. "Further question arises as to how the inputs from which such specified excisable commodity is manufactured are treated by the rule making authority so that the finished excisable commodity produced out of them can earn proforma credit of duty is to be given in connection with the inputs and not the outputs. If the outputs are not specified no further question arises. If they are specified as per rule 56A(1), then the further and more important question will arise as to which inputs can be covered by the scheme of proforma credit procedure. Hence, no scheme of proforma credit is complete without a comprehensive, interconnected and simultaneous consideration of inputs and outputs."

4. Harmonious reading of sub-paras (i) and (ii) and interpretation of the words 'and unless' interconnecting the sub-paras to mean 'and except when' clearly shows that specified finished excisable goods are not entitled to proforma credit benefit if wholly exempt or chargeable to nil rate of duty, "the rule making authority has advisedly employed the words 'and unless' interconnecting sub-paras (i) and (ii) of the proviso which mean 'except when'. When so read, it becomes clear that specified finished excisable goods will not be entitled to the benefit of the proforma credit if (a) they are wholly exempt from excise duty or chargeable to nil rate of duty......Thus a harmonious reading of two sub-paras of the proviso projects the following picture. The specified finished excisable commodity will not get benefit of the proforma if it is wholly exempt from excise duty or chargeable to nil duty. Thus, only those finished excisable goods duly specified under sub-rule (1) of rule 56A will get the benefit of proforma credit, which are exigible to excise duty."

5. Inputs used in the manufacture of specified finished excisable goods must be leviable to duty under the same tariff item as the finished goods or covered by remission or adjustment of duty on inputs sanctioned by the Central Government if they fall under different tariff items. "The inputs which go to manufacture these specified finished excisable goods which bear excise duty must themselves either be exigible to tax under the same tariff item or alternatively even though these inputs are exigible to tax under the different tariff items, then, they must be covered by the specific sanction of the Central Government granting remission or adjustment of duty on these inputs."

HELD: If an imported article is one which has been manufactured or produced, then it must be presumed, for purpose of CVD, that such an article can likewise be manufactured or produced in India; actual manufacture or production in India is not necessary.

HEADNOTE: Rule 56A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Proforma Credit - Inputs relief - proforma credit admissible even if end products (tyres) are exempts: U/Notfn. 95/79-CE, since no correlation is required. CE NOTFN. 95/79-CE

FACT: The issue is whether proforma credit can be availed of by the manufacturers in terms of Notfn. No. 95/79-CE on inputs even if the end product (tyres) listed is liable to nil rate of duly.

HELD: Set off Since Notfn. No. 95/79-CE does not contain a clause to the effect that proforma credit on inputs should be correlated to the duty payable on outputs, non-payment of duty on finished goods does not make the manufacturer ineligible to proforma credit. "Read by itself this notification does not have any condition that there should be any nexus between the inputs and outputs.... The Ld. JDR's argument that goods mentioned in column 5 (final products) are only those which pay duty is not supported by the wordings of the notification. No condition regarding payment of duty is contained any where in the notification. We are further supported in this view by a judgment of the Cegat (SRB) (CCE Bangalore v. Wipro Information Technology, Bangalore) reported in 1988(14) ECR 490 wherein it was held that proforma credit once allowed cannot be recovered subsequently even if finished goods are exempted later on, making proforma credit ineligible, since no interlinking account is provided for in rule."

Minority view:--Interpretation--as per proviso 2 of the Notfn. availability of proforma credit on inputs is directly proportional to the duty payable on the finished product and since tyres were cleared without payment of duty, set off cannot be allowed on the inputs used in the manufacture of tyres. Proviso 2 of Notfn. No. 95/79-CE ".....the extent of the credit that could be taken in respect of the duty paid on the inputs shall be restricted to the duty payable on the end product if it happens to be less than the credit of duty taken on the inputs. What follows from this therefore, is that if the duty payable on the end product is nil, then the extent of exemption that will be available will also be nil........In as much as, no duty in respect of these tyres has been paid, in terms of proviso 2 to the notification, the availability of the credit on the inputs in respect of these tyres will have therefore, to be nil."

FACT: The assessee was engaged in manufacture of texturised Polyster filament yarn. It had not taken any Central excise registration. It cleared goods for home consumption as well as exports without payment of excise duty by availing exemption under Notification No. 30/04. The assessee obtained Central excise registration on 9-10-2009 and on 26-10-2009, filed a refund claim of Cenvat credit of inputs used in the manufacture of texturised Polyster filament yarn exported during the period 1-11-2008 to 7-10-2009. The Assistant Commissioner rejected the refund claim on the ground that refund is permissible only if the dutiable goods are exported under bond or LUT and since the assessee was availing full exemption and was not even registered with Central excise, and fully exempted goods were not exported under bond or LUT, the refund was not permissible. The Asst. Commissioner further observed that as the assessee was not registered with Central excise, therefore, it was not eligible for taking the Cenvat credit and hence question of refund did not arise. It was further held that as the assessee was registered only on 9-10-2009 in view of rule 3(2), it was eligible for only transitional Cenvat credit from 9-10-2010 on the inputs and inputs contained in final products in stock as on 9-10-2010.

On appeal:

HELD: In the instant case the registration certificate was issued only on 9-10-2009 whereas, Cenvat credit has been taken with effect from 1-11-2008. The assessee had availed the benefit of exemption Notification No. 30/2004-C.E. in respect of the indigenous as well as export yarns during the period. Notification No. 30/04 provides for exemption on the finished goods if the Cenvat credit has not been taken. In the normal course, if the assessee was to follow the rules and procedures correctly, it would have taken registration before 1-11-2008, paid duty on the finished yearn and cleared the same for export and thereafter, claim the rebate. As regards the goods manufactured for domestic consumption, it could have reversed the credit as per the formula prescribed by the Government or reverse the credit before the clearance of the goods. However, this was not followed by the assessee because of which the dispute has arisen. [Para 4]

The Tribunal in the case of J.R. Herbal Care India Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (253) E.L.T. 321 (Tri. - Delhi) took a view that there is no provision in the rules that credit was not available to unregistered manufacturers. Manufacturers exempted from the registration do not cease to be a manufacturer of excisable goods. Said case squarely covers the issue in the instant case also. Therefore, in respect of the goods manufactured during the period when the assessee was not registered, credit can be taken subsequently also. This view is further supported by the consistent stand taken by various judicial forums in the case of clandestine removals, even if the duty is paid subsequently, Cenvat credit on inputs used will be available to the assessee/manufacturer subject to the conditions that proper documents showing the payment of duty are available. In the case of SSI units also, wherever SSI benefits have been denied, Cenvat credit has been allowed. Therefore in the instant case also the action of the assessee in taking credit on 9-10-2009 has to be upheld. [Para 5]

The Hon'ble High Court in the case of CCE v. Drish Shoes Ltd. [2010] 27 STT 270 (HP) held that refund of input credit is admissible when exempted goods are exported without execution of bond. Similar was the view taken by the High Court in the case of Repro India Ltd. v. Union of India 2009 (235) E.L.T. 64 (Bom.). Therefore, the conclusion in the impugned order that assessee is not eligible for exemption since the goods have not been exported under bond or LUT, cannot be sustained. [Para 6]

In the case of Salzer Controls Ltd. v. CCE 2003 (160) E.L.T. 1169 (Tri.- Chennai) it was held that benefit of exemption or concession should not be denied whenever intended use of material is established by other evidences and just because of procedural violation, that by itself will not disentitle them from taking the benefit. In this case it is not the case of the department that goods have not been exported or assessee did not have the relevant documents for availing credit or inputs have not been used for the manufacture of exported goods. [Para 7]

HEADNOTE: Rule 5, read with rule 6, of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 and rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002 - Cenvat credit - Refund of - Period August, 2004 to March, 2005 - Whether, an assessee, manufacturing goods chargeable to nil duty, is eligible to avail Cenvat credit of duty paid on inputs under exception clause to rule 6 [as contained in rule 6(5) of 2002 Rules and rule 6(6) of 2004 Rules] which are used in manufacture of goods exported - Held, yes - Whether further in view of provisions of rule 5, a manufacturer, who exports final products which are exempt from duty, can claim refund of Cenvat credit of duty paid on inputs and inputs services used in manufacture and export of said wholly exempted final products - Held, yes [Paras 20 and 21] Circulars & Notifications : Notification No. 11/2002, dated 1-3-2002

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of finished leather, which was wholly exempt from payment of duty. During the period from August, 2004 to March, 2005, the assessee exported manufactured leather. In view of the provisions of rules 5 and 6(6)(v ) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, the assessee claimed refund of Cenvat credit of duty paid on inputs purchased by it to convert raw leather into finished leather. The Adjudicating Authority rejected the refund claim of the assessee.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the refund claim of the assessee holding that the object of exception clause contained in rule 6, was to promote the export of goods manufactured in India, and that in any case, exception clause of rule 6 allowed the credit/refund of Cenvat paid on inputs in the manufacture of excisable products, exported under a bond. On second appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

On appeal to the High Court :

HELD: Rule 3 of the 2004 Rules, as also rule 3 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002 [2002 Rules] which have been repealed by the 2004 Rules, provides for credit of Cenvat paid by a manufacturer on any inputs or capital goods received in a factory for use in or in relation to the manufacture of final products. Rule 6(1) of the 2004 Rules as also the 2002 Rules, says that Cenvat credit shall not be allowed on such quantity of input which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods. Sub-rule (5) of rule 6 of the 2002 Rules, and sub-rule (6) of rule 6 of the 2004 Rules are an exception to rule 6(1). Sub-rule (5)(vi ) of the 2002 Rules, provided that sub-rules (1), (2), (3) and (4) shall not be applicable in case of exempted goods, which are cleared for export under bond, in terms of provisions of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. [Para 9]

Rule 6(6)(v) of the 2004 Rules provides that the provisions of sub-rules (1), (2), (3) and (4) of rule 6, shall not be applicable in case the excisable goods removed without payment of duty are cleared for export under bond in terms of provisions of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. [Para 10]

The only difference between the 2002 Rules and the 2004 Rules is that in case of 2002 Rules, exception clause contained in sub-rule (5) of rule 6 was applicable in case of only exempted goods, whereas exception clause contained in sub-rule (6) of rule 6 of 2004 Rules, applies both to exempted goods, as also goods subject to duty, because the term used in sub-rule (6) is ‘excisable goods’ and not ‘exempted goods’, as was the case in 2002 Rules. [Para 11]

HEADNOTE: Rule 11 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002 - Cenvat credit - Power of Central Government to notify goods for deemed Cenvat credit - Whether Tribunal was justified in allowing deemed credit to assessee in respect of fibre/yarn used in grey fabric which was an indirect input in assessee’s final product, in view of Notification No. 6/2002-CE(NT), dated 1-3-2002 - Held, yes [Para 11] Circulars & Notifications: Notification No. 6/2002 - CE(NT), dated 1-3-2002, Circular No. 702/18/2003-CX, dated 13-3-2003

FACT: The Tribunal allowed deemed credit to the assessee-respondent in respect of fibre/yarn used in grey fabric which was an indirect input in the assessee’s final product, processed fabric, in view of the Notification No. 6/2002-CE(NT), dated 1-3-2002.

On appeal, the revenue/appellant contended that the said notification referred to a table of inputs and final products; that the input of the respondent was grey fabric and not yarn/fibre; that grey fabric was not referred to in the table of inputs mentioned in the said notification and, therefore, the respondent would not be entitled to claim the benefit of the said notification in respect of its manufactured products-processed fabrics. On the other hand, the respondent relied on Circular No. 702/18/2003-CX, dated 13-3-2003. In that context the circular discussed Notification No. 29/96-CE (NT), dated 3-9-1996 which was the predecessor notification to the instant Notification No. 6 pertaining to availment of deemed credit. The Central Board of Excise and Customs, by virtue of the said circular, observed that, although grey fabrics are not included as the declared inputs in the said notification, they are made out of duty paid yarn/fibres, which are declared inputs and have suffered appropriate excise duty. The Board also reiterated its earlier view and observed that the refund of the said unutilized deemed credit of grey fabric was admissible. The respondent submitted that in view of the clarification given by the Board, it was clear that inputs, which formed part of the intermediate products, namely, grey fabrics, were to be considered for the purposes of deemed credit in terms of the Notification No. 6 referred to above.

HELD: Rule 11 makes it clear that the Cenvat credit is to be allowed in respect of the inputs, even if the declared inputs are not used directly by the manufacturer of the final products declared in a notification under rule 11 but are contained in the final products. [Para 8]

A plain reading of the Notification No. 6/2002 - CE(NT), dated 1-3-2002 shows that a distinction has been drawn between the composite mills and other than composite mills. The Explanation 2 to clause (6) of the notification makes it clear as to what is meant by a composite mill. It means a manufacturer who is engaged in the processing of fabrics with the aid of power along with the spinning of yarn from the fibres and weaving or knitting or crocheting of fabrics within the same factory, etc. The respondent was not a composite mill. It manufactured its final product-processed fabrics not by spinning of the yarn from fabrics but from grey fabric purchased from the market. The Explanation 3 was also relevant inasmuch as it clarifies that the provisions of the notification would not apply where the processed fabric itself is used as an input for further processing. The consequence of this Explanation and clarification is that if there is any processed fabric and the same is further processed into the final product, namely, processed fabric, the same would not be eligible for the benefit under the said notification. However, insofar as yarn/fibre is concerned the same, admittedly, finds mention in the table of inputs in Column 2 of the said notification. [Para 10]

The second leg of the definition is an inclusive one. The inclusive definition is a well-recognized device to enlarge the meaning of the word defined. It expands the meaning in the basic definition. [Para 7] In the definition given in rule 2(l )(ii), the inclusive part of the definition expands the scope of ‘input service’ as given in the basic definition by bringing within its ambit, services which would not normally get covered by the main definition: construction and other allied services used for setting up of a factory, for example, have been specifically included, though the use of these services in the setting up of the factory precedes manufacture and the activity is concluded prior to commencement of the manufacturing process. Again, auditing of accounts relating to a final product has been considered to be an ‘input service’ though this service is used after the completion of manufacture of final product and could not have been used directly or indirectly in the manufacturing process. Both the above services, however, have a nexus with and are related to the final product : the setting up of a factory provides the space and machinery for manufacture and auditing ensures proper accounting of the inputs and disposal of the final products. A perusal of the other services in the inclusive part of the definition indicates that use of each of these services is linked to manufacture, storage, transport or sale of the final product. The services of market research, sales promotion and advertising, for example, may not be used in the actual process of manufacture which is necessary for their inclusion in the basic definition of input service, yet they find mention in the inclusive definition as their use does promote sale of the final product. Similar is the case with regard to services used in storage and transportation, accounting, auditing, financing, etc. It is relevant to note here that when the extended definition specifically includes services used for setting up certain buildings, such buildings are restricted to buildings used to house factories and its offices. A manufacturer may construct other types of buildings for its employees such as residential quarters, hospitals, recreation centres, schools, etc. From the nature of the buildings specifically included in the extended definition and the kinds of services included in it, it has to be inferred that construction of only such buildings would be covered as input service which are linked to manufacture, storage, sale, transportation, etc., of the final product. Provision of buildings for housing, schooling, recreation, etc., of workers improves their quality of life and is a welfare measure but they have no nexus with the manufacture, storage or sale of the final products. Even when an extended definition is used, it is necessary to draw a line to exclude categories obviously not intended to be included. A ‘service’ not mentioned in the extended definition has to partake of the characteristics common to the other services specifically mentioned, in order to become an ‘input service’ as per the extended definition. As mentioned above, the common thread running through all the services specifically included in the extended definition is that each of these is linked to manufacture, storage or sale of the final product. Services used for constructing buildings for housing workers and staff, do not have a nexus with the manufacture, sale or storage of the final product and, therefore, such services cannot be considered to be ‘input service’ even as per the extended definition. Therefore, the first question posed for advance ruling was to be answered in the negative. [Para 8]

FACT: The assessee is engaged in the manufacturing of polyester cotton blended yarn and polyester viscose blended yarn and both these products fall under Chapter 55 of the Schedule to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985.

For manufacture of the aforesaid product, the assessee had used the raw material which was an intermediate product and paid excise duty thereupon. The final products were also cleared on payment of excise duty on those finished products.

The assessee exported these goods on payment of central excise duty in CENVAT account and filed rebate claims under the provisions of Rule 18 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 (hereinafter referred to as the 'Rules').

The department opined that the assessee is entitled to one of the two claims for rebate, i.e., either rebate of duty paid on exported goods or the duty paid on inputs used in the exported goods, and not on both of them.

The revisional authority viz. Central Government held that that assessee was entitled to rebate both on the exported goods as well as inputs used in the exported goods.

The High Court held in favour of revenue on ground that out of the two, rule 18 of the Rules permits rebate only qua one of them (viz. either on inputs or on output) and not on both the duties.

HELD: I. Rule 18

Rule 18 stipulates that the Central Government may, by notification, grant rebate of duty paid on such excisable goods OR duty paid on material used in the manufacturing or processing of such goods. Rule 18 is only an enabling provision which empowers the Central Government to issue a notification for grant of these rebates and prescribes the procedure for claiming such rebate(s). [Para 9]

II.Historical perspective of the statutory scheme

Central Excise Rules under the Act were first framed in the year 1944. Rule 12 thereof provided for rebate of duty and Rule 13 enabled exporter to export the goods without payment of duty. As per the said rules it is clear that, from the very beginning, two alternative methods were provided enabling an exporter of goods to get rid of the burden of paying the excise duty; both on excisable goods as well as on materials used in the manufacture of goods. The exporter could either claim rebate when the duty was paid. Or else, he was free not to pay excise duty at all on both types of goods by executing a bond in the prescribed form and fulfilling the conditions prescribed in this behalf.

The grant of rebate, in either of the options, has always been in respect of both kinds of excise duties, i.e. on the final product that is exported as well as on the intermediate product on which excise duty is paid/payable and the same is used as raw material in the manufacture of goods. Under these rules also, Notification No. 41/94-CE(NT), dated 12-9-1994 and Notification No. 42/94-CE(NT), dated 21-9-1994 were issued for grant of rebate of duty on export of all excisable goods, except minerals oils and ship stores and rebate on materials used in manufacture of goods exported out of India, respectively. [Paras 16 & 17]

The very fact that yarn/fibre is mentioned as an input in respect of non-composite mills also makes it clear that the notification is to allow deemed credit in respect of such inputs, although they are not to be used directly by the non-composite mills. HEADNOTE: Rule 57 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Cenvat Credit (Modvat) - OE goods cleared without duty under Chapter X procedure--Whether Modvat admissible--Referred to Larger Bench in view of conflicting decisions

FACT: The appellants receive duly paid bi-metal strips for use in the manufacture of I.C. Engines and parts thereof. They avail of Modvat Credit for the inputs. The appellants cleared certain parts like plain shaft bearings at nil rate of duty by following Chapter X procedure. The Assistant Collector held that credit could not be allowed on inputs used in the manufacture of parts cleared at nil rate of duty as per provisions of Rule 57C of the Central Excise Rules, 1944. This was upheld by the Collector (Appeals).

HELD: Though one to one co-relation of inputs with final product is not prescribed, there appears to be a tacit requirement of reading Rule 57C into the provisions of Rule 57F(3)(i). However in view of the fact that decisions of two Benches run somewhat contrary to each other, the issue "whether credit of duty paid on inputs used in the manufacture of declared final product part of which is cleared without payment of duty could be disallowed" should be placed before a Larger Bench for decision. "Though one to one co-relation is not prescribed under Rule 57F(3)(i), there appears to be a tacit requirement of reading Rule 57C into the provisions of Rule 57F(3)(i). This is the view taken by the East Regional Bench, which we also share to a certain extent. .......Since the issues involves consideration of these points of law and the decisions for two Benches run somewhat contrary to each other, we consider it fit for placing before the larger Bench, for deciding on the following questions.

"Whether, in the context of the provisions of Rule 57C vis-a-vis Rule 57F(3)(i) of the Central Excise Rules, Modvat credit of duty paid on inputs used in the manufacture of declared final products, part of which are cleared free of the whole of duty of excise leviable thereon, in terms of an exemption Notification, could be disallowed by way of reversal of credit of duty on such inputs, which have been used in the manufacture of final products cleared free of duty"?"

cash or by debiting the Cenvat credit availed on inputs used in the manufacture of exported goods can be claimed by the exporter as rebate of duty under rule 18 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. In the instant case, the assessee had paid excise duty on the exported peppermint oil by debiting the Cenvat credit availed on menthol used in the manufacture of exempted menthol crystals and dutiable peppermint oil. [Para 20] Basic argument of the revenue was that, where the duty paid inputs are used in the manufacture of final products which are exempted from payment of excise duty, Cenvat credit on input is not allowable under rule 6(1). In the instant case, it was contended by the revenue that the assessee had neither maintained separate accounts regarding inputs used in the manufacture of exempted/dutiable final products as provided under rule 6(2) nor paid an amount on clearance of exempted menthol crystals as provided under rule 6(3) and, therefore, the assessee could not avail credit of duty paid on menthol (input) and, consequently, the duty paid on peppermint oil by debiting the input credit being not valid the question of allowing rebate of that duty did not arise at all. [Para 21]

It is true that under rule 6(1), credit of duty paid on inputs is not allowable when the inputs are used in the manufacture of exempted final products. But rule 6(2) provides that where the inputs are used in the manufacture of exempted as well as dutiable final products, credit of duty paid on inputs used in the manufacture of dutiable final products is allowable, provided separate accounts regarding the receipt, consumption and inventory of the input used in the manufacture of dutiable final product are maintained. However, rule 6(6) provides that the provisions contained in rule 6(1) to 6(4) shall not apply in certain specified cases, where the excisable goods are cleared without payment of duty. Clause (v) of rule 6(6) provides that where the exempted goods are cleared for export without payment of duty under the Central Excise Rules, 2002, the provisions contained in rule 6(1) to 6(4) shall not apply. Thus, rule 6(6) carves out an exception to the applicability of the provisions contained in rule 6(1) to 6(4) in certain specified cases. [Para 22]

In the instant case, admittedly, the exempted menthol crystals had been cleared for exports under bond without payment of duty and, therefore, the case of the assessee would be covered under rule 6(6)(v) and, consequently, rule 6(1) to 6(4) would not be applicable to the facts of the instant case. In other words, in the instant case, the credit of duty paid on menthol used in the manufacture of exempted menthol crystals was allowable, because, exempted menthol crystals had been exported under bond without payment of duty. [Para 23]

The question then to be considered was, whether excise duty on exported peppermint oil could be paid by debiting Cenvat credit availed on the inputs used in the manufacture of exempted menthol crystals? [Para 24]

Rule 5 specifically provides that where the exempted final product is cleared without payment of duty under bond, the credit of duty paid on input used in the manufacture of the exempted final product shall be allowed to be utilised for payment of duty on any final product by way of adjustment of input credit and where for any reasons such adjustment is not possible, refund of the unutilized input credit would be allowed. [Para 25]

In the instant case, the assessee on export of exempted menthol crystals had utilized the Cenvat credit availed on inputs used in the manufacture of exempted menthol crystals for paying the excise duty on peppermint oil cleared for export as provided under rule 5. Thus, in the facts of the present case, since the credit of duty paid on input used in the manufacture of exempted final product was utilized for payment of excise duty on exported peppermint oil, the assessee, instead of getting refund of input credit under rule 5, was entitled to rebate of duty paid on exported peppermint oil as provided under rule 18 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. [Para 26]

HEADNOTE: Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services - Whether an assessee, which uses inputs exclusively for manufacture of exempted goods and services but makes clearances in any manner specified in sub-rule (6) of rule 6, shall be entitled to credit on inputs exclusively used for production of exempted final products or for provision of exempted services - Held, yes - Whether, there is no justification to collect 10 per cent of sale price of exempted goods manufactured using inputs exclusively meant for manufacture of exempted goods and services - Held, yes - Whether sub-rules (1), (2), (3) and (4) of rule 6 shall not be applicable to case of inputs relatable to excisable goods that are removed without payment of duty either to a hundred per cent EOU or cleared for export under bond in terms of provisions of Central Excise Rules, 2002 - Held, yes [Para 5.2]

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of both, dutiable and exempted bulk drugs. It had opted for not maintaining separate accounts for dutiable and exempted goods as envisaged under rule 6(3). It took credit of duty paid on all the inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods, including exclusive inputs (other than common inputs) and paid 10 per cent on the sale price of exempted goods cleared in domestic market. By the Notification No. 27/2005, dated 16-5-2005 rule 6(3) was amended by inserting Explanation III clarifying that credit shall not be allowed on inputs and input services used exclusively for the manufacture of exempted goods or provision of exempted service. Pursuant to the above amendment show-cause notices were issued to the assessee demanding the Cenvat credit relatable to (i) the exclusive inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods which were cleared on payment at 10 per cent of the sale price of the exempted goods; (ii) the exclusive inputs removed as such; (iii) the exclusive inputs used in the finished goods exported; (iv) the exclusive inputs used in the finished goods removed to 100 per cent EOU; (v) the exclusive inputs lying in stock; (vi) the exclusive inputs used in the finished goods lying in the stock. The demands were confirmed by the Commissioner.

On appeal :

HELD: The Explanation III to rule 6 does not say anything inconsistent with the Cenvat scheme of allowing credit of duty paid on inputs that go into production of goods or services that suffer duty so that there is no cascading effect of goods or services resulting in double taxation. A position that influenced the legislative policy all along is reiterated by expressly denying credit where the final products or services are not subject to tax. The Explanation has been issued for the removal of doubts. The Explanation is in the nature of a clarification and so applies retrospectively. Exceptions to the rule 3 are specified in sub-rule (6) of rule 6. Therefore, an assessee which uses inputs exclusively for the manufacture of exempted goods and services but makes clearances in any manner specified in sub-rule (6) of rule 6 shall be entitled to credit on exclusive inputs used for the production of exempted final products or provision of exempted services. However, in cases not covered by such exceptions, taking of credit on inputs by such assessees shall be irregular in view of the sub-rule (3) of rule 6. Such credit can be recovered along with interest as provided in rule 14. There is no justification to collect 10 per cent of the sale price of exempted goods manufactured using exclusive inputs. There is no legal sanction for such recovery. In the case on hand, sub-rules (1), (2), (3) and (4) of rule 6 shall not be applicable in the case of inputs relatable to excisable goods that are removed without payment of duty either to a hundred per cent EOU or are cleared for export under bond in terms of provisions of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. As regards the credit involved in balance inputs and inputs contained in the finished goods in stock, these demands were premature. The recovery of input credit involved in these cases shall be regulated in the manner indicated, namely, subject to sub-rule (6) of rule 6. [Para 5.2]

It was open to the assessee to claim rebate of duty of the un-utilised input credit under rule 18 of the Central Excise Rules read with Notification No. 21/04-CE (NT) instead of seeking refund under rule 5 of the Cenvat Credit Rules. The inputs in this case had been received from four Jammu units availing of exemption under Notification No. 56/02-CE, namely. Subsequent investigations revealed that these from Jammu suppliers of inputs had made only paper transactions with the assessee to generate Cenvat credit based on bogus invoices without any manufacture.

Assessee's Arguments

While the Menthol/Menthol Crystals, BP/USP, became fully exempt from duty w.e.f. 1-3-2008 under Notification No. 4/08-CE, the other final products remained dutiable. However, all the final products whether exempted or dutiable were being exported out of India. While Menthol/Menthol Crystals, BP/USP were being exported under bond without payment of duty under rule 19 of Central Excise Rules, 2002, the other final products flavouring agents were being cleared on payment of duty and were being exported under rebate claim.

When inputs are used in manufacture of dutiable as well as exempted final products and the exempted final products are exported out of India, the provisions of rule 6 (6) (V) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 would be applicable and the bar of rule 6 (1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules and the liability created under rule 6 (3) (b) would not be attracted.

The words "excisable goods" in rule 6 (6) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 are wide enough to include both dutiable as well as exempted goods.

Amendment to Notification No. 42/01- CE (NT) dated 26-6-2001 by Notification No. 24/10 - CE (NT) dated 26-5-2010 providing that the export of excisable goods which are chargeable to nil rate of duty or are fully exempted from payment of duty, other than the goods cleared by a 100% EOU, shall not be allowed under this notification cannot be given retrospective effect, as this amendment restricts the benefits.

Rule 11 (3) (ii) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 does not apply when a manufacturer manufacturers dutiable as well as exempted final products out of common Cenvat credit availed inputs.

As regards the allegation that the transaction between the supplier units and the assessee regarding supply of Menthol and other raw material were bogus transactions and that only invoices had been issued by the Jammu units without supply of any material, this allegation had not been made in any of show cause notices issued in the present appeals.

Issue Involved

Whether credit was available and if yes, it was refundable to assessee ?

HELD: I. General

In terms of rule 6 (1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, Cenvat credit shall not be allowed on such quantity of input or input services, which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods except in these circumstances mentioned in sub-rule (2). In terms of sub-rule (2) of rule 6 ibid, when a manufacturer avails of Cenvat credit in respect of any input or input services and manufactures such final products which are chargeable to duty as well as the exempted goods, then the manufacturer shall either maintain separate account and inventory for the receipt, consumption of the inputs/input services meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final product and exempted final product and take Cenvat credit only in respect of inputs/input services used in or in relation to manufacture of dutiable final product, or if does not maintain such account and inventory, in accordance with the provisions of sub-rule (3) of rule 6, he shall pay an amount either equal to 10%/5% of the sale price of the exempted final product or equal to the Cenvat credit involved on the inputs/input services used in or in relation to manufacture of exempted final products to be calculated as per the provisions of this sub-rule. [Para 6.1]

HEADNOTE: Rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Input service - Whether since provision of buildings for housing, schooling, recreation, etc., of workers has no nexus with manufacture, storage or sale of final product of assessee-manufacturer, construction services used by assessee for construction of workers’ quarters within factory premises would not fall within ambit of ‘input services’ as defined in rule 2(l) and, consequently, assessee could not avail of credit of such construction services in terms of rule 3 - Held, yes [Para 8]

Rule 3 of the Customs, Central Excise and Service Tax Drawback Rules, 1995 - Drawback - Rates of - Whether where assessee availed of credit of service tax paid on service used in construction of factory sheds and store rooms, in terms of first proviso to rule 3(1), drawback had to be correspondingly reduced and full rate of drawback reimbursing customs, central excise duties and service tax would not be admissible to assessee - Held, yes [Para 12]

FACT: The applicant was engaged in the manufacture of different types of yarn. It proposed to construct within its factory premises, additional sheds for manufacturing and storing of yarn, as also residential quarters for its workers and staff, as a part of its programme to augment the production capacity. It sought advance ruling on the following issues :-

(a)Whether the construction services used for construction of workers’ quarters within the factory premises, fall within the ambit of input services as defined in rule 2(l ) and, consequently, whether, the applicant can avail of the credit of such construction services in terms of rule 3?

(b)Whether the applicant can claim full rate of drawback on export of yarn manufactured by it along with Cenvat credit on construction services used for construction of manufacturing/storage/workers residential quarters within the factory premises?

Regarding the first issue, the applicant stated that the manufacture of yarn was a continuous operation and in order to ensure availability of workers round the clock, it proposed to house the workers in a colony within the factory itself; that continuous availability of workers residing in a colony within the factory would ensure efficient production of yarn; and, therefore, the construction service required for building a residential colony for the workers was indirectly connected with the manufacture and clearance of yarn and such construction service had to be regarded as an input service and Cenvat credit of the service tax paid on such service should be available to it.

As regards the second issue, the applicant submitted that it was entitled to claim the higher rate of drawback allowed in Notification No. 68/2007-Cus. (NT), dated 16-7-2007 for its yarn exports, even when Cenvat credit of the service tax paid on the services used for construction of factory sheds, store rooms and residential colony for workers, had been availed of. According to the applicant, the only condition required to be fulfilled for availing of the higher drawback rate as set out in clause (12)(i) of the above notification was that no Cenvat credit should have been availed of the Central Excise duty on inputs used in the manufacture of yarn export; that this condition was met in its case inasmuch it had availed Cenvat credit on input services; that inputs, i.e., physical goods were distinct from input service; and clause 12(i) nowhere mentions non-availment of Cenvat credit of tax on an input service, as a pre-condition for availing of the higher rate of drawback.

HELD: PER CHITRA SAHA, MEMBER

Whether construction services used for construction of workers’ quarters within factory premises fell within ambit of input services ?

The definition of ‘input services’ under rule 2(l )(ii) is in two parts : the first part gives the basic definition of ‘input service’ while the second part is an inclusive one that specifically mentions certain services to be included within the ambit of ‘input services’. The basic definition limits the scope of input services to those whose use has a nexus directly or indirectly, in or in relation to manufacture and clearance of final products. In Doypack systems, the phrase ‘in relation to’ has been held to be equivalent to or synonymous with ‘pertaining to’ and ‘concerned with’. The use of the service for construction of workers’ residences cannot be said to pertain to or be concerned, directly or indirectly, with manufacture and clearance. [Para 6]

The second leg of the definition is an inclusive one. The inclusive definition is a well-recognized device to enlarge the meaning of the word defined. It expands the meaning in the basic definition. [Para 7]

HEADNOTE: Rule 3 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - General - Whether maintenance of separate books of account for receipt of inputs being used in manufacture of excisable goods is not a condition precedent for purpose of claiming benefit of exemption available on final excisable goods under Notification No. 30/2004 in clearing them without payment of duty - Held, yes - Whether reversal of Cenvat credit availed at input stage amounts to non-availability of said credit and, thus, condition for availing benefit of exemption Notification No. 30/2004 would be satisfied - Held, yes [Paras 6 & 7] Circulars and Notifications : Notification Nos. 29/2004, dated 9-7-2004, 30/2004, dated 9-7-2004; Circular No. 795/28/04-CX, dated 28-7-2004

FACT: The respondent-assessee was engaged in the business of manufacture of cotton fabrics. It used grey cotton, dyes, chemicals, packing material, etc., as inputs for manufacture of cotton fabrics. Prior to February, 2005, the respondent was clearing goods on payment of applicable duty under Notification No. 29/2004-C.E., dated 9-7-2004. It was noticed that the respondent had started availing benefit of both Notifications Nos. 29/2004 and 30/2004 simultaneously from February, 2005. However, the respondent was not maintaining separate accounts for receipt of inputs being used in the manufacture of fabrics subsequently cleared without payment of duty by availing of the benefit of second Notification No. 30/2004-C.E., dated 9-7-2004. According to the revenue, maintenance of such accounts was a mandatory condition. The assessee contended that if the manufacturer reverse credit before clearance, it must be taken that the credit was never availed of, and that neither the Board’s circular nor the clarification issued in the RAC meeting required the manufacturer to maintain separate accounts with regard to the inputs, rather they were required to maintain separate books of account only for the final goods. However, the Commissioner took the view that the respondent had contravened the provisions of the notification read with the clarification issued rendering it liable for penal action under section 11AC. On appeal, following the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Chandrapur Magnet Wires (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 1996 (81) ELT 3 wherein it is held that the reversal of credit of duty originally availed of would amount to the effect as if no credit has been availed, the Tribunal held that the credit availed and reversed would amount to the situation as if the same was not availed, thus, satisfying the condition of Notification No. 30/04-C.E.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: The Commissioner of Central Excise decided the matter against the assessee only on the ground that manufacturer had not maintained separate books of account (i) for the goods availing of the benefit of Notification No. 29 of 2004 and (ii) for the goods availing of the benefit of Notification No. 30 of 2004. He further observed that the relevant circular does not speak of final goods or inputs, but it refers to the goods only and then, he came to the conclusion that the subjected two notifications refer to the aspect of credit being taken or otherwise of inputs and maintenance of separate accounts for inputs is of prime importance. Since this condition was not satisfied, he confirmed the levy of duty, penalty, etc. The finding of the Commissioner of Central Excise was not in consonance with the observations made and the ratio laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Chandrapur Magnet Wires (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 1996 (81) ELT 3. [Para 5]
