III. Rule 6(1) and Rule 6(2) not applies : The provisions of sub-rule (1) of rule 6 of the Cenvat credit Rules, 2004 are subject to the provision of sub-rule (6) of this rule and in the circumstances enumerated in various clauses of Rule 6(6), the provisions of sub-rule (1), (2) and (3) of rule 6 are not applicable. The term "excisable goods" in rule 6 (6) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 is vide enough to include both dutiable as well as exempted goods and the Cenvat credit in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of fully and exempt goods which had been exported under bond/letter of undertaking would be admissible and, as such, the provisions of rule 6 (6) (v) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 would be applicable. The bar provided under rule 6 (1) and the liability created under rule 6 (3) (b) read with rule 6 (2) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 would not be attracted, when the finished goods even if fully exempt from duty, are exported out of India and this bar would be applicable only if the assessee does not export the exempted goods. Manufacturer is entitled for Cenvat credit in respect of inputs used in exported goods, whether exempted or dutiable and the assessee has option either to claim drawback or to claim cash refund of the credit under rule 5 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. Even when the exempted products viz. Menthol crystals had been exported under bond without payment of duty, the case is covered under rule 6 (6) (v) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 and accordingly the Rule 6 (1) to 6 (4) ibid would not be applicable and the assessee would be entitled to the credit of the duty paid on the inputs and the disallowance of the input credit is applicable only when the fully exempted final products made out of Cenvat credit availed inputs are cleared for home consumption. Hence, the revenue's plea that in rule 6 (6) (v), the words "excisable goods" should be interpreted as 'dutiable goods' cannot be accepted. [Para 8.2]

IV. Amendment to Notification No. 42/01-CE(NT) not retrospective :

Notification No. 42/01-CE (NT) dated 26-6-2001 issued under rule 19 (3) of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 prescribes the conditions to be observed and the procedure to be followed for the purpose of export under bond without payment of duty under rule 19 (1) of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. The amendment made to Notification No. 42/01-CE (NT) dated 26-6-2001 by the amending notification dated 26-5-2010 restricts the scope of rule 19 and after this amendment, the goods which are fully exempt from duty or are chargeable to nil rate of duty, cannot be exported under bond or LUT under rule 19 and accordingly, if for manufacture of such exempted goods, any duty paid inputs have been used, the Cenvat credit of the duty paid on the inputs cannot be availed. Since this amendment adversely affects the manufacturers, the same cannot be given retrospective effect. [Para 8.2.2]

V. Refund available

In view of the above discussion, neither the provisions of rule 11 (3) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, nor the provisions of rule 6 (1) ibid are applicable to this case. As regards the Department's plea that the respondent cannot take cash refund of accumulated Cenvat credit under rule 5 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 as well as rebate of duty paid out of the same credit, since in this case, under rule 5 of Cenvat credit Rules, 2004, prohibition is on claiming input duty drawback under Customs and Central Excise duties Drawback Rules, 1995 or the equivalent benefit of input duty rebate under rule 18 of the Central Excise Rules and in this case, neither the input duty drawback under the Drawback Rules nor the input duty rebate under rule 18 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 has been claimed, this plea is not valid. [Para 9]

VI. Adjudication cannot be beyond SCN

On appeal to Tribunal: HELD: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of nylon tyre cord fabric, nylon yarn and nylon chips using caprolactam as the raw material. The caprolactam is polymerized in an uninterrupted and continuous process plant known as main poly-plant. The polymerized material is excluded into nylon strands and then cut into chips known as main poly chips. During the course of polymerization only 90 per cent of the caprolactam is polymerized fully. The rest of 10 per cent is sticking to the nylon strand as a coating in the form of unreacted and partially reacted material referred to as monomer (8.5 per cent) and oligomer (1.5 per cent) respectively. The nylon strand cut to nylon chips are washed with hot water jets. During such washing monomer and oligomer get dissolved and collected as wash water. The said wash water is pumped to monomer recovery plant, where the monomer (caprolactam) is recovered by a process of evolution and distillation. The resultant recovered product is known as MRP lactum. During this process, oligomers are also separated and taken to de-polymerization plant for recovery of caprolactam. The caprolactam recovered on such de-polymerization is called de-poly lactum. Art from oligomer, nylon yarn waste, tyre cord fabric waste, drawn waste, waste chips, etc., which are generated in various manufacturing sections, are also de-polymerized in the commodity polymerization plant resulting in recovery of de-poly lactum. The MRP lactum and de-ploy lactum are polymerized in a batch poly plant. The resultant product is referred to as batch poly chips or non-virgin poly chips. [Para 10]

The assessee in the course of manufacture of tyre cord fabric produced nylon yarn of various deniers. Yarn of 210d is exempted from central excise duty. Hence, the issue arose regarding duty liability of poly chips - both virgin as well as non-virgin - used in the manufacture of such exempted 210d yarn. The duty liability of such virgin poly chips captively used in the manufacture of 210d exempted yarn is not contested. However, the assessee is contesting the duty liability on batch non-virgin poly chips used in the manufacture of 201d yarn. The wash water arising during the course of manufacture of poly chips was put to further process for manufacture of batch non-virgin poly chips. [Para11]

The first issue to be considered is whether batch non-virgin poly chips are marketable and chargeable to duty as excisable goods. The assessee contended that poly chips are not marketable. It contended that the non-virgin poly chips are emerging in the continuous process of manufacture through a parallel recovery process. For marketing poly chips, these are to be packed in nitrogen blanketed containers. Since no such packing is done by it, the product is not marketable and consequently not liable to central excise duty. Admittedly the batch non-virgin poly chips are emerging due to deliberate manufacturing process by the assessee. During the course of polymerization of caprolactam the main virgin poly chips are produced which are washed in the hot water resuling in emergence of pure virgin poly chips and wash water. The wash water is put to further process resulting in the prodcution of batch non-virgin poly chips. Regarding requirement of nitrogen packing, such packing will be required when the product is cleared to some distance. In the instant case, in an integrated chemical plant for captive consumption there is apparently no need for such nitrogen packing as the product is stored and dealt with in controlled environment for the required use. Admittedly non-virgin poly chips are in fact marketed and the assessee itself indicated that one 'S' did market this product and wanted to compare the value of such sale for adopting to excise valuation. Hence special packing required for removal of goods safely to the buyer, which is not required for captive consumption itself, cannot determine the marketability of any product. Accordingly the batch non-virgin poly chips are excisable products. [Para 12]

Thus, in the facts of the present case, since the credit of duty paid on input used in the manufacture of exempted final product was utilized for payment of excise duty on exported peppermint oil, the assessee, instead of getting refund of input credit under rule 5, was entitled to rebate of duty paid on exported peppermint oil as provided under rule 18 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. [Para 26] The argument of the revenue, in the instant case, that the credit of duty paid on menthol was not allowable or had lapsed for the reason that the duty paid menthol had been used in the manufacture of exempted menthol crystals, could not be accepted, because, admittedly the exempted menthol crystals had not been cleared for home consumption but had been cleared for export under bond and, therefore, rule 6(1) to 6(4) would not apply, but rule 6(6)(v) would apply. In other words, non-allowability of input credit under rule 6(1) to 6(4) is applicable only when the inputs used in the manufacture of exempted final products are cleared for home consumption without payment of duty and not when exempted final products are cleared for export without payment of duty under bond. In the instant case, exempted menthol crystals had been exported without payment of duty under bond and, therefore, the assessee was entitled to take the credit of duty paid on menthol used in the manufacture of exempted menthol and utilize that credit for paying duty on clearance of peppermint oil. Since peppermint oil was exported on payment of duty, the assessee was entitled to claim rebate of duty paid on exported peppermint oil under rule 18 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. [Para 27]

In the result, it was held that, in the facts of the instant case, since the exempted menthol crystals as well as dutiable peppermint oil manufactured out of duty paid menthol had been exported by the assessee, the provisions of rule 6(1) to 6(4) were not applicable and, as per rule 5, the assessee was entitled to avail the Cenvat credit of duty paid on menthol used in the manufacture of exempted menthol crystals and utilize the said credit for payment of duty on clearance of peppermint oil either for home consumption or for export. In the instant case, since the peppermint oil had been exported on payment of duty, the assessee was entitled to claim rebate of the duty paid on peppermint oil. [Para 28]

For all the aforesaid reasons, the petition filed by the Commissioner failed. [Para 29]

availability of Cenvat credit to beneficiary

There was no merit in the contention of the assessee that there was no condition in the exemption notification, dated 10-6-2003 about non-availability of Cenvat credit to the beneficiary of such notification. Even otherwise availability of Cenvat credit depends upon the provisions of law comprised under the Cenvat Credit Rules and they do not stand modified by any exemption notification. [Para 75]

Clearance of goods for export under bond There is no doubt that rule 6(6) excludes the goods cleared for export under bond from the applicability of the provisions of law comprised under rule 6(1). At the same time, rule 3 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 relates to the entitlement of credit in relation to the duty paid on the inputs. The Commissioner did not seem to have taken into consideration the effect of these provisions of law while rejecting the claim based on the contention of the assessee about clearance of goods for export under bond. Certainly the adjudicating authority would have to consider this point with reference to those inputs which were stated to have been used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final goods which were cleared for export under the bond. The assessee would have to establish actual export of such final goods. [Para 78]

It was also submitted by the assessee that it was entitled for rebate under rule 18 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 in respect of duty paid on the inputs going into the manufacture of goods for export purposes by unit availing area based exemption under the Notification No. 50/2003-CE. Undoubtedly, rule 18 provides that where the goods are exported, the Central Government may by notification grant rebate of duty paid on such excisable goods or duty paid on the materials used in the manufacture or processing of such goods and the rebate shall subject to such condition or limitation if any and fulfilment of such procedure as has been specified in the notification. The rule 18 lays down procedure for claiming rebate on duty paid on the raw materials used in the manufacture of the goods exported to various countries. It is for the assessee to have claimed rebate of duty by following proper procedure in that regard if it so desires. That could not be a justification to insist for availment of Cenvat credit contrary to the provisions of law comprised under the rules applicable to the matter. [Para 79]

Whether the assessee had availed credit during the period from 1st January to 10-1-2005 or not has to be ascertained by verifying the records. This aspect can very well be dealt with along with the claim of the assessee regarding the entitlement of benefit under rule 6(6)(v) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 which relates to the subject of export of goods under bond. [Para 80]

Conclusion

(i )The Cenvat credit availed on the inputs being in stock on the day the assessee opted for exemption from payment of duty under Notification No. 50/2003, dated 10-6-2003 was required to be reversed.

(ii )It is not necessary that an exemption notification should specifically provide for non-availability of Cenvat credit facility in relation to the duty paid on inputs which are to be utilized in the goods availing the exemption benefit under such notification.

(iii )The question as to whether the goods cleared by the assessee for export under bond could not be considered as the exempted goods, and that, therefore, the manufacturer thereof was entitled to avail Cenvat credit in respect of duty paid on the inputs utilized in manufacture of such final goods; and that whether the assessee was entitled for the rebate as sought to be contended would have to be considered by the adjudicating authority afresh. [Para 81]

Inputs Cement and Steels — Credit allowed upto 31-3-2011: On plain reading of Explanation 2 of the definition of Input in rule 2(k), as amended on 07.07.2009, said explanation would apply in respect of the goods used in the manufacture of capital goods, which are further used in the factory of the manufacturer. Thus, it is clear that input Cement and Steel used in the factory of manufacturer shall not be eligible input credit. This explanation is applicable only to the manufacturer and not the service provider. It is to be read strictly as per plain meaning of the statute. There is no indication in the Explanation that it would apply to the service provider. So, the denial of input credit on Cement and Steel before and after amendment of Explanation 2 of definition Input, cannot be sustained. [Para 8]

B. Other inputs and capital goods used for construction of port/jetty are eligible

The adjudicating authority observed that —

the inputs and capital goods were used in the construction of Port Jetty, Port buildings and Warehouse services, which are not output service i.e. Port services.

inputs and capital goods were used for maintenance & repair of machines used in the Port area and for other general use in the Port area.

construction of Port is exempted service in view of the Notification No. 25/2007-ST dated 22.05.2007 and no CENVAT credit is eligible on exempted services. [Para 9]

On close reading of input definition under Rule 2(k) of the Rules as above, it is clear that Clause (i) covers all goods, except as specified, used in or in relation to the manufacture of final product. On the other hand, Clause (ii) in Rule 2(k) covers all goods except specified therein, used for providing any output service. In short, Clauses (i) and (ii) are applicable for manufacturer and output service provider respectively. The present case relates to output service provider. There is no dispute that the assessee herein are not manufacturer and covered under Clause (ii) of input definition. The words all goods, if read with used for providing any output service in Clause (ii) of Rule 2(k) of Rules 2004, make it clear that any goods other than specified in the said Clause, used for providing any output service, would be treated as input and covered under the said definition. Further, the particular expression used for providing any output service in the said Clause (ii) in Rule 2(k) have widened the scope of definition of input in respect of output service.

The definition of capital goods under Rule 2(a) of the Rules provides the goods, specified in sub-clauses (i) to (vii) of Clause (A) used for providing output service, would be treated as capital goods.

Similarly, the definition of input service in Rule 2(l) of Rules 2004, is in two parts. Clauses (i) and (ii) of Rule 2(l) cover the service provider and the manufacturer respectively. The present case relates to output service provider. The expression any service, if read with used by a provider of taxable service for providing an output service in Clause (i) of Rule 2(l) of the Rules, 2004 had widened the scope of input service in respect of output service provider.

It is well settled that literal interpretation would prevail, where the plain words of statute are clear, unambiguous and not absurd or unjust. When words of statute are clear and meaning is unambiguous, intention of statute gets irrelevant. The plain meaning of the statute should not be distorted by following the interpretation based on intention. [Para 11]

Port Service means any service provided or to be provided to any person, by a port or any person authorised by the port, in relation to goods or vessels, in any manner; Section 67 of the said Act, the value of any taxable service shall be the gross amount charged by the service provider for such service provided or to be provided by him. [Para 16]

Port is a harbour where ships load and unload cargo; any place where persons and cargo are allowed to enter a country and where customs officials are stationed. It is a place for the loading and unloading of the cargoes of vessels, and the collection of duties or customs upon imports and exports. A port is a place intended for loading or unloading goods; hence includes the natural shelter surrounding water, as also sheltered water produced by artificial jetties, etc. A port is a place where a vessel can lie in a position of more or less shelter from the elements, with a view to the loading or discharge of cargo. The word port must be construed in its usual and limited popular or commercial sense as a place where ships are in the habit of coming for the purpose of loading or unloading, embarking or disembarking.

HEADNOTE: Rule 5, read with rule 6, of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Refund of - Assessee was engaged in manufacture of goods, which were exempted from duty - Assessee had exported said goods and cleared same under bond - Whether assessee was entitled to refund of service tax paid on services used in manufacture of exported goods cleared under bond in view of rules 5 and 6 - Held, yes [Paras 6 and 7]

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of Psyllium Seed Husk and was exporting the entire products. It claimed refund of service tax paid on services used in the manufacture of exported goods cleared under bond. The original authority rejected the refund claim of the assessee on the ground that the goods of the assessee were exempted from duty and, therefore, the refund claim was unsustainable. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the action of the original authority.

On appeal :

HELD: The finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) was that the assessee availed Cenvat credit on input services used in or in relation to manufacture of unconditionally exempted goods. Rule 6(1) provides that Cenvat credit shall not be allowed on such quantity of inputs or input services which are used in the manufacture of exempted goods or exempted services. Rule 6(6) provides that proviso to sub-rule (1) of rule 6 shall not apply in case of exported goods removed without payment of duty cleared for export under bond in terms of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. In the instant case, there was no dispute that the assessee cleared the goods under bond. So rule 6(6) would be applicable. The original authority observed that as the goods were exempted, there was no requirement for furnishing bond. According to him, there was no requirement of furnishing bond and, therefore, it did not come within the purview of rule 6(6). This issue had already been settled by the Bombay High Court in the case of Repro India Ltd. v. Union of India [Writ Petition No. 6951 of 2007, dated 6-12-2007] in favour of the assessee. [Para 5]

Further, the Tribunal in the case of CCE v. Drish Shoes Ltd. 2009 (90) RLT 686 (New Delhi - CESTAT) following the decision of the High Court in the case of Repro India Ltd. (supra) held that inputs used in manufacture of exempted final product which is exported, input credit and its refund are admissible under rules 5 and 6. [Para 6]

In the instant case, there was no dispute that the goods were exported and not liable to any duty. The issue was settled by the High Court and the Tribunal in favour of the assessee as stated above. [Para 7]

In view of the above, impugned order was to be set aside and the appeal of the assessee was to be allowed. [Para 8]

Officer 1997 (91) ELT 34 (SC), goods used in an activity, without which manufacturing, operations, though theoretically possible, are not commercially feasible, have to be treated as ,'used in the manufacture of the final products'. When the expression 'used in manufacture' has been interpreted in the above manner, the scope of the expression 'used in or in relation to manufacture whether directly or indirectly' would be much wider. [Paras 6 and 6.1] Definition of 'input' does not depend on what ought to be used but what is commercially expedient to use and the expression 'in relation to' has a wide connotation. Therefore, for determining the eligibility of a particular item for Cenvat Credit, what has to be seen is as to whether without use of that item or without the activity in which that item is used, the manufacture of final product, though theoretically feasible. is commercially expedient or possible or not.

It is nobody's case that manufacturing activity is commercially feasible with malfunctioning machinery, and leaking pipes, tubes and tanks. Therefore repair and maintenance of plant and machinery, though by itself not a manufacturing activity, has to be treated as an activity in relation to manufacture and inputs used in repair & maintenance would have to be treated as goods used in relation to manufacture. [Para 6.1]

Mere dismissal of SLP without giving any reason does not lay down any law; hence, judgment in SAIL v. CCE 2008 taxmann.com 532 (Kol. - CESTAT), against which SLP was dismissed in Steel Authority of India Ltd. v. Commissioner - 2008 (229) ELT A127 (SC), is not binding. [Para 7]

Though Apex Court in case of Grasim Industries Ltd. v. Union of India 2011 (273) ELT 10 has held that repair & maintenance of machinery is not manufacture and therefore steal scrap, arising in course of the said activity is not excisable; but, this judgment does not help the department, as for determining the eligibility for Cenvat Credit of an item used in an activity, what is relevant is as to whether without that activity in which the item, in question, is used, manufacturing operation are commercially feasible, and it is not relevant as to whether that activity by itself amounts to manufacture.

When three other High Courts have held that welding electrodes used for repair and maintenance of plant and machinery are eligible for Cenvat Credit, it is these judgments which will hold the field; hence, contrary view of Andhra Pradesh High Court was not to be followed. [Para 8]

The question for consideration would arise as to whether the assessee was entitled to avail the cenvat credit of duty paid on the inputs used in the manufacture of HB wire and could clear such product on payment of 8 per cent of value of said product in terms of provisions of rule 6(3)(b). HELD: The product 'HB wire' is admittedly specified in the Central Excise Tariff and in terms of provisions of section 2(d) of the Central Excise Act, the same has to be held as excisable goods. The same attract duty at the rate of 16 per cent ad valoram. As admitted by the assessee, there is no exemption notification in respect of said goods. The provisions of rule 6(3)(b) get attracted only when common cenvatable inputs stand used by the assessee for the manufacture of dutiable as also exempted goods. Going through the said rule leads to hold that payment of a particular amount only to neutralize availed cenvat credit is only in respect of exempted final product. Admittedly, in the instant case, the assessee's final product does not attract duty at all on account of being a non manufactured product. As such, question of exemption of the same does not arise. On the one hand, the assessee is taking a stand that no duty is required to be paid on the galvanized wire inasmuch as there was no manufacturing activity involved and thus reason that it is not paying full rate of duty of 16 per cent on the said product at the time of clearance of the same. On the other hand, it is claiming the applicability of rule 6(3)(b) on the ground that said product is dutiable but exempted. Such an interpretation if adopted would lead to total chaos. Even at the cost of repetition, it may be observed that assessee has not cleared its final product on full payment of duty of 16 per cent in which case credit could have been allowed to it, as per settled proposition of law. [Para 7]

As rule 6(3)(b) is applicable only in respect of exempted products, one has to decide as to what are the exempted goods. The answer lies in the provisions of rule 2(d) of Central Excise Rules, 2002. [Para 8]

As per rule 2(d) of the Central Excise Rules, exempted goods are excisable goods, which stand exempted from payment of duty of excise leviable thereon. If no duty of excise is leviable on account of non manufacture, the question of exemption of same does not arise. As such, goods cannot be held to be exempted goods. Thus making the applicability of rule 6(3)(b) as nil. [Para 9]

The problem can also be tackled from other angle. Rule 3 of the Central Credit Rules allows a manufacturer or producer of final product to avail the credit of duty paid on the inputs, which are to be used by it in the manufacture of final product. If there is no manufacturing activity involved, the said rule debars the availment of credit at the ab initio stage itself. Inasmuch as no manufacturing activity was involved in the instant case as neither the wire drawing process nor the galvanization process involved any manufacturing activity, the credit itself was not available to the assessee under the said rule so as to be further neutralized in terms of rule 6(3)(b).

In view of the aforesaid, provisions of rule 6(3)(b) would not be applicable to instant case. [Para 10]

The definition of 'input service' under rule 2(l) precisely covers any service used by a provider of taxable service for providing an output service, any service used by a manufacturer in or in relation to manufacture of final product and inclusive part of the definition, services used in relation to setting up, modernisation, renovation or repair of a factory, premises of a provider of output service or an office relating to such factory or premises, etc. The expression 'any service' read with 'for providing an output service' would cover wide encompass of the definition of input service. HEADNOTE: Rule 57, read with Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Interpretation - Words  phrases--Duty-paid, non-duty paid, Nil rate, Appropriate Rate--Non-duty paid inputs does not cover only goods clandestinely removed without payment of duty; it means 'duty not paid'. Assessment--Includes payment at 'nil' rate of duty. Appropriate rate of duty includes 'rate of duty'. Duty rate--Nil rate of duty applies both to Tariff and exemption notifications. 'Chargeable to nil rate of duty' applies to the Tariff only. CE Rule 57A, 57G(2); Notfn. 203/83-CE

Rule 57 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Deemed credit--Galvanised wire received from manufacturer thereof without payment of duty; not available

FACT: The appellants manufacture stranded wires from galvanised wires for which they took Modvat credit as deemed credit without producing duty-paying documents, The lower authorities held that deemed credit was not allowable as the manufacturers of the inputs had availed of the exemption notification 203/83-CE and not paid any duty and one of the conditions for getting deemed credit was that inputs should be non-duty-paid or charged to nil rate of duty.

HELD: Interpretation--Non-duty-paid inputs does not cover only goods which have been clandestinely removed without payment of duty since the reference is obviously only to goods which have been removed without payment of duty. Hence non-duty-paid means not duty-paid. Hence goods cleared free of duty under an exemption notification means appropriate duty, which includes nil duty, has been paid. "We do not agree with the contention that the expression non-duty paid would cover only goods which have been clandestinely removed without payment of duty. ........Since the expression non-duty paid has been used with reference to goods lying in a factory, Customs Area or a warehouse they cannot obviously be goods which have been removed without payment of duty. Thus non-duty paid means not duty paid. ........If the goods have been cleared free of duty by virtue of an exemption notification it would amount to their being cleared on payment of appropriate duty which includes nil duty."

2. Deemed credit--Where nil duty is paid at the input stage, no duty credit is available as Modvat credit provides credit of duty paid on inputs towards payment of duty on the final products, the literal meaning of 'paid' as actually paid in cash is applicable for permitting credit as the deemed credit facility depends on the payment of duty. "The purpose of modvat credit is different and is to avoid the cascading effect of duty paid at different stages by providing credit of duty on the inputs for being utilised towards payment of duty on the final products. Where duty is exempt by notification, nil duty is paid. ........Where nil duty is paid at the input stage there is nothing to cascade and there is no duty credit available........the literal meaning of the expression paid as actually paid in cash need not be accepted will not apply in respect of permitting credit of duty paid. ........the deemed credit facility does not rule out the payment of duty which will be the case when complete exemption is available. On the contrary it is dependent on it, as it should be."

3. Interpretation--charged to nil rate of duty in the deemed credit order means that nil rate has been applied; it is immaterial as to whether it is per the Tariff or under an exemption notification; it does not mean that it is chargeable to nil rate of duty under the Tariff only. "The expression used........is charged to nil rate of duty, and not chargeable to nil rate of duty. Charged to nil rate of duty will only mean that nil rate has been applied. Whether the nil rate applied is as per the tariff or in terms of an exemption notification will be immaterial. ........Thus charged to nil rate of duty has not been used in the deemed credit order dated 7.4.1986 with reference to chargeability under the First Schedule of the Tariff only."

4. Deemed credit--purchase from a manufacturer does not necessarily constitute purchase from the open market for availing deemed credit. "The question was whether purchase from another manufacturer was purchase from the open market and this was answered in the affirmative. This does not automatically apply in the present case relating to deemed credit matter in the manner claimed by the appellants."

5. Amendment which is not repugnant to or in addition to the provisions subsisting earlier can be retrospectively applied to a past order even if it was superseded. "We also feel that the argument that the amendment cannot be retrospectively applied to a past order particularly as the latter had been superseded may not be in order as the said amendment is not repugnant to or in addition to the provisions subsisting earlier."

FACT: The assessee manufactures final product, namely, blanket out of woollen fibres. The blankets attract only Basic Excise Duty (for short BED) and does not attract either Additional Excise Duty (Goods of Special Importance) [for short 'AED(GSI)'] or Additional Excise Duty (Textiles and Textile Articles) [for short AED(T&TA)]. With effect from 1-4-1994, the assessee became entitled to avail credit of duty paid on the inputs (tops etc.) used in or in relation to the manufacture of manmade yarn. With effect from the said date, the assessees became entitled to avail credit of duty paid on the inputs used in or in relation to the manufacture of blankets falling under Chapter 63.

Vide Notification No. 24/94CE (NT), dated 20-5-1994 issued under rule 57A, AED(T&TA) paid on input can be utilised for payment of AED(T&TA) on the final product. Similarly, AED(GSI) paid on the input can be utilised for payment of AED(GSI) on the final product. Similar provision contained in Notification No. 5/94(NT), dated 1-3-1994 also issued under rule 57A.

With effect from 3-9-1996, the assessees became entitled to avail credit of duty paid on the inputs used in or in relation to the manufacture of fabrics falling under Chapter 55.

The assessee, inter alia, took the credit of Basic Excise Duty and AED(T&TA) on one of the inputs viz. Manmade tops falling under Chapter 55 of the Tariff Act used in or in relation to the manufacture of yarn from 1-3-1994. The yarn manufactured by the assessees was subject to BED and AED(T&TA).

The assessee utilised the credit of BED paid under section 3 on the tops towards the payment of BED and the additional duty of excise payable under the additional duties of excise (Goods of Special Importance) Act. However, under a mistake of law, the assessee did not utilise the credit of AED (T&TA) on the tops towards the payment of duty on any other final products viz. Fabric, Blanket, Shawls etc.

Owing to introduction of Cenvat Scheme from 1-4-2000, rule 57AB(2)(b) provided that AED (T&TA) and AED (GSI) paid on input can be utilised for payment of AED (T&TA) or AED (GSI). This position contained upto 30-6-2001.

Later, Cenvat Credit Rules, 2001 provided that AED (T&TA) and AED (GSI) paid on input can be utilised for payment of AED (T&TA) or AED (GSI) 'respectively' (word respectively was added).

Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002 maintained the aforesaid position of law.

Between January 2003 to April, 2003, the assessees utilised this AED (T&TA) credit for payment of BED and AED (GSI).

The department argued that said use of AED (T&TA) was impermissible.

HELD: Cross-utilization not permitted :

If one peruses the scheme of credit of duties paid on excisable goods used as inputs under the Central Excise Rules, 1944, one finds that in rule 57A as was prevailing in 1995-96 and thereafter until the Notification was issued by the Government, the credit of these duties was not permissible. [Para 49]

The credit was allowed vide Notification issued in 1995 but there was no cross utilisation permissible and from the inception. In other words, the credit of specified duties allowed in respect of inputs insofar as it relates to the additional duty of excise in terms of the 1978 Act shall be utilised only towards payment of duty of excise leviable under 1978 Act on the final products or as the case may be on the inputs. Similar is the position with regard to the 1957 Act. [Paras 49 & 50]

Thereafter, even the Notification dated 28-2-1999 does not alter this position. All that the Cenvat credit Rules or the Central Excise Rules prevalent clarify is that credit of specified duty insofar as it relates to duty paid under the 1957 and 1978 Acts can be availed of and subject to the restrictions. The position remains the same even under the notifications subsequently issued. [Para 50]

Even under rule 57AB, the situation has not undergone any change from the one noted hereinabove. When the Cenvat credit Rules, 2001 came into force on 1-7-2001, there as well, by rule 3, Cenvat credit was allowed to be taken but did not permit any cross utilisation. [Paras 51 to 54]

Since this condition was not satisfied, he confirmed the levy of duty, penalty, etc. The finding of the Commissioner of Central Excise was not in consonance with the observations made and the ratio laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Chandrapur Magnet Wires (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 1996 (81) ELT 3. [Para 5] In this case, Court’s attention was drawn to the departmental circular according to which in a case where the manufacturer produces dutiable final products and also final goods which are exempt from duty, it is not reasonably possible to segregate inputs utilised in manufacture of the dutiable final products from the final products which are exempt from duty. Based on this, the Court held that the manufacturer may take credit of duty paid on all the inputs used in the manufacture of final products, on which duty will have to be paid and in view of this clarification by the Departmental circular, the Court saw no reason as to why the assessee should not make a debit entry in the credit account before removal of the exempted final product; and, hence, it cannot be said that the assessee had taken credit for the duty paid on the inputs utilised in the manufacture of the final exempted product under rule 57A. The Court, therefore, took the view that the claim for exemption of duty on the disputed goods cannot be denied on the plea that the assessee had taken the credit of the duty paid on the inputs used in manufacture of these goods. The ratio laid down in this decision was squarely applicable to the facts of the instant case and maintenance of separate books of account at the initial stage cannot be considered to be a condition precedent for the purpose of claiming the benefit of exemption to the respondent-assessee. [Para 6]

Even rule 6(3) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 says that notwithstanding anything contained in sub-rules (1) and (2), the manufacturer or the provider of output service, opting not to maintain separate accounts, shall follow either of the following conditions, as applicable to him. Even otherwise rule 3 says that the manufacturer or producer of the final product or provider of output services shall be allowed to take credit on various items enumerated therein. This issue had come up for consideration before the Allahabad High Court in the case of Hello Minerals Water (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India 2004 (174) ELT 422, wherein it is held that reversal of Modvat credit amounts to non-taking of credit on the inputs. Hence, the benefit of the notification granting exemption/rate of duty has to be given on the final products since the reversal of credit on the input was done. Accordingly, the Tribunal’s order in the instant case was justified. [Para 7]

HEADNOTE: Rule 57 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Cenvat Credit - Modvat - EOUs--Credit not admissible for goods cleared to EOUs free of duty

FACT: Appellants manufacture Pumpable Slurry Explosives (PSE) and supply the same free of duty to a 100% Export Oriented Unit (EOU). The appellants want to be allowed to accumulate Modvat credit on inputs of PSE for utilisation later as and when they start clearing the goods on payment of duty.

HELD: Modvat--credit is not admissible as no duty leviable on the final product (PSE) cleared by the appellants. "A reading of the various Central Excise Rules and the Scheme of the MODVAT set out therein shows that the facility of MODVAT Credit is available in respect of duty paid on inputs used in or in relation to the manufacture of the specified final product and for utilizing the credit so allowed towards payment of duty of excise leviable on the final product. When, therefore, there is no duty leviable on the final products which have been cleared from the appellants' factory, the question of allowing them the MODVAT Credit on the inputs would not arise. Rule 57C of the Central Excise Rules clearly envisages that no credit of the specified duty paid on the inputs used in the manufacture of a final product shall be allowed if the final product is exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon or is chargeable to nit rate of duty. ...In view of above, we hold that there is no force in the appellants' plea......."

HEADNOTE: Rule 9A of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002 - Cenvat Credit - Transactional provisions for textile and textile articles - Appellant, a manufacturer of cotton knitted garments and cotton knitted fabrics, made fabrics from yarn (duty paid) and then made garments from fabrics - Appellant availed Cenvat Credit on total quantity/value of duty paid yarn - Whether there is no dispute about fact that every manufacturing process would automatically result in some kind of a loss such as evaporation, creation of by-product etc, and, therefore, total quantity of inputs that went into making of finished product represented inputs of such products in entirety - Held, yes - Whether appellant was right in making a claim for Cenvat Credit, with reference to total quantity and value of inputs that went into making of fabric - Held, yes [Paras 13  16] [In favour of assessee]CENVAT: A textile manufacturer is entitled to claim Cenvat Credit on total quantity and value of inputs, i.e., yarn inclusive of manufacturing loss that went into making of finished product i.e., fabric

FACT: The appellant was a manufacturer of Cotton knitted garments and cotton knitted fabrics. It used yarn on which excise duty was paid. It availed Cenvat Credit on duty paid yarn that had gone into making of fabric.

A show-cause notice was issued on the ground that the appellant had wrongly availed CENVAT Credit on the stock declared and had utilized the same for payment of duty towards clearance of knitted garments manufactured by it.

The Adjudicating Authority disallowed the claim for Cenvat Credit and imposed penalty along with interest.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) disallowed a claim for Cenvat Credit and upheld the appellant guilty of claiming CENVAT Credit to which appellant was not entitled.

On second appeal, the Tribunal upheld the Order-in-Original.

On appeal before the High Court:

HELD: What the appellant did was to make a claim for CENVAT credit in respect of the total quantity and value of goods that had gone into the making of fabric. Under Rule 9A, the appellant is admittedly entitled to credit, equivalent to the duty paid on inputs of finished product, lying in stock or in process or contained in finished products lying in stock as on 31-3-2003. Rule 9A deals with three items. They are (i) finished products lying in stock (ii) the products lying in process and (iii) those contained in finished products. The appellant has not made a claim in respect of the entire quantity and value of the inputs that had gone into the making of the finished products. [Para 9]

Incidentally, it should be pointed out that the appellant uses yarn, on which, excise duty is paid. This yarn is made into fabric and the fabric is made into garment. Their claim for credit was confined only to the duty paid on the yarn that had gone into the making of fabric. The claim of the appellant is that about 5 per cent of the quantity and value of yarn is lost while making it into a fabric and that therefore, they are entitled to take credit for the entire quantity and value of input that had actually produced the fabric that was lying in store. [Para 10]

To put it in simple terms, what the appellant claimed was that if X kg of fabric was lying in stock on the relevant date, the inputs that had gone into the making of the said quantity was X plus something. The only question that falls for consideration is as to whether that something is actually entitled to CENVAT credit or not? [Para 11]

Keeping the above in mind, it is seen that there are three expressions used. They are (i) input of such furnished product, (ii) lying in stock or in process and (iii) contained finished product [Para 12]

To say that what is contained in finished product is only a quantity of all the inputs of the same weight as that of the finished product would presuppose that all manufacturing processes would never have an inherent loss in the process of manufacture. The expression 'inputs of such finished product' contained in 'finished products' cannot be looked at theoretically with its semantics. It has to be understood in the context of what a manufacturing process is. If there is no dispute about the fact that every manufacturing process would automatically result in some kind of a loss such as evaporation, creation of by-products, etc., the total quantity of inputs that went into the making of the finished product represents the inputs of such products in entirety. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: Section 5A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Power to grant exemption from duty of excise - Period from 13-3-2002 to 15-9- 2002 - Assessee, manufacturer of grey fabrics, claimed exemption under Notification No. 14/2002-CE, dated 1-3-2002 under which grey fabrics are chargeable to nil rate of duty subject to two conditions, viz., assessee paying duty on yarn before claiming exemption and assessee not claiming Cenvat credit before claiming exemption - Whether since assessee paid duty on yarn on deferred basis before clearance of grey fabrics and credit available on payment of duty on input (yarn) was never utilized by it, both conditions of said exemption Notification were satisfied and, hence, item No. 1 of Table to said Notification would apply and grey fabrics would attract nil rate of duty - Held, yes [Para 8] Circulars & Notifications - Notification No. 14/2002-CE, dated 1-3-2002

FACT: The assessee, engaged in weaving grey fabrics out of spun yarn from raw cotton in one of its composite mills, opted for exemption under Notification No. 14/2002-CE under which grey fabrics, not subjected to any process, are chargeable to nil rate of duty subject to the condition that the said fabrics were made from textile yarn on which appropriate duty of excise stood paid and no credit for duty paid on inputs had been taken under CENVAT Credit Rules. However, since the assessee was not in a position to ascertain the variety and quantity of yarn entering into the manufacture of export production of grey fabrics meant for home consumption, the assessee instead of paying duty on yarn at spindle stage opted to pay duty on yarn on deferred basis at the time of clearance of grey fabrics for home consumption. According to the revenue, the assessee had failed to pay duty on yarn at the spindle stage and, secondly, it had taken credit for the duty paid on inputs under CENVAT Credit Rules, 2002 and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to claim nil rate of duty as it failed to comply with the two-fold conditions mentioned in item No. 1 of the Table to the said Notification. Consequently, a demand was raised for differential duty on the ground that the assessee had failed to pay the duty on yarn at the spindle stage. The demand was confirmed by the adjudicating authority. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the assessee for the payment of duty on yarn at the time of clearance of grey fabrics instead of payment of duty on yarn at the spindle stage. The order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was upheld by the Tribunal.

On revenue’s appeal to the Supreme Court :

HELD: Under the notification, mode of payment has not been prescribed. Further, exemption is given to the final product, namely, grey fabric. Under the Act, levy is on manufacture but payment is at the time of clearance. Under the Act, payment of duty on yarn has to be at the spindle stage. However, when one comes to the Exemption Notification No. 14/2002-CE, the requirement is that exemption on grey fabrics is admissible subject to the assessee paying duty on yarn before claiming exemption and subject to the assessee not claiming CENVAT credit before claiming exemption. The question of exemption from payment of duty on grey fabrics arises on satisfaction of the said two conditions. In the instant case, payment of duty on yarn on deferred basis took place before clearance of grey fabrics on which exemption was claimed. Therefore, payment was made before the stage of exemption. Similarly, on payment of duty on the input (yarn), the assessee got the credit which was never utilized. That, before utilization the entry had been reversed which amounted to not taking credit. Hence, in the instant case, both the conditions were satisfied and item No. 1 of the Table to Notification No. 14/2002-CE would apply and, accordingly, the grey fabrics would attract nil rate of duty. [Para 8]

Accordingly, the appeal filed by the department failed and the same was to be dismissed. [Para 10]

The expression 'inputs of such finished product' contained in 'finished products' cannot be looked at theoretically with its semantics. It has to be understood in the context of what a manufacturing process is. If there is no dispute about the fact that every manufacturing process would automatically result in some kind of a loss such as evaporation, creation of by-products, etc., the total quantity of inputs that went into the making of the finished product represents the inputs of such products in entirety. [Para 13] If the purport of Rule 9A is not understood in this manner, every manufacturer will have to pay excise duty on the quantity and value of inputs, which go to the making of a finished product, whose weight will never be equivalent to the sum total of the weight of all the inputs. Therefore, this is not the way to understand Rule 9A. [Para 14]

Right from the stage of issue of show-cause notice upto the stage of the order of the Tribunal, the claim of the appellant that they incur a manufacturing loss to the extent of 5 per cent of the total quantity of the finished product, has not been disputed by the department. In cases where there is a dispute about the existence of a loss and in cases where there is a dispute with regard to the quantum of loss, the questions may have to be left open. But, in cases where the quantum of manufacturing loss claimed at 5 per cent by the appellant is never disputed by the department from the stage of issue of the show-cause notice upto the stage of the order of the Tribunal, the interpretation given to Rule 9A cannot be accepted. [Para 15]

Therefore, the appellant was right in making a claim for CENVAT credit, with reference to the total quantity and the value of the inputs that went into the making of the fabric. [Para 16]

"In so far as Alfa Alumina is concerned, we find that this item is used in the process of manufacture of POY and Polyester Flat yarn. Section 2, read with First Schedule, of the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 - Classification - Processed Rubber Compound Sheet - Assessee was manufacturing processed rubber compound in sheet form - Assessee claimed classification thereof under sub-heading 4005.10 (Nil rate) - Department argued that sub-heading 4005.10 applies to goods manufactured without taking input credit; since, in this case, input credit had been taken, therefore, goods were classifiable under sub-heading 4005.90 - Assessee argued that credit was taken only on minor items viz., consumables and not on major items viz., 'raw rubber and fillers' - HELD : Classification itself was dependent upon whether input credit was taken or not; there is nothing like major or minor item - Once manufacturer has taken credit of any input, output goes out of sub-heading 4005.10 and is classifiable under sub-heading 4005.90 - Demand was upheld [Para 6] [In favour of revenue]Excise  Customs : Where NIL rate of duty is based upon condition that no credit of inputs had been taken, assessee cannot claim said benefit if he had taken credit even on minor inputs/consumables

Rule 6, read with rules 3 and 9, of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted service - Whether availability of Cenvat credit depends upon provisions of law comprised under Cenvat Credit Rules and they do not stand modified by any exemption notification - Held, yes - Assessee, a manufacturer, undertook expansion programme at its factory in order to avail exemption of duty liability on finished goods under Notification No. 50/2003-CE, dated 10-6-2003 - It filed a declaration in that regard on 10-1-2005 - On that day, it had some of inputs in stock, which were procured prior to that day and were either lying in store or contained in goods in manufacturing process or contained in finished goods in stock - It was case of assessee that credit taken in respect of duty paid on inputs lying in stock on 10-1-2005, was already utilized prior to 10-1-2005 and, therefore, said credit could not be denied to it, nor could be ordered to be reversed - Case of department was that as per Cenvat Credit Rules, credit in respect of duty paid on inputs is admissible provided it is availed and utilized in or in relation to manufacture of final goods which are not exempt from payment of duty - Whether though Cenvat credit is earned from payment of duty on inputs procured for use in manufacture of dutiable and non-exempted final products, mere use of such credit towards payment of duty on such final product does not amount to complete utilization of such credit till and until inputs on which such credit is earned are also used in manufacture of dutiable and non-exempted final products; this is irrespective of fact that there is no co-relation between inputs on which credit is earned and final product in respect of which such credit is used for payment of duty thereon - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Cenvat credit availed on inputs lying in stock on day assessee opted for exemption from payment of duty under Notification No. 50/2003, dated 10-6-2003, would be required to be reversed - Held, yes - Whether regarding question as to whether goods cleared for export under bond cannot be considered as exempted goods, and manufacturers thereof are entitled to avail Cenvat credit in respect of duty paid on inputs utilized in manufacture of such final goods, one has to take into consideration effect of provisions of rules 6(6) and 3 - Held, yes [Issue of goods cleared for export under bond was remanded] [Paras 74 to 79] Circulars and Notifications : Notification No. 50/2003-CE, dated 10-6-2003 , Notification No. 21/2004-CE (N.T.) , dated 6-12-2004 , Notification No. 19/2004-CE (N.T.) , dated 6-9-2004 , Notification No. 20/2004-CE (N.T.) , dated 6-9-2004

Section 3(1) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, read with sections 3 and 5A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Charge/levy - Additional Duty of Customs/CVD - Assessee imported Nylon Filament Yarn and claimed exemption in respect of CVD under Excise Notification No. 6/2002-CE (Entry 122) - Department denied exemption on ground that : (a) vide condition No. 20, exemption is subject to condition that 'no credit is taken under CENVAT Credit Rules in respect of inputs/capital goods used in manufacture of goods'; and (b) said condition was impossible of being complied with because no credit was otherwise allowable on inputs/capital goods used in imported goods - HELD : If an imported article is one which has been manufactured or produced, then it must be presumed, for purpose of CVD, that such an article can likewise be manufactured or produced in India; actual manufacture or production in India is not necessary - For quantification of CVD in such a case, it has to be imagined that article imported had been manufactured or produced in India and then to see what amount of excise duty was leviable thereon - Hence, assessee was entitled to exemption from payment of CVD [Paras 7 and 8] [In favour of assessee]Excise  Customs : Where excise duty in India is NIL subject to 'not taking of credit on inputs/capital goods', an importer is entitled to said exemption in respect of 'CVD equal to excise duty' and in his case, CVD would be equal to excise duty i.e., NIL
