Section 2, read with 1st Schedule, of the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 - Classification - Slub Yarn or Normal Yarn - Tariff Headings 55.06 and 56.06 - Period from July, 1994 to March, 1995 - Assessee manufactured blended yarn containing 52 per cent viscose fibre and 48 per cent polyester fibre and during spinning process, a special effect was given by using an electronic device to make it 'slub yarn' - Assessee sought classification under Tariff Heading 55.06 'synthetic staple fibres, carded, combed or otherwise processed for spinning', being a final product eligible for input credit - Revenue sought classification under Tariff Heading 56.06 'Gimped, Chenille or Loop wale Yarn', being final product not eligible for input credit - HELD : All types of special yarns requiring special treatment are different from normal yarn (Heading 55.06) and are covered by 56.06 - Assessee had manufactured goods with special mechanical stimulation which created an effect of thick and thin features in yarns while spinning to impart slub effect - Thus, 'slub' yarns were not normal yarns and were classifiable under Heading 55.06 [Paras 3 to 6] [In favour of revenue]Excise  Customs : Blended yarn made of viscose fibre and polyester fibre with special mechanical stimulation creating an effect of thick and thin features in yarns while spinning to impart slub effect, known as 'slub' yarn, is classifiable under Heading 55.06

Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat Credit - available - in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of goods cleared to 100% Export Oriented unit at nil rate of duty -appeal allowed in view of earlier decisions

Section 5A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Exemption - Central Excise - Notification No. 84/87-CE - Polyester fibre tow - used in manufacture of staple fibre cleared free of duty under Notification No. 191/85-CE dt. 28.8.85 for supply to KVIC - tow entitled to exemption under Notification No. 84/87-CE though no duty paid on staple fibre in view of purpose and intention behind Notification No. 191/85 - subsequent Notification No. 76/92-CE dt. 1.7.92 amending Notification No. 191/85 to be considered as clarificatory in nature and retrospective in effect (Para 4)

Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat Credit - CC8 - used as an additive, mixed and used along with residual fuel oil for raising temperature of oil to required level - eligible input under Rule 57A as its use is essential in relation to manufacture of final product i.e. polyester fibre and it is not covered by excluded category - appeal allowed.

Rule 57F of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - final product cleared under Rule 191B/191BB for use in manufacture of export goods under bond - input credit not deniable - appeal rejected (Para 7)

Rule 57C of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - inputs sent without payment of duty in terms of Notification No. 33/90-CE dt. 5.9.90 to manufacturers of final product for export under old Rule 191BB of Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Rule 57C not attracted as Notification No. 33/90-CE neither grants exemption nor uses the words nil rate of duty - credit admissible - appeal allowed.

Rule 57C and  57CC of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - inputs are used in manufacture of parts which are captively used in manufacture of exempted or nil duty rated final products - duty is paid on such parts and credit of duty paid on the parts is not taken - Rule 57C and 57CC are not attracted in such case - input credit admissible - appeals rejected (Para 4)
Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Boron Nitrate suspension - used in manufacture of polyester film - eligible input (Para 6)

Rule 11 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002 - Cenvat credit - Power of Central Government to notify goods for deemed Cenvat credit - Whether Tribunal was justified in allowing deemed credit to assessee in respect of fibre/yarn used in grey fabric which was an indirect input in assessee’s final product, in view of Notification No. 6/2002-CE(NT), dated 1-3-2002 - Held, yes [Para 11] Circulars & Notifications: Notification No. 6/2002 - CE(NT), dated 1-3-2002, Circular No. 702/18/2003-CX, dated 13-3-2003

Section 5A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Exemption - Central Excise - Notification No. 191/85-CE - Polyester fibre - 'Manufacturer' - Interpretation - word 'manufacturer' in the notification referred to manufacturer of fabrics and not to manufacturer of fibre - duty not demandable from the manufacturer of fibre as the liability to pay duty was on the manufacturer of fabrics on his failure to produce end use certificate - appeal allowed (Para 5)

Section 35L (b) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Notification No. 95/ 83 - Exemption notification presupposes that the duty is otherwise payable on the finished products specified therein - Final products cleared by the assessee at nil rate of duty - None of the inputs for which proforma credit had been taken went into production of dutiable goods - Respondent cannot take advantage of the notification

Rule 57 A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat Credit - Dowtherm Diphyl - used for maintaining required heat in the equipment for manufacture of nylon and polyester filament yarn - eligible input under Rule 57A as used in relation to manufacture of final product.

Section 2(f) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Manufacture - Dutiability--Polyester waste generated daring the manufacture of polyester fibre and tops from duty paid polyester waste is liable to duty again--Manufacture--Conversion of polyester polymer waste into monomer and its reconversion to polymer by successive processes of depolymerisation and polymerisation constitute manufacture even though the final product has the same physical and chemical properties as that of the original product and falls under same tariff heading

Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Tungsten wire and Triethylene Glycol - used in or in relation to manufacture of final product (polyester film) - eligible inputs - appeals rejected (Para 5)

facts.text:
The Appellants purchased duty paid crimped uncut waste, cut it into polyester fibre by fibre cutting machine and made sub-standard mixed yarn. It was alleged against the appellants that they had manufactured polyester fibre out of polyester crimped uncut waste with the held of the aforementioned processes without obtaining Central Excise licence for manufacture of fibre, and without complying with the other Central Excise formalities, including payment of duty on the fibre.

It was held that post drawn waste is generated only after the material which goes into the manufacture of fibre attains necessary qualities of fibre. It has, therefore, for all purposes, to be treated as fibre, but since it confirms to the category of waste, as stipulated in Notfn. No. 53/72-CE dated 17.3.1972 it was allowed to be cleared from the factory on payment of duty at concessional rates as provided for in the said Notification.

Once it is agreed that post drawn waste which was processed by the appellants was cleared as fibres, although on concessional rate of duty, being waste, the relaxation under the same Tariff item would naturally amount to double taxation which is not advisable under law.

The assessee was manufacturing yarn and was making its clearances as follows :

(a)

domestic clearances under full exemption under Notification 30/2004 (which was subject to no Cenvat credit condition); and

(b)

export clearances on payment of unconditional concessional duty of 4 per cent under Notification 29/2004 and claiming rebate thereof.

The assessee did not take any input credit but only took credit of capital goods.

The Department argued that :

(a)

since goods were already exempt under Notification 30/2004, hence, payment of duty under Notification 29/2004 was not a duty but only a deposit and even export clearances continued to be 'exempted goods' and

(b)

therefore, no credit could be allowed under Rule 6(4) on capital goods exclusively used for manufacture of 'exempted goods' only.

The appellants manufacture man-made polyester fibre falling under CETI 18 using duty-paid ethylene glycol of CETI 68 and DMT in addition to other inputs. Set-off of duty paid on ethylene glycol claimed under Notfn. 201/79-CE was refused by the Asstt. Collr. for various reasons. After filing a new classification list, set-off was claimed under the amendment to the proviso which said that proforma credit could not be denied or varied on the grounds that part of the input was non-excisable waste. An appear was filed to the CCE contending that the duty-paid ethylene glycol was captively consumed in the manufacture of polyester fibre and even the waste is recycled and captively used in the manufacture of DMT. When the Asstt. Collr. held that proforma credit was applicable only for a limited amount, a second appeal was filed to the CCE, and a third appeal against the demand of duty. The CCE (Appeals) decided three appeals in favour of the appellants, but the Tribunal decided otherwise. This appeal was then filed.

The appellants manufacture polyester fibre yarn. In 1975 they were awarded a contract by Imperial Chemical Industries, Singapore for manufacture of blended yarn to be exported to an ICI customer in Sri Lanka. ICI Singapore supplied free of cost one of the raw materials, dimethyl terephthalate (DMT) for manufacture of the polyester fibre yam which was to be blended with viscose staple fibre yarn for production of the blended yarn to be exported to Sri Lanka. The appellants obtained Customs Clearance Permits (CCPs) for the DMT so supplied. The conditions of the CCPs were that the polyester fibre would be manufactured from the imported DMT under Customs bond, the blending with viscose fibre would be carried out under excise supervision (manufacture in bond), and thereafter the blended yam would be exported to Sri Lanka. However, the Customs authorities were not in a position to permit manufacture of polyester fibre under bond and declined the appellants' request for such manufacture, as a result of which the appellants could only clear the DMT after paying the customs duty in force at the time. The DMT thus cleared on payment of duty was used for manufacture of polyester fibre, which in turn was blended with indigenous viscose fibre to produce blended yam which was duly exported. Subsequently, on 2.8.1976, a notification was issued which fully exempted imported DMT from customs duty, but as the import of DMT in their case was prior to that date, the appellants were not entitled to avail of that exemption. The appellants then filed a claim for drawback of the customs duty paid by them on the DMT, and the rejection of this claim at all levels up to the High Court has led to the present appeals to the Supreme Court. The plea of the appellants is that the drawback permissible was equal to the excise duty on the manufacture of blended yarn. As they had not paid any excise duty in view of manufacture under excise supervision, the question of drawback of excise duty did not arise. The fact that the drawback was equal to the excise duty payable indicated, according to them, that the customs duty element had not been considered while computing drawback.

The appellant, a Textile factory, purchased in the open market synthetic fibre waste or crimped uncut waste as alleged by Central Excise Officers below, and converted it into polyester fibre with a "tow cutting machine" to manufacture blended yarn. Collector Delhi confirmed the demand of duty on the polyester fibre manufactured by the appellants.

Ratio of decision:--It was held that there is no duty liability, as fibre, on the product manufactured out of "crimped uncut waste" by a tow cutting machine as it was earlier cleared out of the factory of manufacture as fibre waste on payment of duty.

The appeal was therefore allowed.

The appellants manufacture low price polyester cotton fabrics after obtaining polyester yarn at a concessional rate of duty in pursuance of policy decision of Government of India and therefore are not liable to pay on fents, rags and chindies 8% in excess of total quantity of clearance of the goods in question.

The appellants manufacture low price polyester cotton fabrics after obtaining polyester yarn at a concessional rate of duty in pursuance of policy decision of Government of India and therefore are not liable to pay on fents, rags and chindies 8% in excess of total quantity of clearance of the goods in question.

The assessee is engaged in the manufacturing of polyester cotton blended yarn and polyester viscose blended yarn and both these products fall under Chapter 55 of the Schedule to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985.

For manufacture of the aforesaid product, the assessee had used the raw material which was an intermediate product and paid excise duty thereupon. The final products were also cleared on payment of excise duty on those finished products.

The assessee exported these goods on payment of central excise duty in CENVAT account and filed rebate claims under the provisions of Rule 18 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 (hereinafter referred to as the 'Rules').

The department opined that the assessee is entitled to one of the two claims for rebate, i.e., either rebate of duty paid on exported goods or the duty paid on inputs used in the exported goods, and not on both of them.

The revisional authority viz. Central Government held that that assessee was entitled to rebate both on the exported goods as well as inputs used in the exported goods.

The High Court held in favour of revenue on ground that out of the two, rule 18 of the Rules permits rebate only qua one of them (viz. either on inputs or on output) and not on both the duties.

w.e.f. 1-3-2008, and just because in course of processing of the raw menthol for manufacture of menthol crystals BP/USP and Menthol BP/USP, some residual oil is obtained which on further processing is converted into flavouring materials which are dutiable, it cannot be said that the provisions of rule 11(3) read with rule 6 (1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 would not be applicable. Assessee's argument that materials in the instant case were not exclusively and solely used in the manufacture of exempt goods and therefore, the provisions of rule 11 (3) would not apply, is unfounded, fallacious and patently wrong as sub-rule (3) (ii) of rule 11 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 does not make any exception in respect of export goods as is evident from the words "whether cleared for home consumption or for export" in this sub-rule.

In view of section 5A(1A), exemption was mandatory. A harmonious construction of section 5A (1A) of Central Excise Act, 1944 with rule 6 (6) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 would be that the term "excisable goods" in this sub-rule should be read as "dutiable goods".

Notification No. 24/10-CE (NT) dated 26-5-2010 providing that the export of excisable goods which are chargeable to nil rate of duty or are fully exempted from duty, other than the goods cleared by 100% EOU, is not allowed under bond should be treated as retrospective amendment.

As per proviso to rule 5 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 no refund shall be allowed if the manufacturer inter alia claims rebate in respect of such duty. In the instant case, no segregation of duty paid on inputs was made in reference to the final products and the refund and rebate were claimed from a common basket of input credit.

Menthol falling under heading 29061100 of the Central Excise Tariff happened to be both input as also the export product in the subject case involving no manufacturing process in between. As per rule 3 (5) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 to which when Cenvat credit availed inputs or capital goods are cleared as such, an amount equal to the credit availed in respect of such inputs or capital goods shall be payable under the cover of invoices.

It was open to the assessee to claim rebate of duty of the un-utilised input credit under rule 18 of the Central Excise Rules read with Notification No. 21/04-CE (NT) instead of seeking refund under rule 5 of the Cenvat Credit Rules. It is inexplicable as to why the assessee avoided such obvious legitimate course for tax neutralization in respect of their exempted products which were exported.

The inputs in this case had been received from four Jammu units availing of exemption under Notification No. 56/02-CE, namely. Subsequent investigations revealed that these from Jammu suppliers of inputs had made only paper transactions with the assessee to generate Cenvat credit based on bogus invoices without any manufacture.

Assessee's Arguments

While the Menthol/Menthol Crystals, BP/USP, became fully exempt from duty w.e.f. 1-3-2008 under Notification No. 4/08-CE, the other final products remained dutiable. However, all the final products whether exempted or dutiable were being exported out of India. While Menthol/Menthol Crystals, BP/USP were being exported under bond without payment of duty under rule 19 of Central Excise Rules, 2002, the other final products flavouring agents were being cleared on payment of duty and were being exported under rebate claim.

When inputs are used in manufacture of dutiable as well as exempted final products and the exempted final products are exported out of India, the provisions of rule 6 (6) (V) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 would be applicable and the bar of rule 6 (1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules and the liability created under rule 6 (3) (b) would not be attracted.

The words "excisable goods" in rule 6 (6) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 are wide enough to include both dutiable as well as exempted goods.

Amendment to Notification No. 42/01- CE (NT) dated 26-6-2001 by Notification No. 24/10 - CE (NT) dated 26-5-2010 providing that the export of excisable goods which are chargeable to nil rate of duty or are fully exempted from payment of duty, other than the goods cleared by a 100% EOU, shall not be allowed under this notification cannot be given retrospective effect, as this amendment restricts the benefits.

Rule 11 (3) (ii) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 does not apply when a manufacturer manufacturers dutiable as well as exempted final products out of common Cenvat credit availed inputs.

The respondent-assessee was engaged in the business of manufacture of cotton fabrics. It used grey cotton, dyes, chemicals, packing material, etc., as inputs for manufacture of cotton fabrics. Prior to February, 2005, the respondent was clearing goods on payment of applicable duty under Notification No. 29/2004-C.E., dated 9-7-2004. It was noticed that the respondent had started availing benefit of both Notifications Nos. 29/2004 and 30/2004 simultaneously from February, 2005. However, the respondent was not maintaining separate accounts for receipt of inputs being used in the manufacture of fabrics subsequently cleared without payment of duty by availing of the benefit of second Notification No. 30/2004-C.E., dated 9-7-2004. According to the revenue, maintenance of such accounts was a mandatory condition. The assessee contended that if the manufacturer reverse credit before clearance, it must be taken that the credit was never availed of, and that neither the Board’s circular nor the clarification issued in the RAC meeting required the manufacturer to maintain separate accounts with regard to the inputs, rather they were required to maintain separate books of account only for the final goods. However, the Commissioner took the view that the respondent had contravened the provisions of the notification read with the clarification issued rendering it liable for penal action under section 11AC. On appeal, following the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Chandrapur Magnet Wires (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 1996 (81) ELT 3 wherein it is held that the reversal of credit of duty originally availed of would amount to the effect as if no credit has been availed, the Tribunal held that the credit availed and reversed would amount to the situation as if the same was not availed, thus, satisfying the condition of Notification No. 30/04-C.E.

On revenue’s appeal :

The assessee, engaged in weaving grey fabrics out of spun yarn from raw cotton in one of its composite mills, opted for exemption under Notification No. 14/2002-CE under which grey fabrics, not subjected to any process, are chargeable to nil rate of duty subject to the condition that the said fabrics were made from textile yarn on which appropriate duty of excise stood paid and no credit for duty paid on inputs had been taken under CENVAT Credit Rules. However, since the assessee was not in a position to ascertain the variety and quantity of yarn entering into the manufacture of export production of grey fabrics meant for home consumption, the assessee instead of paying duty on yarn at spindle stage opted to pay duty on yarn on deferred basis at the time of clearance of grey fabrics for home consumption. According to the revenue, the assessee had failed to pay duty on yarn at the spindle stage and, secondly, it had taken credit for the duty paid on inputs under CENVAT Credit Rules, 2002 and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to claim nil rate of duty as it failed to comply with the two-fold conditions mentioned in item No. 1 of the Table to the said Notification. Consequently, a demand was raised for differential duty on the ground that the assessee had failed to pay the duty on yarn at the spindle stage. The demand was confirmed by the adjudicating authority. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the assessee for the payment of duty on yarn at the time of clearance of grey fabrics instead of payment of duty on yarn at the spindle stage. The order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was upheld by the Tribunal.

On revenue’s appeal to the Supreme Court :

The applicant was engaged in the manufacture of different types of yarn. It proposed to construct within its factory premises, additional sheds for manufacturing and storing of yarn, as also residential quarters for its workers and staff, as a part of its programme to augment the production capacity. It sought advance ruling on the following issues :-

(a)Whether the construction services used for construction of workers’ quarters within the factory premises, fall within the ambit of input services as defined in rule 2(l ) and, consequently, whether, the applicant can avail of the credit of such construction services in terms of rule 3?

(b)Whether the applicant can claim full rate of drawback on export of yarn manufactured by it along with Cenvat credit on construction services used for construction of manufacturing/storage/workers residential quarters within the factory premises?

Regarding the first issue, the applicant stated that the manufacture of yarn was a continuous operation and in order to ensure availability of workers round the clock, it proposed to house the workers in a colony within the factory itself; that continuous availability of workers residing in a colony within the factory would ensure efficient production of yarn; and, therefore, the construction service required for building a residential colony for the workers was indirectly connected with the manufacture and clearance of yarn and such construction service had to be regarded as an input service and Cenvat credit of the service tax paid on such service should be available to it.

As regards the second issue, the applicant submitted that it was entitled to claim the higher rate of drawback allowed in Notification No. 68/2007-Cus. (NT), dated 16-7-2007 for its yarn exports, even when Cenvat credit of the service tax paid on the services used for construction of factory sheds, store rooms and residential colony for workers, had been availed of. According to the applicant, the only condition required to be fulfilled for availing of the higher drawback rate as set out in clause (12)(i) of the above notification was that no Cenvat credit should have been availed of the Central Excise duty on inputs used in the manufacture of yarn export; that this condition was met in its case inasmuch it had availed Cenvat credit on input services; that inputs, i.e., physical goods were distinct from input service; and clause 12(i) nowhere mentions non-availment of Cenvat credit of tax on an input service, as a pre-condition for availing of the higher rate of drawback.

The assessee manufactures final product, namely, blanket out of woollen fibres. The blankets attract only Basic Excise Duty (for short BED) and does not attract either Additional Excise Duty (Goods of Special Importance) [for short 'AED(GSI)'] or Additional Excise Duty (Textiles and Textile Articles) [for short AED(T&TA)].

With effect from 1-4-1994, the assessee became entitled to avail credit of duty paid on the inputs (tops etc.) used in or in relation to the manufacture of manmade yarn. With effect from the said date, the assessees became entitled to avail credit of duty paid on the inputs used in or in relation to the manufacture of blankets falling under Chapter 63.

Vide Notification No. 24/94CE (NT), dated 20-5-1994 issued under rule 57A, AED(T&TA) paid on input can be utilised for payment of AED(T&TA) on the final product. Similarly, AED(GSI) paid on the input can be utilised for payment of AED(GSI) on the final product. Similar provision contained in Notification No. 5/94(NT), dated 1-3-1994 also issued under rule 57A.

With effect from 3-9-1996, the assessees became entitled to avail credit of duty paid on the inputs used in or in relation to the manufacture of fabrics falling under Chapter 55.

The assessee, inter alia, took the credit of Basic Excise Duty and AED(T&TA) on one of the inputs viz. Manmade tops falling under Chapter 55 of the Tariff Act used in or in relation to the manufacture of yarn from 1-3-1994. The yarn manufactured by the assessees was subject to BED and AED(T&TA).

The assessee utilised the credit of BED paid under section 3 on the tops towards the payment of BED and the additional duty of excise payable under the additional duties of excise (Goods of Special Importance) Act. However, under a mistake of law, the assessee did not utilise the credit of AED (T&TA) on the tops towards the payment of duty on any other final products viz. Fabric, Blanket, Shawls etc.

Owing to introduction of Cenvat Scheme from 1-4-2000, rule 57AB(2)(b) provided that AED (T&TA) and AED (GSI) paid on input can be utilised for payment of AED (T&TA) or AED (GSI). This position contained upto 30-6-2001.

Later, Cenvat Credit Rules, 2001 provided that AED (T&TA) and AED (GSI) paid on input can be utilised for payment of AED (T&TA) or AED (GSI) 'respectively' (word respectively was added).

Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002 maintained the aforesaid position of law.

Between January 2003 to April, 2003, the assessees utilised this AED (T&TA) credit for payment of BED and AED (GSI).

The department argued that said use of AED (T&TA) was impermissible.

The appellants receive duly paid bi-metal strips for use in the manufacture of I.C. Engines and parts thereof. They avail of Modvat Credit for the inputs. The appellants cleared certain parts like plain shaft bearings at nil rate of duty by following Chapter X procedure. The Assistant Collector held that credit could not be allowed on inputs used in the manufacture of parts cleared at nil rate of duty as per provisions of Rule 57C of the Central Excise Rules, 1944. This was upheld by the Collector (Appeals).

Polyester filament yarn, both textured and non-textured, was manufactured by the petitioner in their Nainital factory, designated as an 'A' class backward area. Classified under CETI 5402.20 and 5403.20 and dutiable under Notification 53/87-CE, it was exempt from 50% of the duty leviable under Notification 186/89-CE provided certain conditions were fulfilled. Though this notification was valid till 31st October 1990, it was rescinded by Notification 187/89-CE dated 30th October 1989. Full duty was demanded for goods cleared on that date though the petitioner contended that the public was made aware of it only later and it was not actually published on that date.

The appellants manufactured polyester viscose blended yarn and cotton polyester yarn. They took Cenvat credit on the polyester fibre which was the input. The revenue proceeded against the appellants on ground that in use of polyester in production the normal process loss can be limited only to 2 to 3 per cent. However, the actual loss in case of the appellants was much more. Therefore, the duty was demanded from the appellants on certain quantity of polyester fibres on which Modvat credit was taken. Besides that penalty was also imposed on the appellant. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) set aside order of the original authority.

On appeal :

The Tribunal allowed deemed credit to the assessee-respondent in respect of fibre/yarn used in grey fabric which was an indirect input in the assessee’s final product, processed fabric, in view of the Notification No. 6/2002-CE(NT), dated 1-3-2002.

On appeal, the revenue/appellant contended that the said notification referred to a table of inputs and final products; that the input of the respondent was grey fabric and not yarn/fibre; that grey fabric was not referred to in the table of inputs mentioned in the said notification and, therefore, the respondent would not be entitled to claim the benefit of the said notification in respect of its manufactured products-processed fabrics. On the other hand, the respondent relied on Circular No. 702/18/2003-CX, dated 13-3-2003. In that context the circular discussed Notification No. 29/96-CE (NT), dated 3-9-1996 which was the predecessor notification to the instant Notification No. 6 pertaining to availment of deemed credit. The Central Board of Excise and Customs, by virtue of the said circular, observed that, although grey fabrics are not included as the declared inputs in the said notification, they are made out of duty paid yarn/fibres, which are declared inputs and have suffered appropriate excise duty. The Board also reiterated its earlier view and observed that the refund of the said unutilized deemed credit of grey fabric was admissible. The respondent submitted that in view of the clarification given by the Board, it was clear that inputs, which formed part of the intermediate products, namely, grey fabrics, were to be considered for the purposes of deemed credit in terms of the Notification No. 6 referred to above.

The 'assessee' is engaged in the manufacture of polyester chips, polyester staple fibre, polyester filament yarn and other goods.

Advance licence is issued under the EXIM Policy. The holder of the advance licence could procure imported raw material against the said licence for manufacture of finished goods. However, as per para 7.7 of the EXIM Policy 1997-2002, the advance licence holder intending to source the materials from indigenous source in lieu of direct import had the option to source them against advance release orders denominated in foreign exchange/Indian rupees. In such a case, the licence was to be invalidated for direct import and permission in the form of ARO was to be issued entitling the supplier of the goods the benefits of deemed export.

The advance licence holder category buyers got their licences invalidated/surrendered. Thereafter, DGFT issued licence in favour of the assessee herein permitting it to procure the goods duty free from indigenous manufacturers and on the supply of this material to such buyers, treating the same as 'deemed exports', thereby earning the benefits of duty drawback.

The assessee had been selling polyester staple fiber to two classes of domestic buyers, in addition to exporting the same in the international market. One of the category of domestic buyers were those who were having advance licence and the other category without any such licence. The assessee had issued two different price lists. Those buyers who had advance licence but agreed to surrender the said licence, were offered price of Rs. 37.50 per kg. Other category, with no such licence, were sold the goods at Rs. 50 per kg. As per the assessee, it was exporting polyester staple fiber during the relevant period at an average price of Rs. 36 per kg against its own advance licence for exports.

The goods that were cleared as 'deemed exports' to advance licence holders were at a price lower than what was being charged to the other buyers who did not hold an advance licence.

The department alleged that the reason for selling the goods to the aforesaid particular class of buyers at a lesser price was that the assessee had received 'additional consideration' and, therefore, its inclusion was necessitated having regard to the formula provided for arriving at the 'transaction value' contained in the statutory scheme.

On surrender of advance licence with the aforesaid buyers, the assessee could receive drawback from the Government/Director General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) as per the Export-Import (EXIM) Policy and this was stated to be the additional consideration.

The assessee argued that 'additional consideration' under section 4 refers only to the additional consideration flowing from the buyer to the assessee and in the present case no such additional consideration flew from the advance licence buyers of the 'deemed exports'.

The assessee was engaged in manufacture of texturised Polyster filament yarn. It had not taken any Central excise registration. It cleared goods for home consumption as well as exports without payment of excise duty by availing exemption under Notification No. 30/04. The assessee obtained Central excise registration on 9-10-2009 and on 26-10-2009, filed a refund claim of Cenvat credit of inputs used in the manufacture of texturised Polyster filament yarn exported during the period 1-11-2008 to 7-10-2009. The Assistant Commissioner rejected the refund claim on the ground that refund is permissible only if the dutiable goods are exported under bond or LUT and since the assessee was availing full exemption and was not even registered with Central excise, and fully exempted goods were not exported under bond or LUT, the refund was not permissible. The Asst. Commissioner further observed that as the assessee was not registered with Central excise, therefore, it was not eligible for taking the Cenvat credit and hence question of refund did not arise. It was further held that as the assessee was registered only on 9-10-2009 in view of rule 3(2), it was eligible for only transitional Cenvat credit from 9-10-2010 on the inputs and inputs contained in final products in stock as on 9-10-2010.

On appeal:
The issue is whether proforma credit can be availed of by the manufacturers in terms of Notfn. No. 95/79-CE on inputs even if the end product (tyres) listed is liable to nil rate of duly.

The appellants imported 930 MT of polyester chips falling under CTA H. 39.01/06 from Yugoslavia. The goods were warehoused at Kota and were cleared against 10 Ex-Bond Bills of Entry during the period 30.11.1985 to 17.2.1986. The appellants filed a refund claim for Rs. 29,46,143.81 on the ground that goods being polyester resins, the basic duty of customs leviable was only 75% in terms of Notification No. 36/83-Cus. dated 1.3.1983 (as amended) as against 100% levied on the goods. The claim was rejected by the Asstt. Collector on the ground that 'polyester chips' had been specifically excluded from the purview of Notification No. 36/83-Cus. This order was confirmed by the Collector (Appeals). The assessee argued that, during the period of dispute, Menthol Crystals BP/USP and Menthol BP/USP were being exported out of India under bond in terms of rule 19 of the Central Excise Rules, and, therefore, in terms of the provisions of rule 6(6)(v) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, they were eligible for the input duty credit.

When final products became fully and unconditionally exempt from duty, there was no question of their export under bond.

In terms of the provisions of rule 11 (3) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 assessee was required to reverse the Cenvat credit involved on the cenvated inputs lying in stock, cenvated inputs in process and cenvated inputs contained in finished product lying in stock as on 1-3-2008 and the balance amount of Cenvat credit, if any left, would lapse.

Even if the final product -Menthol Crystals BP/USP and Menthol BP/USP had been exported out of India, the provisions of rule 6(6)(v) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 would not be attracted and the assessee would not be entitled for Cenvat credit in respect of inputs, as the final products were fully exempt from duty and there is no question of their export under bond without payment of duty or under letter of undertaking in terms of the provisions of rule 19 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 read with Notification No. 42/01-CE (NT), dated 26-6-2001.

Entire inputs were put into processing to manufacture Menthol Crystals BP/USP and Menthol BP/USP, both exempt absolutely and unconditionally w.e.f. 1-3-2008, and just because in course of processing of the raw menthol for manufacture of menthol crystals BP/USP and Menthol BP/USP, some residual oil is obtained which on further processing is converted into flavouring materials which are dutiable, it cannot be said that the provisions of rule 11(3) read with rule 6 (1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 would not be applicable.

held.text:
Total set-off of duty paid on ethylene glycol used in the manufacture of polyester fibre must be allowed even if some part of it is contained in the methanol which is a by-product of the chemical reaction during manufacture. Since the formation of methanol cannot be prevented by using less ethylene glycol, it is obvious that the final product is polyester fibre, not methanol. ".....it is clear that the Tribunal should have held that even though a part of the ethylene glycol was contained in the by-product methanol, yet the credit of duty could not be reduced to the extent of the ethylene glycol contained in the methanol as ineligible. ......ethylene glycol was used in the manufacture of polyester fibre. It appears that methanol arises as a part and parcel of the chemical reaction during the process of manufacture when ethylene glycol interacts with DMT to produce polyester fibre. It is not possible to use a lesser quantum of the ethylene glycol to prevent methanol from arising for producing a certain quantity of polyester fibre. Thus, the quantity of ethylene glycol required to produce a certain quantum of polyester fibre is determined by the chemical reaction. It may be mentioned herein that it is not as if the appellants have used excess ethylene glycol wantonly to produce the methanol. It is clear that the appellants are not engaged in the production of methanol but in the production of polyester fibre. That position is undisputed. Therefore, it appears that the Tribunal erred when it held that the appellants were not entitled to a part of the credit of duty since ethylene glycol when it interacts with DMT also gives rise to methanol."

2. Set-off of duty paid on inputs can only be denied if the final product is totally exempt from duty. So credit of duty cannot be denied on non-excisable methanol which arose during the manufacture of dutiable polyester fibre. "....the only situation where the credit of the duty paid on the inputs could be denied was only where the final products were wholly exempt from the duty of excise or chargeable to nil rate of duty. In the present case, the excisable goods, namely, polyester fibre were not wholly exempt from duty nor chargeable to nil rate of duty. It cannot be read in the notification that the notification would not be available in case non-excisable good arise during the course of manufacture. In fact, the Tribunal seems to have erred in not bearing in mind that exemption notification was pressed in service in respect of polyester fibre which is excisable goods and not in respect of methanol which arises as a by-product as a part and parcel of chemical reaction."

3. Trade notice clarifying rule 56A must be considered in interpreting exemption Notfn. 201/79-CE since it is applicable to both. "On an analysis and comparison of aforesaid, it is clear that the clarification in the form of trade notice issued by the Pune Collect prate in respect of rule 56A was as much applicable to that rule as to notification No. 201/79. .....exemption notifications are meant to be implemented and trade notices in these matters clarify the stand of the Government for the trade. It is clear, therefore, that the Tribunal failed to interpret the words of the exemption notification No. 201/79 properly and fully. .....it appears further on a comparison of the rule 56A and the notification No. 201/79 that these deal with the identical situation."

4. Methanol arising during the process of manufacture of polyester fibre through chemical reaction is a product which can be said to be used to its manufacture. "Just because methanol arises as a part and parcel of the chemical reaction during the process of manufacture, it cannot be said that methanol was not used in the manufacture of polyester fibre."

Rule 3 of the 2004 Rules, as also rule 3 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002 [2002 Rules] which have been repealed by the 2004 Rules, provides for credit of Cenvat paid by a manufacturer on any inputs or capital goods received in a factory for use in or in relation to the manufacture of final products. Rule 6(1) of the 2004 Rules as also the 2002 Rules, says that Cenvat credit shall not be allowed on such quantity of input which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods. Sub-rule (5) of rule 6 of the 2002 Rules, and sub-rule (6) of rule 6 of the 2004 Rules are an exception to rule 6(1). Sub-rule (5)(vi ) of the 2002 Rules, provided that sub-rules (1), (2), (3) and (4) shall not be applicable in case of exempted goods, which are cleared for export under bond, in terms of provisions of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. [Para 9]

Rule 6(6)(v) of the 2004 Rules provides that the provisions of sub-rules (1), (2), (3) and (4) of rule 6, shall not be applicable in case the excisable goods removed without payment of duty are cleared for export under bond in terms of provisions of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. [Para 10]

The only difference between the 2002 Rules and the 2004 Rules is that in case of 2002 Rules, exception clause contained in sub-rule (5) of rule 6 was applicable in case of only exempted goods, whereas exception clause contained in sub-rule (6) of rule 6 of 2004 Rules, applies both to exempted goods, as also goods subject to duty, because the term used in sub-rule (6) is ‘excisable goods’ and not ‘exempted goods’, as was the case in 2002 Rules. [Para 11]

The scheme of the 2002 Rules as also the 2004 Rules shows that Cenvat credit/refund is allowed on the inputs of all manufactured goods which are not exempt from duty, as is clear from a combined reading of rule 3 and sub-rule (1) of rule 6 of 2002 Rules, as also the 2004 Rules, so as to avoid indirect double taxation on inputs. However, this rule is not absolute. It is subject to exception clause, contained in rule 6(5) of the 2002 Rules and rule 6(6) of the 2004 Rules, and one of the exceptions is in respect of excisable goods, which are cleared for export under bond in terms of the provisions of Central Excise Rules, 2002. [Para 16]

Sub-rule (5) of rule 6 of the 2002 Rules was applicable only in case of exempted goods. That meant that the exception was not applicable in case of dutiable goods. It appears that this led to anomalous situations. For example, if the goods were dutiable and were exported, credit for Cenvat could not be claimed in respect of input of those goods, at least under the aforesaid exception clause. To overcome this kind of anomalous situation, exception clause contained in sub-rule (6) of rule 6 of 2004 Rules has been made applicable to all excisable goods. [Para 17]

Thus, there was no merit in the submission of the revenue that term ‘excisable goods’ used in sub-rule (6) of rule 6 of 2004 Rules, meant only dutiable goods. [Para 18]

An assessee manufacturing goods chargeable to nil duty, is eligible to avail Cenvat credit of duty paid on the inputs under the exception clause to rule 6, as contained in rule 6(5) of the 2002 Rules and rule 6(6) of the 2004 Rules, used in the manufacture of such goods, if the goods are exported. [Para 20]

Further it is clear from a bare reading of rule 5 of the 2004 Rules that a manufacturer, who exports the final products which are exempt from duty, can claim refund of Cenvat credit. [Para 21]

The Explanation III to rule 6 does not say anything inconsistent with the Cenvat scheme of allowing credit of duty paid on inputs that go into production of goods or services that suffer duty so that there is no cascading effect of goods or services resulting in double taxation. A position that influenced the legislative policy all along is reiterated by expressly denying credit where the final products or services are not subject to tax. The Explanation has been issued for the removal of doubts. The Explanation is in the nature of a clarification and so applies retrospectively. Exceptions to the rule 3 are specified in sub-rule (6) of rule 6. Therefore, an assessee which uses inputs exclusively for the manufacture of exempted goods and services but makes clearances in any manner specified in sub-rule (6) of rule 6 shall be entitled to credit on exclusive inputs used for the production of exempted final products or provision of exempted services. However, in cases not covered by such exceptions, taking of credit on inputs by such assessees shall be irregular in view of the sub-rule (3) of rule 6. Such credit can be recovered along with interest as provided in rule 14. There is no justification to collect 10 per cent of the sale price of exempted goods manufactured using exclusive inputs. There is no legal sanction for such recovery. In the case on hand, sub-rules (1), (2), (3) and (4) of rule 6 shall not be applicable in the case of inputs relatable to excisable goods that are removed without payment of duty either to a hundred per cent EOU or are cleared for export under bond in terms of provisions of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. As regards the credit involved in balance inputs and inputs contained in the finished goods in stock, these demands were premature. The recovery of input credit involved in these cases shall be regulated in the manner indicated, namely, subject to sub-rule (6) of rule 6. [Para 5.2]

In the case of CCE v. Drish Shoes Ltd. [2010] 27 STT 270 the High Court of Himachal Pradesh held that an assessee manufacturing goods chargeable to nil duty is eligible to avail of Cenvat credit paid on the inputs, under the exception clause to rule 6(1) as contained in rule 6(6), used in the manufacture of such goods, if the goods are exported. The High Court relied on a Division Bench’s judgment of the Bombay High Court in Repro India Ltd. v. Union of India 2008 (88) RLT 481 dealing with a similar situation involving entitlement to the Cenvat credit of duty paid on inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods which were exported. [Para 5.3]

The above judgments of the High Courts pertain to exception contained in sub-rule (6) of rule 6 relating to excisable goods removed without payment of duty and cleared for export under a bond in terms of provisions of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. The exception is with reference to sub-clause (v) of rule 6(6). A similar exception applies to excisable goods removed without payment of duty to a 100 per cent Export Oriented Undertaking as per clause (ii) of rule 6(6). Therefore, the impugned order was not sustainable to the extent it confirmed demand of the Cenvat credit relatable to inputs used in the manufacture of excisable goods which were exported or were cleared to a 100 per cent EOU without payment of duty. [Para 5.4]

The impugned order demanded interest on the credit of duty paid on inputs cleared as such. On a conjoint reading of rule 6(1) and rule 14, unless it was shown that the assessee had not used the credit involved and the same had remained an entry in its Cenvat account, the impugned demand of interest was in accordance with law. The dispute relating to the interest was to be remanded for a fresh decision by the Commissioner after verifying the facts. As regards the penalty, it was to be held that the same was not sustainable in view of the fact that the dispute involved provisions now being interpreted. The impugned order was to be set aside. The appeal was to be allowed by way of remand. [Para 5.5]

Wording of rule 56A(1) and (2) read with the proviso attached to sub-(2) clearly shows that specification of excisable goods means specification finished excisable goods for which the credit procedure laid down in sub-rule (sic) attracted. "In our view, the question has to be answered in the light of the express language of rule 56A (1) and (2) read with the proviso attached to sub-rule (2) as held the field at the relevant time ....in the context of the caption to rule 56A (1), it must held that specification of excisable goods would be specification of the finished excisable goods. Once that specification is made under sub-rule (1) of rule 5 procedure of sub-rule (2) would get attracted, as provided by sub-rule (1) of 56A itself Once that eventuality takes place, the entire machinery of sub-rule (2) of rule 56A will be made available for the specified excisable goods in question..... ....When the procedure laid down under sub-rule (2) gets attracted to the specified excisable goods, the entire sub-rule (2) would get attracted and not sub-rule dehors the proviso. On the express language of sub-rule (2) of rule 56A, it must be held that proviso which forms a part and parcel of sub-rule (2) also gets attracted case of special excisable goods, duly notified in the official gazette by the Central Government under sub-rule (1) of rule 56A.......it is sufficient to note that the specified finished excisable goods, procedure of sub-rule (2) alongwith the proviso gets attracted."

2. "No credit rule" applies to finished excisable goods in the manufacture which duty paid inputs mentioned in the later part of the proviso to sub-rule (2) 56A have been used. "Thus, the proviso contemplates no credit rule in connection with the finished excisable goods which are made up of material or component parts, as are dealt with in the later part of the proviso.....a conjoint reading of caption of rule 56A with sub-rule (1) clearly indicates that excisable goods that are to be specified under sub-rule (1) will be those excisable goods which are finished excisable goods and which utilise duty paid material or component parts in their manufacturing process."

3. Proforma credit scheme is a composite, well-knit scheme for the workability of which both inputs and outputs have to be considered comprehensively together. "Further question arises as to how the inputs from which such specified excisable commodity is manufactured are treated by the rule making authority so that the finished excisable commodity produced out of them can earn proforma credit of duty is to be given in connection with the inputs and not the outputs. If the outputs are not specified no further question arises. If they are specified as per rule 56A(1), then the further and more important question will arise as to which inputs can be covered by the scheme of proforma credit procedure. Hence, no scheme of proforma credit is complete without a comprehensive, interconnected and simultaneous consideration of inputs and outputs."

4. Harmonious reading of sub-paras (i) and (ii) and interpretation of the words 'and unless' interconnecting the sub-paras to mean 'and except when' clearly shows that specified finished excisable goods are not entitled to proforma credit benefit if wholly exempt or chargeable to nil rate of duty, "the rule making authority has advisedly employed the words 'and unless' interconnecting sub-paras (i) and (ii) of the proviso which mean 'except when'. When so read, it becomes clear that specified finished excisable goods will not be entitled to the benefit of the proforma credit if (a) they are wholly exempt from excise duty or chargeable to nil rate of duty......Thus a harmonious reading of two sub-paras of the proviso projects the following picture. The specified finished excisable commodity will not get benefit of the proforma if it is wholly exempt from excise duty or chargeable to nil duty. Thus, only those finished excisable goods duly specified under sub-rule (1) of rule 56A will get the benefit of proforma credit, which are exigible to excise duty."

5. Inputs used in the manufacture of specified finished excisable goods must be leviable to duty under the same tariff item as the finished goods or covered by remission or adjustment of duty on inputs sanctioned by the Central Government if they fall under different tariff items. "The inputs which go to manufacture these specified finished excisable goods which bear excise duty must themselves either be exigible to tax under the same tariff item or alternatively even though these inputs are exigible to tax under the different tariff items, then, they must be covered by the specific sanction of the Central Government granting remission or adjustment of duty on these inputs."

Whether construction services used for construction of workers’ quarters within factory premises fell within ambit of input services ?

The definition of ‘input services’ under rule 2(l )(ii) is in two parts : the first part gives the basic definition of ‘input service’ while the second part is an inclusive one that specifically mentions certain services to be included within the ambit of ‘input services’. The basic definition limits the scope of input services to those whose use has a nexus directly or indirectly, in or in relation to manufacture and clearance of final products. In Doypack systems, the phrase ‘in relation to’ has been held to be equivalent to or synonymous with ‘pertaining to’ and ‘concerned with’. The use of the service for construction of workers’ residences cannot be said to pertain to or be concerned, directly or indirectly, with manufacture and clearance. [Para 6]

The second leg of the definition is an inclusive one. The inclusive definition is a well-recognized device to enlarge the meaning of the word defined. It expands the meaning in the basic definition. [Para 7]

In the definition given in rule 2(l )(ii), the inclusive part of the definition expands the scope of ‘input service’ as given in the basic definition by bringing within its ambit, services which would not normally get covered by the main definition: construction and other allied services used for setting up of a factory, for example, have been specifically included, though the use of these services in the setting up of the factory precedes manufacture and the activity is concluded prior to commencement of the manufacturing process. Again, auditing of accounts relating to a final product has been considered to be an ‘input service’ though this service is used after the completion of manufacture of final product and could not have been used directly or indirectly in the manufacturing process. Both the above services, however, have a nexus with and are related to the final product : the setting up of a factory provides the space and machinery for manufacture and auditing ensures proper accounting of the inputs and disposal of the final products. A perusal of the other services in the inclusive part of the definition indicates that use of each of these services is linked to manufacture, storage, transport or sale of the final product. The services of market research, sales promotion and advertising, for example, may not be used in the actual process of manufacture which is necessary for their inclusion in the basic definition of input service, yet they find mention in the inclusive definition as their use does promote sale of the final product. Similar is the case with regard to services used in storage and transportation, accounting, auditing, financing, etc. It is relevant to note here that when the extended definition specifically includes services used for setting up certain buildings, such buildings are restricted to buildings used to house factories and its offices. A manufacturer may construct other types of buildings for its employees such as residential quarters, hospitals, recreation centres, schools, etc. From the nature of the buildings specifically included in the extended definition and the kinds of services included in it, it has to be inferred that construction of only such buildings would be covered as input service which are linked to manufacture, storage, sale, transportation, etc., of the final product. Provision of buildings for housing, schooling, recreation, etc., of workers improves their quality of life and is a welfare measure but they have no nexus with the manufacture, storage or sale of the final products. Even when an extended definition is used, it is necessary to draw a line to exclude categories obviously not intended to be included. A ‘service’ not mentioned in the extended definition has to partake of the characteristics common to the other services specifically mentioned, in order to become an ‘input service’ as per the extended definition. As mentioned above, the common thread running through all the services specifically included in the extended definition is that each of these is linked to manufacture, storage or sale of the final product. Services used for constructing buildings for housing workers and staff, do not have a nexus with the manufacture, sale or storage of the final product and, therefore, such services cannot be considered to be ‘input service’ even as per the extended definition. Therefore, the first question posed for advance ruling was to be answered in the negative. [Para 8]

Rule 11 makes it clear that the Cenvat credit is to be allowed in respect of the inputs, even if the declared inputs are not used directly by the manufacturer of the final products declared in a notification under rule 11 but are contained in the final products. [Para 8]

A plain reading of the Notification No. 6/2002 - CE(NT), dated 1-3-2002 shows that a distinction has been drawn between the composite mills and other than composite mills. The Explanation 2 to clause (6) of the notification makes it clear as to what is meant by a composite mill. It means a manufacturer who is engaged in the processing of fabrics with the aid of power along with the spinning of yarn from the fibres and weaving or knitting or crocheting of fabrics within the same factory, etc. The respondent was not a composite mill. It manufactured its final product-processed fabrics not by spinning of the yarn from fabrics but from grey fabric purchased from the market. The Explanation 3 was also relevant inasmuch as it clarifies that the provisions of the notification would not apply where the processed fabric itself is used as an input for further processing. The consequence of this Explanation and clarification is that if there is any processed fabric and the same is further processed into the final product, namely, processed fabric, the same would not be eligible for the benefit under the said notification. The conclusion as well as the reasoning adopted by the Tribunal were to be agreed with. The Tribunal was of the view that rule 11 empowers the Central Government to declare the inputs on which the duty of excise or additional duty of customs shall be deemed to have been paid at such rate as may be specified in the notification and to allow the Cenvat credit of such duty deemed to have been paid even if the declared inputs are not used directly by the manufacturer of the final products declared in the notification but are contained in the final products. The Tribunal went on to examine the said Notification No. 6/2002 (NT) in the light of rule 11, as also in the light of the clarification given in the circular of 13-3-2003. Thereafter, the Tribunal came to the conclusion that the contention of the revenue was not correct inasmuch as the said Notification No. 6/2002 had been issued under rule 11, which clearly provides that the deemed credit would be available even if the declared inputs are not used directly by the manufacturer of the final products declared in the notification but are contained in the said final products. [Para 11]

In fact, the provisions of rule 11 are very clear. Grey fabrics in the instant case, though not mentioned in the table of inputs referred to in the notification, are comprised of yarn/fibre which are the inputs in respect of the grey fabrics. Grey fabrics are also not processed fabrics and, therefore, are not covered by the Explanation 3 to clause (6) of the said notification. The processed fabrics are the final products containing the yarn/fibre which is the requirement under rule 11. Thus, although the yarn/fibre was contained in the final product yet, it was not directly used by the respondent in its manufacturing process. It came in indirectly, being a constituent of the grey fabric. The requirement of rule 11 stood satisfied. [Para 12]

If the interpretation sought to be given by the revenue was to be accepted then Serial No. 2 of the table in the notification would become redundant, because there would be no non-composite mill which could take the benefit of the notification inasmuch as all the inputs refer only to yarn/fibre and do not include the intermediate product-grey fabric. The very fact that yarn/fibre is mentioned as an input in respect of non-composite mills also makes it clear that the notification is to allow deemed credit in respect of such inputs, although they are not to be used directly by the non-composite mills. Therefore, the issue was to be decided in favour of the assessee. [Para 13]

The appeal was dismissed. [Para 14]

Ahmedabad Manufacturing and Calico Printing Co. Ltd......their dutiability has to be determined on the basis of their form and character after completion of the final carbonisation process."

Modvat--credit is not admissible as no duty leviable on the final product (PSE) cleared by the appellants. "A reading of the various Central Excise Rules and the Scheme of the MODVAT set out therein shows that the facility of MODVAT Credit is available in respect of duty paid on inputs used in or in relation to the manufacture of the specified final product and for utilizing the credit so allowed towards payment of duty of excise leviable on the final product. When, therefore, there is no duty leviable on the final products which have been cleared from the appellants' factory, the question of allowing them the MODVAT Credit on the inputs would not arise. Rule 57C of the Central Excise Rules clearly envisages that no credit of the specified duty paid on the inputs used in the manufacture of a final product shall be allowed if the final product is exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon or is chargeable to nit rate of duty. ...In view of above, we hold that there is no force in the appellants' plea......."

In the instant case, the raw material (POY) which is unsuitable for manufacture of fabric, undergoes texturising which is a thermo mechanical process of stretching, heating, cooling, twisting and untwisting and heating for final setting and with addition of oil it becomes texturised yarn which is a raw material for manufacture of fabric. It also undergoes twisting process by revolving on aluminium bobbins to produce warp yarn for the purpose of weaving. Thus, after the processing, texturised yarn or warp yarn continues to be raw material for the manufacture of fabric or weaving of fabric. Even while describing the processing involved in the assessee’s case, it was clear that although the raw material (POY) underwent some change, yet it continued to be the suitable raw material for the manufacture or weaving of fabric. Viewed in this context, the processing did not amount to manufacture at all. The test of manufacture laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Delhi Cloth & General Mills Co. Ltd. AIR 1963 SC 791 clearly showed that even a series of changes brought about by the processes should take the commodity to the point where it was commercially recognized as distinct and new article which had emerged as a result of the processes. Judged from this test of manufacture, the processed yarn continued to be the raw material for the purpose of manufacture of fabric or weaving of fabric.

In this view of the matter. the assessee was not eligible for investment allowance.

The duty paid menthol was used in the manufacture of menthol crystals and peppermint oil emerged as a by-product and both these final products were liable for excise duty under the Central Excise Act, 1944. By a Notification No. 4/2008, dated 1-3-2008, excise duty on menthol (raw materials) as well as menthol crystals was exempted. Thus, with effect from 1-3-2008, excise duty became payable only on peppermint oil (by-product) [Para 19]

Excise duty paid on exported goods either in cash or by debiting the Cenvat credit availed on inputs used in the manufacture of exported goods can be claimed by the exporter as rebate of duty under rule 18 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. In the instant case, the assessee had paid excise duty on the exported peppermint oil by debiting the Cenvat credit availed on menthol used in the manufacture of exempted menthol crystals and dutiable peppermint oil. [Para 20]

Basic argument of the revenue was that, where the duty paid inputs are used in the manufacture of final products which are exempted from payment of excise duty, Cenvat credit on input is not allowable under rule 6(1). In the instant case, it was contended by the revenue that the assessee had neither maintained separate accounts regarding inputs used in the manufacture of exempted/dutiable final products as provided under rule 6(2) nor paid an amount on clearance of exempted menthol crystals as provided under rule 6(3) and, therefore, the assessee could not avail credit of duty paid on menthol (input) and, consequently, the duty paid on peppermint oil by debiting the input credit being not valid the question of allowing rebate of that duty did not arise at all. [Para 21]

It is true that under rule 6(1), credit of duty paid on inputs is not allowable when the inputs are used in the manufacture of exempted final products. But rule 6(2) provides that where the inputs are used in the manufacture of exempted as well as dutiable final products, credit of duty paid on inputs used in the manufacture of dutiable final products is allowable, provided separate accounts regarding the receipt, consumption and inventory of the input used in the manufacture of dutiable final product are maintained. However, rule 6(6) provides that the provisions contained in rule 6(1) to 6(4) shall not apply in certain specified cases, where the excisable goods are cleared without payment of duty. Clause (v) of rule 6(6) provides that where the exempted goods are cleared for export without payment of duty under the Central Excise Rules, 2002, the provisions contained in rule 6(1) to 6(4) shall not apply. Thus, rule 6(6) carves out an exception to the applicability of the provisions contained in rule 6(1) to 6(4) in certain specified cases. [Para 22]

In the instant case, admittedly, the exempted menthol crystals had been cleared for exports under bond without payment of duty and, therefore, the case of the assessee would be covered under rule 6(6)(v) and, consequently, rule 6(1) to 6(4) would not be applicable to the facts of the instant case. In other words, in the instant case, the credit of duty paid on menthol used in the manufacture of exempted menthol crystals was allowable, because, exempted menthol crystals had been exported under bond without payment of duty. [Para 23]

The question then to be considered was, whether excise duty on exported peppermint oil could be paid by debiting Cenvat credit availed on the inputs used in the manufacture of exempted menthol crystals? [Para 24]

Rule 5 specifically provides that where the exempted final product is cleared without payment of duty under bond, the credit of duty paid on input used in the manufacture of the exempted final product shall be allowed to be utilised for payment of duty on any final product by way of adjustment of input credit and where for any reasons such adjustment is not possible, refund of the unutilized input credit would be allowed. [Para 25]

Interpretation of Notification: Words and phrases--The expression 'used in the manufacture' occurring in Notfn. 201/79-CE encompasses any process integrally related to the manufacture of marketable goods (as defined by the Supreme Court); therefore, paper tubes and discs are 'inputs' entitled to set off since without their use the final products cannot be transported or marketed. "We, therefore, have to respectfully take the observation of the Supreme Court into consideration to interpret the expression 'used in the manufacture' occurring in the said notification. In the present case, it has been explained that without the three articles in question, the appellants would not be able to manufacture and to market their goods, namely, rayon tyre yarn, cord etc. The goods have to be wound around the cord and the discs have to be used as stiffeners.......... it is clear that the yarn cannot be transported and marketed without the help of these two articles. ............In the light of the discussion above, and following the ratio of the judgments cited before us, we hold that out of the three articles, for which the appellants claimed credit, two, which have paid duty under Tariff item No. 68, have been used by the appellants in the manufacture of the finished goods and are, therefore, 'inputs' in terms of Notification No. 201/79-CE."

2. Cardboard boxes, in which yarn is packed, are not 'inputs' since yarn is a complete product ready for sale even without being packed in boxes. "The same observation does not, however, apply to the cardboard boxes because even without being packed in the boxes, the yarn, which is wound on the tubes, is a completed product and can be bought and sold. The boxes are necessary only to protect the already manufactured yarn from elements and dirt and to transport the same to the market."

There is no provision for transfer of credit on intermediary products from one unit to another of the same manufacturer. Polyester chips would be covered by entry 'Polyester resins' against Sr. No. 1(iv) of the Table annexed to Notification No. 36/83-Cus., even after its amendment.
