ACCE (2011) 272 ELT 353 (Mad HC DB) [In this case, the assessee had reversed the Cenvat credit on inputs. Why this was done is not clear]. Such rebate is limited to the Cenvat credit on inputs/capital goods - Honda Motorcycles Ltd. In re (2011) 272 ELT 473 (GOI) [In this case, assessee paid excise duty more that the Cenvat availed on purchased goods. It was held that no duty was payable as no manufacturing activity was carried out].

Exempted goods cannot be cleared under bond and Cenvat credit of inputs cannot be availed - Notification No. 42/2001-CE(NT) has been amended w.e.f 26-5-2010 to provide that exempted goods cannot be cleared under bond [In CBE&C circular No. 928/18/2010-CX dated 28-6-2010, it has been stated that assessee should follow procedure under Notification No. 21/2004-CE(NT) dated 6-9-2004 to obtain rebate of duty paid on inputs].

Earlier, in following cases, Tribunal/Court had held that this is permissible.

Exempted goods can also be cleared under bond (besides excisable and non-excisable goods) - Tuffropes v. CCE (2009) 233 ELT 544 (CESTAT) - based on an unreported decision of Bombay High Court in a writ petition - same view in CCE v. Global Pharmatech (2008) 229 ELT 313 (CESTAT SMB) - view confirmed in Repro India v. UOI (2009) 235 ELT 614 (Bom HC DB).

In CCE v. Drish Shoes (2010) 27 STT 270 (HP HC DB), assessee exported goods which were wholly exempt from excise duty. It was held that even then, assessee is entitled to obtain refund of service tax on services specified in rule 6(5), as the term 'excisable goods' is wider than 'exempted goods'.

In Tufropes P Ltd. v. CCE (2009) 238 ELT 106 (CESTAT), it was held that exempted goods can be exported under bond and in such case, Cenvat credit is available inputs used in manufacture of such exempted products, in view of rule 6(5)(vi) of Cenvat Credit Rules - same view in Sandoz v. CCE (2009) 237 ELT 532 (CESTAT) * CC v. Sharp Menthol (2010) 252 ELT 536 (CESTAT SMB) - view confirmed in UOI v. Sharp Menthol India (2011) 31 STT 175 = 10 taxmann.com 190 = 270 ELT 212 (Bom HC DB) * UOI v. Sharp Menthol (India) Ltd. (2015) 50 GST 148 = 55 taxmann.com 117 (SC).

In Punjab Steel Industries v. CCE (2008) 226 ELT 587 = 2008-TIOL-1004 (CESTAT), it has been held that Cenvat credit of inputs used in exempted goods for export is permissible and refund can be claimed under rule 5 - quoted and followed in Sandoz P Ltd. v. CCE (2009) 237 ELT 532 (CESTAT) - same view in Jyoti Overseas v. CCE (2009) 22 STT 527 (CESTAT SMB).

Now these decisions are not valid w.e.f. 26-5-2010.

Bond and CT-1 by merchant exporter

18.3-1 Merchant exporter is required to execute a bond so that goods can be cleared by the supplier-manufacturer without payment of duty.

The bond can be executed by merchant-exporter in form B-1. Merchant exporter registered with recognised Export Promotion Council and Star Export Houses do not have to furnish any security/surety while executing bond, unless they have come to adverse notice of department. - CBE&C circular No. 613/4/2001-CX dated 31-1-2002, confirmed in CBE&C circular No. 711/27/2003-CX dated 30-4-2003. - - - If bond is executed by merchant exporter, he will obtain certificates in form CT-1 from Superintendent of Central Excise.

The exporter shall ensure that debit in bond does not exceed the credit available in the bond any time. Goods can be cleared by manufacturer on the strength of this certificate, without payment of duty. Forms of bond, letter of undertaking and CT-1 certificate have been given in Notification No. 42/2001-CE(NT). If export is through merchant exporter, ARE-1 form should be signed both by manufacturer as well as merchant exporter.

What about those who did not reverse in GSTR-3B in case of inverted duty structure on textile products w.e.f. 1-8-2018? - The clarification above applies to registered persons who have already reversed the ITC required to be lapsed in terms of the said notification through return in FORM GSTR-3B. What about those registered persons who are yet to perform this reversal? Clarification - All those registered persons required to make the reversal in terms of the said notification and who have not yet done so, may reverse the said amount through FORM GST DRC-03 instead of through FORM GSTR-3B - Sr. No. 2 of para 57 of CBI&C Circular No. 125/44/2019-GST dated 18-11-2019.

9.21-1 Consequences if credit to be lapsed on textile products reversed after August 2018?

What shall be the consequence if any registered person reverses the amount of credit to be lapsed, in terms the said notification, through the return in FORM GSTR-3B for any month subsequent to August, 2018 or through FORM GST DRC-03 subsequent to the due date of filing of the return in FORM GSTR-3B for the month of August, 2018?

Clarification - (a) As the registered person has reversed the amount of credit to be lapsed in the return in FORM GSTR-3B for a month subsequent to the month of August, 2018 or through FORM GST DRC-03 subsequent to the due date of filing of the return in FORM GSTR-3B for the month of August, 2018, he shall be liable to pay interest under section 50(1) of the CGST Act on the amount which has been reversed belatedly. Such interest shall be calculated starting from the due date of filing of return in FORM GSTR-3B for the month of August, 2018 till the date of reversal of said amount through FORM GSTR-3B or through FORM GST DRC-03, as the case may be. (b) The registered person who has reversed the amount of credit to be lapsed in the return in FORM GSTR-3B for any month subsequent to August, 2018 or through FORM GST DRC-03 subsequent to the due date of filing of the return in FORM GSTR-3B for the month of August, 2018 would remain eligible to claim refund of unutilized ITC on account of accumulation due to inverted tax structure w.e.f. 01.08.2018. However, such refund shall be granted only after the reversal of the amount of credit to be lapsed, either through FORM GSTR-3B or FORM GST DRC-03, along with payment of interest, as applicable - Sr. No. 3 of para 57 of CBI&C Circular No. 125/44/2019-GST dated 18-11-2019.

9.21-2 Imitation Zari - No Refund of ITC of GST paid on polyester film/plastic film w.e.f. 20-10-2023

In case of Imitation zari thread or yarn made out of metallised polyester film/plastic film falling under heading 5605, refund of ITC of polyester film/plastic film will not be available w.e.f. 20-10-2023 - Sr. No. 6AA of Notification Nos. 5/2017-CT (Rate) and 5/2017-IT (Rate) both dated 28-6-2017 inserted w.e.f. 20-10-2023.

Imitation zari threat or yarn threat falls under heading 5605 and GST rate is 5% - CBIC circular No. 205/17/2023-GST, dated 31-10-2023.

If unbranded goods are cleared independently and not along with branded goods, SSI exemption is available for unbranded goods. - CCE v. Cipra Plastics 2001(130) ELT 813 (CEGAT). Same provision applies for calculating limit of Rs. 150 lakhs. However, goods manufactured in rural area under other's brand name will have to be included for calculating the limit of Rs 150/400 lakhs, as these are exempt from duty upto first Rs 150 lakhs - view prima facie held as correct in Chamundi Foods v. CCE 2006 (201) ELT 361 (CESTAT) and Chamundi Foods v. CCE 2007 (212) ELT 424 (CESTAT) - contrary view in CCE v. Shanti Industries (2008) 232 ELT 363 (CESTAT), where it was held that goods manufactured in rural area (whether branded or unbranded) is exempt and hence is not required to be considered for calculation of SSI exemption limit [seems arguable case].

In Nebulae Health Care v. CC (2007) 209 ELT 125 (CESTAT), it was held that if a manufacturer manufactures goods under brand name of others and also own products, he can avail Cenvat credit in respect of branded products and avail SSI exemption in respect of own products - view confirmed in CCE v. Nebulae Health Care (2015) 52 GST 621 = 62 taxmann.com 29 = 325 ELT 431 (SC).

[In CCE v. Ramesh Food Products 2004 (174) ELT 310 (SC), it was held that simultaneous availment of Cenvat credit on some products and exemption on some other products is not permissible. However, in that case, the issue was different].

Branded Goods manufactured under loan license and cleared on payment of duty - In Tanmed Pharmaceuticals v. CCE 2005 (190) ELT 190 (CESTAT), it has been held that clearances of goods manufactured under loan license with brand name of others, and cleared on payment of full duty, is not required to be included for purpose of SSI exemption limit - relying on CCE v. Medopharm 2004 (175) ELT 754 (CESTAT) - same view in Omega Pharmaceuticals v. CCE 2006 (196) ELT 332 (CESTAT) * Hema Laboratories v. CCE (2010) 256 ELT 255 (CESTAT).

If H form is submitted, it is acceptable as proof of export. Value of such exports is not required to be considered for purpose of SSI exemption - Pioneer Magnesia Works v. CCE (2010) 251 ELT 316 (CESTAT).

Intermediate products/captive consumption when final product eligible for SSI exemption - Value of intermediate products manufactured while producing final products which are eligible for SSI exemption cannot be considered for calculating limits of Rs. 400 lakhs, if both intermediate product and final product are eligible for SSI concession [Same provision for calculating limit of Rs. 150 lakhs].

Goods captively consumed by SSI unit for manufacture of specified final products are exempt from duty - confirmed in CCE v. Jalaram Wood Crafts 2003 AIR SCW 1860 * Ramuka v. CCE 2000(117) ELT 44 (CEGAT) * Lohia Sheet Products v. CCE 2000(118) ELT 372 (CEGAT). Value of captively consumed parts is not to be included for calculating aggregate value of clearances. - CCE v. S A Ivy Pumps (2001) 138 ELT 333 (CEGAT) * Cholomandal Marine v. CCE (2007) 211 ELT 496 (CESTAT) * CCE v. Lakshmi Light Metal Industries (2014) 300 ELT 403 (CESTAT).

Job work amounting to manufacture done under specified notifications to be excluded - Job work which amounts to manufacture will be excluded while calculating exemption limit of Rs. 400 lakhs, only if such job work is done under specified notifications. These notifications are - No. 214/86-CE, 83/94-CE or 84/94-CE. [SSI exemption notifications amended w.e.f. 11-8-2003] This turnover will be excluded for calculating exemption limit of Rs. 150 lakhs also. - confirmed in Moon Chemicals v. CCE (2009) 240 ELT 688 (CESTAT SMB) - following Moon Chemicals v. CCE (2007) 215 ELT 434 (CESTAT).

In CCE v. Midas Pre-Cured Tread (2009) 236 ELT 26 (Ker HC DB), it has been held that this amendment is with prospective effect and has no retrospective effect - same view in CCE v. Mustangs Rubbers (2009) 237 ELT 257 (Ker HC DB).

(2015) 49 GST 519 = 53 taxmann.com 350 (SC). In this case, assessee was manufacturing plastic pouches which were exempt from duty. For manufacturing plastic pouches, assessee was manufacturing plastic film as intermediate product, which was dutiable. It was confirmed that when final product is exempt from excise duty, it cannot be termed as 'specified goods'. Hence, value of intermediate product is includible for calculating limit of Rs 150 lakhs. [Earlier, in Universal Electrical v. CCE (2001) 70 ELT 279 (CEGAT), CCE v. Gadgets India (1994) 71 ELT 835 (CEGAT) [View confirmed in CCE v. Universal Electrical Industries 2003 AIR SCW 1929 = 153 ELT 266 (SC) and CCE v. Jalaram Wood Crafts 2003 AIR SCW 1860], Vindhyachal Process v. CCE (2001) 136 ELT 1382 (CEGAT) etc. it was held that even in such case, the intermediate product is not includible. However, now, the SSI exemption notification has been amended and as per annexure to the notification, 'goods chargeable to nil rate or exempt from whole of duty' are not 'specified goods'. (Now, w.e.f. 1-3-2006, this annexure has been changed but second proviso has been added to notification No. 8/2003-CE, which clarifies that the exemption as contained in SSI exemption notification is not applicable to goods which are chargeable to nil rate of duty or are exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon). Hence, these decisions are now not valid. SC had admitted departmental appeal in case of Vindhyachal Process, but departmental appeal has been dismissed - 167 ELT A98, may be because the issue was not properly presented].

Export to Bhutan- - Export to Bhutan will have to be included for calculating exemption limit of Rs 400 lakhs. This turnover is includible even if export is without payment of duty under international contract [same provision applies for calculation of limit of Rs 150 lakhs] - confirmed in R&D Engineers v. CCE (2007) 210 ELT 715 (CESTAT SMB). [Till 1-3-2016, even exports to Nepal were includible]

Export to Nepal will be treated as normal export w.e.f. 1-3-2012. However, the SSI notification was not amended. Now, Nepal has been excluded from definition of 'clearance for home consumption' w.e.f. 1-3-2016. Thus, only export to Bhutan will be considered for calculating limit of turnover i.e. export to Bhutan will be treated as 'clearance for home consumption'. Export to Nepal will not be considered for calculating the limit of Rs 150 lakhs.

However, in Ketan Pottery Works v. UOI (2016) 54 GST 301 = 66 taxmann.com 259 (Guj HC), it has been held that Nepal turnover would be treated at par with other exports w.e.f. 1-3-2012 and would not be considered for calculating turnover limit of Rs. 400 lakhs, in view of revision in Indo-Nepal treaty. Continuance of reference to 'Nepal' in the SSI exemption notification after 1-3-2012 is unconstitutional as it is discriminatory.

Goods manufactured to be included even if later rejected and returned - In Orex Pharma P Ltd. v. CCE 2003 (154) ELT 425 (CEGAT), assessee manufactured certain goods and cleared the same. These were rejected and returned. It was held that this turnover cannot be excluded for calculating limit of Rs. 400 lakhs as subsequent return does not have effect of nullifying the earlier clearances. [same provision for Rs. 150 lakhs also].

Goods cleared with payment of duty - Goods cleared with payment of duty are also to be included while calculating SSI exemption limit - Kinjal Electricals v. CCE (2004) 169 ELT 246 (CESTAT).

In U V Laboratories v. CCE (2012) 276 ELT 266 (CESTAT), assessee paid duty on some goods (manufactured on loan license basis) and claimed SSI exemption on other goods. It was held that value of both the goods should be clubbed for computing clearances for SSI exemption.

[Same provision applies for calculation of limit of Rs 150 lakhs].

Sometimes, a manufacturer wants to avail Cenvat on some products and exemption on some other products - e.g. he may be manufacturing some articles where buyers require Cenvat while some other products where buyer does not want to avail Cenvat. This is permissible only where assessee is manufacturing goods under brand name of others as well as other goods. Exemption to be availed for all factories if assessee? - If a manufacturer has more than one factories, he has to avail the option in respect of all factories. He cannot opt to avail Cenvat in respect of one factory and avail SSI exemption in respect of other factory, as the slab-wise exemption is for all factories of manufacturer together. - CBE&C Circular No. 172/6/96-CX dated 6-2-1996. - view upheld in CCE v. Janardan Plywood (2015) 52 GST 418 = 61 taxmann.com 44 = 323 ELT 46 (Uttara HC DB).

However, this view has not been accepted by tribunal.

In Polylinks P Ltd. v. CCE 2004 (165) ELT 335 (CESTAT), it was held that assessee can avail SSI exemption in respect of goods manufactured in one unit and not avail SSI exemption in another unit - relying on CCE v. Munjal Gases 2003(156) ELT 1006 = 55 RLT 402 (CEGAT) - followed in Ceear Electronics v. CCE 2005 (187) ELT 229 (CESTAT) - same view in CCE v. Kingslay Industries (2005) 187 ELT 171 (CESTAT) - departmental appeal admitted for hearing by SC - 218 ELT A70.

In CCE v. Sagar Chlorate (2009) 235 ELT 478 (CESTAT), assessee paid normal rate of duty in respect of one unit while availing concessional rate in respect of other unit. It was held that this is permissible and there is no short payment of duty (as in fact, he had paid excess duty).

In CCE v. Innovative Teck Pack (2008) 224 ELT 340 (SC), assessee took Cenvat credit in one factory and paid duty while in other factory, he did not avail Cenvat credit and did not pay duty on same product. It was held that this is permissible.

[In view of aforesaid decision of SC, the decision in CCE v. Ramesh Food Products 2004 (174) ELT 310 (SC) will not apply in such cases].

Contrary view has been held in CCE v. Wonderpack Industries (2010) 260 ELT 289 (CESTAT) [In this case, assessee did not appear before Tribunal and not a single case law has been discussed in the decision].

SSI unit can avail Cenvat on inputs used in exported products - SSI unit can opt not to avail Cenvat credit on goods sold for home consumption. However, the unit can avail Cenvat on inputs used for exported final products. He has to maintain separate accounts right from raw material stage to final production of export production as well as for home consumption. Drawback Rules, 2017 - Section 75(2) of Customs Act (and Section 37 of Central Excise Act in case of products covered under Central Excise even after 1-7-2017) allows Central Government to frame rules for purpose of the Act. Under these powers, 'Customs and Central Excise Duties Drawback Rules, 2017' have been notified w.e.f. 1-10-2017. No RCMC required for post export remission schemes like duty drawback, RoDTEP, RoSCTL- Schemes such as Duty Drawback, Rebate of State and Central Taxes and Levies (RoSCTL), and Remission of Duties and Taxes on Export Products (RoDTEP) fall under the category of remission-based schemes. These schemes are aimed at remitting duties or taxes on exported goods. For these remission-based schemes, the requirement of an RCMC (Registration-Cum-Membership Certificate) does not apply. Exporters can claim benefits under these schemes without obtaining an RCMC - DGFT trade notice No. 19/2024-25 dated 4-10-2024.

58.1-1 Drawback of customs duty paid on input goods

As per rule 2(a) of Customs and Central Excise Duties Drawback Rules, 2017, Drawback, in relation to any goods manufactured in India and exported, means the rebate of duty excluding IGST and Compensation Cess, chargeable on any imported materials or excisable materials used or taxable services used as input services in manufacture of such goods [The words in italics inserted in 2017 Rules]

Rebate of safeguard duty paid on inputs if final product is exported - If inputs on which safeguard duty has been paid are actually used for manufacture of final product which is exported, the exporter can claim rebate of safeguard duty paid on inputs. This is because the All India duty drawback rates do not include incidence of safeguard duty - MF(DR) circular No. 23/2015-Cus dated 29-9-2015.

Countervailing duty on subsidized article not considered in duty drawback rate - Countervailing duty on subsidized article levied under section 9 of Customs Tariff Act is not considered in All Industry duty drawback rate. However, its drawback is available. Hence, inputs on which these duties are paid are used in manufacture of exported goods, the duty is eligible for duty drawback under brand rate. If the imported goods are exported as such, its refund is permissible under section 74 of Customs Act - MF(DR) circular No. 49/2017-Cus dated 12-12-2017.

Meaning of 'manufacture' - 'Manufacture' includes processing of or any other operation carried out on such goods, and the term 'manufacturer' shall be construed accordingly [rule 2(e) of Customs and Central Excise Duties Drawback Rules, 2017].

The definition is very wide. Simple processing will be eligible for 'drawback'.

What is 'export' for purpose of duty drawback - 'Export' means (a) taking out of India to a place outside India or (b) taking out from a place in Domestic Tariff Area (DTA) to a Special Economic Zone (SEZ) and (c) including loading of provisions or store or equipment for use on board a vessel or aircraft proceeding to a foreign port. [Rule 2(c) Customs and Central Excise Duties Drawback Rules, 2017].

Thus, duty drawback is available not only on physical exports but also in case of goods supplied to SEZ or to store or equipment supplied to aircraft/vessel going abroad.

Processing also eligible for Drawback - Drawback is allowable if any manufacture, process or any operation is carried out in India [section 75(1) of Customs Act]. Thus, drawback is available not only on manufacture, but also on processing and job work, where goods may not change its identity and no 'manufacture' has taken place.

58.1-2 Drawback - When not eligible

Section 75 of Customs Act, 1962 provide some disallowances or cases when drawback allowed can be recovered. Further, section 76(2) of Customs Act, 1962 authorises Central Government to issue notifications prohibiting drawback if the goods are likely to be smuggled back to India after export. Drawback Rules, 2017 also provide for some disallowances. These are summarised below :

If sale proceeds of export goods are not received within time stipulated by RBI

If no customs is paid on the inputs

If imported inputs were obtained under Advance Authorisation without payment of duty

If importer avails DFIA

Goods manufactured under Customs Bond where inputs were obtained without payment of duty

Goods manufactured by EOU or a unit in Special Economic Zone (as they obtain inputs without payment of duty)

In case of negative value addition - i.e. selling price of exported goods is less than value of imported goods i.e. foreign exchange spent on import of raw material is more than FOB Value of exports.

Jute batching oil used in manufacture of jute yarn, twist, twine etc.

Packing materials used in relation to export of jute yarn, jute fabrics and jute manufacture.

UTILISATION OF CENVAT CREDIT IN RESPECT OF INPUTS ON WHICH CREDIT IS AVAILED BUT THE INPUTS ARE EXPORTED AS SUCH UNDER BOND

It has been represented to the Board that the field formations have taken a view that credit on inputs cleared as such for export under bond cannot be allowed to be utilised for payment of duty on final products cleared for home consumption nor can it be refunded in cash. In this regard, it has been stated that aforesaid facilities are available where inputs are used in the manufacture of export products and not in the case where inputs have themselves been exported. This doubt has arisen on account of the proviso to rule 57F(4) according to which duty availed on inputs used in the manufacture of final product exported under bond could be utilised towards payment of duty on goods cleared for home consumption or refunded in cash.

2. The matter has been examined by the Board.

3. Rule 57A(1) provides for the general scheme of MODVAT given in section V(AA) of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 and it indeed mentions that credit of duty will be allowed for utilising towards payment of duty of excise leviable on the final products. Whereas rule 57F is a more specific provision regarding manner of utilisation of the inputs and the manner of utilisation of the credit allowed in respect of duty paid thereon. Rule 57F(1)(ii) permits removal of the inputs as such for export under bond. Proviso to rule 57F(4) deals with manner of utilisation of credit in cases of export of 'final products' or 'intermediate products' under bond. Export of inputs as such under bond were treated as 'final product' by virtue of 'deemed manufacture' clause (i.e., the expression as if such inputs have been manufactured in the same factory) under the erstwhile rule 57F(1)(ii) which covered all such cases within the ambit of proviso to rule 57F(4). This expression was omitted by Notification No. 28/95-C.E.(N.T.), dated 29-6-1995 with a view to simplify the clearance procedure, which has created a doubt in respect of utilisation of credit in such cases. It is not the intention of the Government to debar such manufacturer-exporters from utilising credit. Clearance of inputs as such for export under bond can still be treated at par with 'final product' and the manner of utilisation of credit in such cases will be governed by the provisions of the proviso to rule 57F(4).

4. It is also observed that in case such inputs are cleared on payment of duty by debit in RG-23A Part II account by virtue of rule 57F(4)(iii), the manufacturer will be entitled for rebate under rule 12(1)(a) of the Central Excise Rules. He is however, put to disadvantage if he opts for export under bond procedure.The exports under 'claim of rebate' and 'export under bond' should be at parity, since, intention of both the procedures is to make duty incidence 'nil'. It is also an established principle that rules should be interpreted in a manner which do not render them redundant.

5. Accordingly, it is clarified that the Modvat credit in RG-23A Part II account against the export of inputs as such under bond can be utilised in the same manner as is provided for a final product under proviso to rule 57F(4). Obviously, it follows from this that such inputs should be allowed to be exported under bond without any reversal of the credit.

Hence, duty is payable as if they are removed as waste and scrap - same view in CCE v. Crompton Greaves 2004 (174) ELT 231 (CESTAT), in respect of cut sheets arising in manufacture of electrical stamping and laminations.

Removal of waste lubricating oil after use is not removal 'as such' - Nahar Spinning Mills v. CCE (2010) 256 ELT 92 (CESTAT).

Such removal does not affect SSI concession - Small scale industries are exempt from duty upto prescribed turnover. Board has clarified that if inputs are cleared as such on payment of 'amount', such sale will not be considered for calculating SSI exemption limit. This is correct, as the clearance is not of 'manufactured goods'.

Inputs received cannot be sent under CT-3 without reversal of Cenvat credit -EOU notification says that inputs should be obtained under CT-3 directly from the manufacturer of inputs. Issue is, can a manufacturer who has received inputs and has taken Cenvat credit on them clear the same to EOU unit under CT-3 certificate without reversal of Cenvat credit? (Obviously, he is not manufacturer of those inputs).

CCE (2016) 334 ELT 107 (CESTAT).

If input becomes waste during manufacture, Cenvat credit is not required to be reversed - Foil Pack India v. CCE (2007) 216 ELT 616 (CESTAT) * Monika Electronics v. CCE (2006) 204 ELT 468 (CESTAT SMB) * Titan Industries v. CCE (2009) 237 ELT 730 (CESTAT). In Kirloskar Electric Co. v. CCE 2002(144) ELT 647 (CEGAT), it was held that if sheets are cut to requisite length and left over portion of sheets are cleared, it cannot be said that inputs are removed 'as such'. Hence, duty is payable as if they are removed as waste and scrap - same view in CCE v. Crompton Greaves 2004 (174) ELT 231 (CESTAT), in respect of cut sheets arising in manufacture of electrical stamping and laminations.

Removal of waste lubricating oil after use is not removal 'as such' - Nahar Spinning Mills v. CCE (2010) 256 ELT 92 (CESTAT).

Such removal does not affect SSI concession - Small scale industries are exempt from duty upto turnover of Rs. 100 lakhs. Concessional duty is payable from Rs. 50 lakhs to Rs. 100 lakhs. Board has clarified that if inputs are cleared as such on payment of 'amount', such sale will not be considered for calculating limit of Rs. 100 or Rs. 300 lakhs. This is correct, as the clearance is not of 'manufactured goods'.

Inputs received cannot be sent under CT-3 without reversal of Cenvat credit - EOU notification says that inputs should be obtained under CT-3 directly from the manufacturer of inputs. Issue is, can a manufacturer who has received inputs and has taken Cenvat credit on them clear the same to EOU unit under CT-3 certificate without reversal of Cenvat credit? (Obviously, he is not manufacturer of those inputs).

There were contrary decisions. Finally, in Lakshmi Automatic Loom Works v. CCE (2008) 232 ELT 428 (CESTAT 3 member bench), it has been held that he cannot do so. Procurement under CT-3 is permissible only if inputs are procured directly from the manufacturer of those inputs.

In Lakshmi Machine Works v. CCE (2005) 184 ELT 61 (CESTAT) also, it was held that he cannot do so and hence he has to reverse Cenvat of duty taken by him on his inputs [This decision has been stayed by Madras High Court - 196 ELT 325].

Earlier, in Lakshmi Synthetic Machinery v. CCE (2005) 184 ELT 109 (CESTAT), it was held that he can do so and he need not reverse Cenvat credit taken on the inputs - same view in Ghardia Chemicals v. CCE 2006 (196) ELT 325 (CESTAT) * Resil Chemicals v. CCE (2009) 241 ELT 132 (CESTAT SMB). Now these decisions stand overruled.

In view of contrary decisions, in Lakshmi Machine Works v. CCE (2009) 236 ELT 550 (CESTAT), the issue was referred to large bench.

Sale of factory does not mean removal of inputs and capital goods - In Metzeller Automotive v. 9.6

Zero rated transactions and exempted transactions

Concept of 'zero rated' transaction and 'exempt' transaction has been incorporated in rule 6(6) and 6(7) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

Certain final products and output services are 'zero rated' i.e. tax is not payable on final product in certain specified circumstances. However, credit will be available on the inputs and input services i.e. credit will not have to be reversed.

Distinction between 'zero rated transaction' and 'exempt transaction' is that in case of 'zero rated transaction', credit is available on tax paid on inputs and inputs and services, while in case of exempt transactions, credit of tax paid on inputs and input services is not available.

9.6-1 Supply to EOU/SEZ, export of goods, deemed exports or gold manufacture, supply of ethanol are 'zero rated'

Rule 6(6) of Cenvat Credit Rule states that provisions of rule 6(1), 6(2), 6(3) and 6(4) are not applicable , if excisable final product is despatched without payment of duty, in following cases —

(a)

Final product is despatched to SEZ unit, EOU, EHTP or STP and to SEZ developer for their authorised operations (Actually, supply to SEZ is 'export' and not 'deemed export') [The words 'SEZ Developer for their authorised operations' were added w.e.f. 31-12-2008] [Rules 6(6)(i), 6(6)(ii) and 6(6)(iii) of Cenvat Credit Rules]

(b)

Final product is supplied to United Nations or an international organisation for their official use or supplied to projects funded by them, which are exempt from duty [Rule 6(6)(iv) of Cenvat Credit Rules]

(c)

Goods supplied for use of foreign diplomatic missions or consular missions or career counselling offices or diplomatic agents in terms of Notification No. 12/2012-CE dated 17-3-2012 [Rule 6(6)(iva) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-7-2010] (earlier Notification No. 6/2006-CE dated 1-3-2006,)

(d)

When final product is exported under bond without payment of duty [Rule 6(6)(v) of Cenvat Credit Rules]

(e)

Gold or silver falling within Chapter 71, arising in course of manufacture of copper or zinc by smelting [Rule 6(6)(vi) of Cenvat Credit Rules]

(f)

Goods supplied against International Competitive Bidding or power project from which power supply has been tied up through tariff based competitive bidding or to a power project awarded to a deve-loper through tariff based competitive biddings in terms of Notification No. 12/2012-CE dated 17-3-2012, if such goods are exempt from customs duty when imported in India [Rules 6(6)(vii) of Cenvat Credit Rules] (earlier Notification No. 6/2006-CE dated 1-3-2006)

(g)

Supplies made for setting up of solar power generation projects or facilities [Rule 6(6)(viii) of Cenvat Credit Rules, inserted w.e.f. 8-5-2012]

(h)

Clearance of ethanol without payment of excise duty, produced from molasses generated from cane crushed in sugar season in 2015-16, for supply to public sector oil companies for blending with petrol [The clause was added w.e.f. 7-10-2015]

In such case, assessee need not reverse Cenvat credit or pay any 'amount'.

9.6-2 Exports are 'zero rated' - No Cenvat reversal exported

As per rule 5 of Cenvat Credit Rules, if the final products are exported, the Cenvat credit is not required to be reversed. Assessee can utilise credit for payment of duty on other products. If this is not possible, he can get refund.

As per rule 6(6)(v) of Cenvat Credit Rules, rule 6(1) to 6(4) are not applicable to goods exported under bond.

If final product is exported, Cenvat credit cannot be denied - CCE v. VVF Ltd. (2006) 195 ELT 57 (CESTAT).

Metallic Yarn

The metallic yarn is manufactured from polyester films. They are dyed permanently with silver and golden colour and the film are then made in very thin and fine fibre in the form of threads. It is not made by spinning. The metallic yarn is not a yarn but it is only a fibre. It is not covered under Entry Nos. 33 and 33-A of the Notification No. 3391/1.7.1962, as amended by Notification No. 902/1.2.1968. [Commissioner of Sales Tax v. Prakash Agencies, 1980 STJ 159 by Allahabad High Court].

Metallic yarn, manufactured from polyester film, made in very thin and fine fabric in thread form is not manufactured by spinning.

Two things are obvious—one that although what is manufactured by the assessee is known as metallic yarn but in fact it is not yarn and it does not satisfy the requirement of yarn. It is further clear that it is not made by spinning.

If it is not yarn, it could not be filature or artificial silk yarn. [Commissioner of Sales Tax v. Memorex Company, 1980 UPTC 905, decided on 13.8.1979 by Allahabad High Court].

EXPORT AND CENTRAL EXCISE

Duty free exports

18.1 Exports are priority of any country.

Goods and services are to be exported, taxes are not to be exported. WTO stipulates free and fair global trade. Giving export incentives will be against principle of fair trade and hence export incentives are not allowed under WTO. However, goods and services can be made free of domestic taxes.

No stoppage of export consignment or stoppage of manufacturing - Exports are vital for our economy. Any stoppage in export consignment means loss of export orders to the exporter and loss of foreign exchange to the country.

Hence, it has been provided that movement of export consignment will not be interrupted and no export consignment shall be withheld for any reason whatsoever by any agency of Central/State Government. In case of any doubt, customs authorities may ask for an undertaking that the export is on sole responsibility of the exporter [para 2.42 of FTP].

No seizure shall be made by any agency so as to disrupt the manufacturing activity and schedule of export goods. In exceptional cases, the concerned agency may seize the stock on basis of prima facie evidence. Such seizure should be lifted within seven days [para 2.42.1 of FTP]

Inputs free of duty for export production - In relation to Central Excise and Customs, following are the concessions/incentives for exports :

(1)

Exemption from duty on final products (or refund of duty paid).

(2)

Exemption/Refund of excise and customs duties paid on inputs.

Exporting units need raw materials without payment of customs/excise duty, to enable them to compete with world market. Government has devised following schemes for this purpose :

(a)

Special Economic Zones at various places where inputs are allowed to be imported without payment of duty and finished goods are exported

(b)

Export Oriented Undertakings (EOU)

(c)

Permission to avail Cenvat on inputs for other similar products

(d)

Refund of duty on inputs if Cenvat credit cannot be used

(e)

Duty Drawback Scheme

(f)

Schemes of Advance License, DEPB and DFRC.

Elaborate procedures have been prescribed for the above, to ensure that the benefits are not misused.

Exports free of duty on finished product - Exports of almost all excise goods except hides, skin and leather and salt and exports to all countries except to Bhutan are exempt from Central Excise Duties. Exports to Bhutan do not qualify for export incentives as payment is received in Indian rupees. As per Rule 2(d) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 'exempted goods' means goods which are exempt from whole of duty of excise leviable thereon and includes goods which are chargeable to 'Nil' rate of duty and goods in respect of which the benefit of an exemption under Notification No. 1/2011-CE, dated the 1st March, 2011 or under entries at serial numbers 67 and 128 of Notification No. 12/2012-CE, dated the 17th March, 2012 is availed

Intermediate products received by unit covered under Cenvat - A manufacturer covered under Cenvat can send his inputs for job work outside the factory. An intermediate product may get produced at the factory of job worker. In such case, the intermediate product can be brought from the factory of job worker without payment of duty, if it is used in manufacture of final product and duty is payable on final product.

Intermediate products used captively for exported goods - Intermediate products manufactured and used within the factory for manufacture of final products are exempt from duty, even if CT-3 certificate is not issued and Central Excise (Removal of Goods at Concessional Rate of Duty for Manufacture of Excisable Goods), Rules [earlier Chapter X] procedure is not followed subject to the condition that documents/records are available with manufacturer that the intermediate goods have been used for export purpose only - CBE&C circular No. 229/63/96-CX dated 8-7-1996, amended vide 303/19/97-CX dated 11-3-1997.

CCE 1995 (77) ELT 350 (CEGAT). Same view in Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd. v. CCE 1995 (79) ELT 111 (CEGAT). In view of this, no duty is payable on intermediate product if final product is cleared for export under bond without payment of duty.

Goods manufactured for defence /Government, etc. - Some goods are exempt from duty if they are supplied to defence, railways, defence stores, Indian Navy, or if manufactured in ordnance factories, mint, prison, mine, Government tool rooms, etc. In such cases, if an intermediate product gets produced while manufacturing final product, such intermediate product is also exempt from duty - Notification No. 83/1992 dated 16-9-92.

Intermediate products manufactured by exempted SSI unit - A small scale unit with turnover less than Rs. 150 lakhs is exempt from duty, if it does not avail Cenvat on inputs. Such SSI unit may manufacture an intermediate product, which is used in manufacture of final product. In such cases, no duty is payable on such intermediate product even if final product is cleared without payment of duty [As clarified in SSI exemption notifications]. In Ramuka v. CCE 2000(117) ELT 44 (CEGAT), it was held that meaning of this explanation is that goods manufactured by SSI and captively consumed are exempt from duty.

However, if final product is fully exempt under any other notification, duty will be payable on intermediate product, or its value will be considered for calculating limit of Rs. 100/400 lakhs. In Super Polyfabriks Ltd. v. CCE 1999(114) ELT 1019 (CEGAT), it was held that if intermediate product manufactured by SSI unit is not eligible for SSI exemption, the unit will have to pay duty on such intermediate product even if final product is eligible for SSI exemption.

Intermediate products used in manufacture of specified final products - In case of some final products as specified in Notification No. 10/1996-CE dated 23-7-1996, intermediate product 'consumed' for manufacture of final product is exempt from duty even if final product is exempt from duty (e.g. some food products falling under chapters 15 and 21, fertilizers, newsprint, artificial limbs, ball point pens).

In Ruchi Soya Industries v. CCE (2008) 221 ELT 87 (CESTAT), it was held that 'Consumption' does not mean the intermediate product should be so used as to lose its identity. It is sufficient if they are present in final product In this case, it was held that HDPE jar/metal containers captively consumed for packing of final product exempted under Notification No. 10/1996-CE are entitled to exemption - same view in Ruchi Soya Industries v. CCE (2008) 221 ELT 569 (CESTAT).

In a further circular No. 19/2005-Cus dated 21-3-2005, it was reiterated that All Industry Rates cannot be denied on the ground that some duty free materials have been used in manufacture. The All Industry Rate cannot be arbitrarily altered in case of individual exporters. The reason is the All industry Rates are fixed on basis of weighted average of consumption of imported/indigenous inputs and have no relation to the actual consumption pattern or actual duty incidence suffered on inputs of a particular exporter or individual consignments exported under drawback claim.

Despite these clear circulars, in Rubfila International Ltd. v. All Industry Rate (AIR) of Duty Drawback allowed even if some non duty paid inputs used - CBIC vide Circular No. 19/2005- Customs, dated 21-3-2005 has clarified that the concept of AIR of duty drawback is that the rates are determined taking into account the average duties paid on the inputs and in determining the rates, the average (weighted average) consumption of imported/indigenous inputs of a representative cross- section of exporters is taken into account. It is not open to the field formations to probe whether certain exempted inputs have been used in the manufacture of the export goods. Thus, AIR cannot be denied on that ground - CBIC Instruction No. 1/2025 dated 28-2-2025.

Upper limit of drawback rate - All Industry Duty drawback rate shall not exceed 33% of market price of export goods - rule 9 of Customs and Central Excise Duties Drawback Rules, 2017.

Value cap - In case of some cases, value cap has been fixed. In such cases, maximum drawback allowable per unit of quantity has been specified (This is to avoid misuse by over-valuation of export goods].

Drawback in case of composite articles - In case of composite articles, rate of drawback applicable to various constituent materials can be extended to composite article according to net content of such articles on the basis of self-declaration to be furnished by exporter. Drawback in case of goods packed as CKD/SKD - If goods are exported in CKD/SKD condition, these will be classifiable as complete and finished products, if the article has essential character of complete or finished article. Hence, goods exported in CKD/SKD/unassembled condition shall be entitled to All industry Rate of Drawback, if there is evidence to substantiate claim that all components/parts constituting complete export product are being exported - MF(DR) circular No. 26/2005-Cus dated 8-6-2005.

Classification of handicraft for duty drawback - Assessing Authority should normally accept certificates issued by Development Commissioner (Handicrafts)/EPCH (Export Promotion Council for Handicrafts). Drawback schedule is aligned with Customs Tariff at 4 digit level but this alignment is not applicable to Artware/Handicraft items. The Artware/Handicraft items should be classified according to the constituent material. However, for drawback purposes, it will be treated as 'Artware/Handicraft' under drawback schedule. In case of composite article, it should be classified as if that constituent material which predominates in it by weight - CBI&C circular No. 3/2010-Cus dated 12-2-2010.

9.10-1 Cenvat credit can be reversed after clearance

The Supreme Court decision in Chandrapur Magnet and other Tribunal were on basis of facts of the case that assessee had reversed Cenvat credit before clearance. However, this does not mean that the provision does not apply if reversal is done after clearance. If assessee has taken Cenvat credit through mistake and reverses after clearance, the principle should apply.

In Hello Minerals Water v. UOI 2004 (174) ELT 422 (All HC DB), it was held that reversal can be even subsequent to clearance of final product — followed in CST v. Amola Holdings (2009) 22 STT 161 = 29 VST 54 (CESTAT) — same view in Luthara Dyg v. CCE (2010) 252 ELT 113 (CESTAT) * CCE v. Diplast Plastics (2010) 257 ELT 397 (P&H HC DB).

In Ruchi Infrastructure v. CCE (2008) 224 ELT 123 (CESTAT), it was held that if Cenvat credit is reversed though later with interest, payment of 10% ‘amount’ is not required — same view in Sri Sarvaraya Sugars v. CCE (2010) 251 ELT 418 (CESTAT) * CCE v. Foram Glazed Tiles (2011) 267 ELT 461 (Guj HC DB).

In Hi-line Pens P Ltd. v. CCE 2003 (158) ELT 168 (CEGAT), it was held that requirement in Cenvat Rules is reversal of credit taken in excess of what is due. Time of reversal is not material for this (i.e. it can be reversed subsequent to removal of final product). In this case, it was held that if Cenvat credit is reversed, 8% ‘amount’ is not payable (now 5%).

If Cenvat credit is reversed with interest, demand is not sustainable — Eurokem Laboratories v. CCE (2008) 226 ELT 397 (CESTAT SMB) [‘with interest’ means assessee must have reversed at a later stage].

However, in Spentex Industries v. CCE (2010) 253 ELT 225 (CESTAT), it has been held that once Cenvat credit is taken by assessee (debited in favour of assessee) with discretion to utilise it at their sweet will, it amounts to utilisation of Cenvat credit, irrespective of its actual utilisation or remaining idle.

In Hind Lamps Ltd. v. CCE (2010) 250 ELT 237 (CESTAT), it was held that reversal should be before clearance. If it is after clearance, payment of ‘amount’ is required.

47.1-3 Advance Authorisation provisions at a glance

Provisions are contained in following Customs Notifications - (a) No. 21/2023-Cus dated 1-4-2023 for physical exports (b) No. 22/2023-Cus dated 1-4-2023 for deemed exports (c) No. 23/2023-Cus dated 1-4-2023 for exports against Advance Authorisation for Annual Requirement (d) No. 24/2023-Cus dated 1-4-2023 for exports of prohibited items (e) No. 27/2023-Cus dated 1-4-2023 for fabrics.

Basic provisions are as follows.

Purpose of the scheme - Purpose of scheme of Advance Authorisation to enable exporter to obtain imported material required to manufacture final product, which will then be exported.

Actual User Condition and no transfer of authorisation and material - Material imported must be actually used for manufacture of final goods. The authorisation and the material cannot be sold or transferred.

Exemption from duties to imported material - Imports of material under Advance Authorisation are exempt from basic customs duty, additional customs duty, IGST, GST Compensation Cess, safeguard duty, Countervailing duty and anti dumping duty. However, imports against advance authorisation for deemed exports are not exempt from IGST and GST Compensation Cess.

Bond if materials imported before discharge of export obligation - if materials are imported before discharge of export obligation., importer shall execute a bond with surety or security, for payment of duty and interest @ 15% if export obligations not fulfilled.

Bond if materials imported after discharge of export obligation - If materials are imported after discharge of export obligation, and if material is cleared without payment of IGST and GST Compensation Cess, the importer shall execute bond that the material will be utilised in his factory or factory of supporting manufacturer. If IGST and GST Compensation Cess is paid at the time of imports, then such bond is not required.

Common bond for various export promotion schemes - Authorisation holders can execute a common bond for imports under three specified schemes i.e. Advance Authorisation, DFIA and EPCG. Facility will be available financial year wise. Form and procedure has been prescribed in MF(DR) circular No. 11(A)/2011-Cus dated 25-2-2011.

Bond jointly with supporting manufacturer if import is by merchant exporter - Bond is required to be jointly executed with supporting manufacturer, if import is by merchant exporter.

Import and export should be from specific ports. ICD or land customs station - Import under advance authorisation should be from specified ports, ICD or land customs only, unless specific permission is obtained - Para 1(ix) of Notification No. 21/2023-Cus dated 1-4-2023.

Material can be sent to job worker - Material imported can be sent to job worker. In Sanvijay Rollong and Engineering v. CC (2013) 287 ELT 33 (Bom HC DB), it was held that goods obtained under Advance Authorisation can be sent to job worker for manufacture and then sold if the export obligation was fulfilled. This is not transfer of imported material.

Defective material can be re-exported - Defective material can be re-exported after proper documentation.

However, in case of other Advance Authorisations, material can be imported even after goods are expected. Even those goods are subject to Actual User Condition.

SION - "SION" means Standard Input Output Norms notified by DGFT - Para 11.54 of FTP 2023. There is provision for self ratification and self declaration of SION.

47.1-4 Difference between Advance Authorisation and DFIA

Purpose of both Advance Authorisation and Duty Free Import Authorisation (DFIA) is to enable import of material without duty for manufacture of final product, which is to be exported. However, there are some distinctions, as below.

ANNEX 9.1

[PARA 9.2-6]

CIRCULAR NO. 754/70/2003-CX, DATED 9-10-2003

AVAILMENT TO CREDIT ON INPUTS USED EXCLUSIVELY FOR THE MANUFACTURE OF EXEMPTED FINISHED GOODS

I am directed to say that Board's attention has been drawn to the availment of credit on inputs falling under Chapters 28 and 29 used exclusively for the manufacture of exempted goods by certain assessees manufacturing finished goods falling under Chapter 30 of Schedule to Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985. It has been reported that these assessees are subsequently reversing an amount @ 8% of the price of the exempted goods under clause (b) of sub-rule (3) of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002.

2. The matter has examined in Board in the context of admissibility of such credit or otherwise. In this connection, your attention is invited to sub-rule (1) of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002 which prescribes that no Cenvat credit shall be allowed on such quantity of inputs which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods. The said sub-rule makes an exception of the circumstances in which such credit on inputs used for the exempted goods can be availed. Sub-rule (2) of the said rule gives an option to the manufacturer to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of inputs meant for use in for the manufacture of exempted and dutiable goods and in case, he does not opt for the separate records, clause (b) of sub-rule (3) requires a manufacturer to pay an amount equal to 8% of the total price of the exempted goods excluding sales tax and other taxes as paid. Thus, it is clear that the option to maintain the separate accounts or payment of 8% of the price of the exempted goods can be exercised only in respect of common inputs used for the manufacture of dutiable and exempted goods. Where any inputs are clearly identifiable as used only in or in relation to the manufacture of final products which are exempt from payment of duty, CENVAT credit is not admissible on such inputs which are used exclusively for the manufacture of exempted final products. The circumstances specified in sub-rule (2), sub-rule (3) do not cover, or envisage availment of credit on inputs used exclusively for the manufacture of exempted final products.

3. It is therefore, clarified that no credit can be taken on inputs which are used exclusively in or in relation to the manufacture of exempted final products. It may also be seen that this position was the same in erstwhile Central Excise Rules, 1944 and there has been no change in this principle. The procedural facility is prescribed to take care of the practical difficulties which may be faced by the manufacturers using the same inputs in both dutiable and exempted final products. Necessary action to recover the credit wrongly availed of, if any, may be taken at your end.

2. The matter has been examined by Board. As per sub-rule (1) of rule 6 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2002, the credit is not available on inputs which are used in the manufacture of exempted goods. North Sun Enterprises (2012) 284 ELT 75 (CESTAT).

In Sterlite Opticals v. CCE (2012) 282 ELT 392 (CESTAT), assessee paid excise duty under bona fide belief that the activity carried out by him is 'manufacture'. He availed Cenvat credit of inputs. The payment of duty was accepted by department. It was held that even if activity is not 'manufacture', it is case of removal of inputs 'as such' and Cenvat credit is reversible. Thus, entire exercise is revenue neutral and demand is not sustainable.

In one case, Tribunal observed that if the activity does not amount to manufacture, there can be no question of levy of duty and if duty is levied, Cenvat credit cannot be denied by holding that there is no manufacture. This view was upheld in CCE v. Creative Enterprises (2009) 235 ELT 785 (Guj HC DB) * Perfo Chem v. CCE (2015) 315 ELT 237 (CESTAT).

If department accepts duty (though not payable), it cannot refuse Cenvat credit on inputs, since department cannot approbate and reprobate, as held in Laxmindco Steel P Ltd. v. CCE 2006 (202) ELT 629 (CESTAT SMB).

In Rico Auto Industries v. CCE 2003 (157) ELT 170 = 57 RLT 271 (CEGAT), it was held that inputs can be removed 'as such' or 'after processing' under Cenvat Credit Rules. Hence, even if there is no 'manufacture', no further amount is payable - followed in Sona Koyo Steering Systems v. CCE (2007) 5 STR 15 (CESTAT) [Strictly legally, in such case, it should be shown as 'amount' in invoice and not 'duty'].

If supplier has paid excise duty on wire drawn (though not legally payable during the relevant time), the buyer is eligible to avail Cenvat credit if supplier had not obtained refund of duty paid by them on drawn wire - BCL Springs v. CCE 2005 (185) ELT 56 (CESTAT).

Similarly, in Owens Bilt Ltd. v. CCE 1998(101) ELT 642 (CEGAT), it was held that once duty is paid at the manufacturer's end, the jurisdictional Assistant/Deputy Commissioner at user's end has no jurisdiction to decide whether duty was payable or not - followed in Goa Industrial Products v. CCE 2005 (181) ELT 222 (CESTAT).

Duty paid at full rate without availing concession - If assessee has paid duty at tariff rate without availing concessional rate, the buyer can get full Cenvat credit. - CCE v. Noel Pharmaceuticals 1999 (113) ELT 66 (CEGAT).

In Bharat Chemicals v. CCE (2004) 170 ELT 568 (CESTAT), tariff rate was 20%, but effective rate by way of exemption notification was 10%. Assessee was paying duty @ 10% for home clearances, but was paying duty @ 20% for goods exported and claiming rebate of full duty paid on export goods. It was held that he is entitled to full rebate, as rebate is of 'duty paid' and not 'duty payable'. [He was paying higher duty as he had excess balance in Cenvat credit account].

Cenvat credit if process incidental to manufacture - Purification and filtration of chemical to make it marketable in international market is process incidental to manufacture of the product and hence is covered in definition of 'manufacture' and hence is eligible for Cenvat credit - CCE v. Alok Enterprises (2010) 259 ELT 333 (Bom HC DB).

Buyer can avail Cenvat credit, if supplier paid duty, even though not payable - If supplier had paid excise duty (though not payable), buyer is eligible to avail Cenvat credit. See case law in earlier part of this chapter.

Cenvat credit in case of export of final products and taxable services

30.2 All exports of goods and services are tax free. Relief is given in respect of both input taxes/duties and taxes/duties on final product/output services.

Export Benefits - So far as excise is concerned, two major export incentives are available to a manufacturer (a) No duty is payable on finished products exported (b) Duty paid on inputs/tax paid on input services is refunded/not charged or Cenvat credit is allowed to be used for other final products.

Duty paid on inputs and service tax on input services used for exported final products not to be reversed - As an export incentive, no excise duty is payable on products exported. Supplies to SEZ are 'exports'. Similarly, goods can be supplied to units in EOU, EHTP or STP without payment of duty [these are 'deemed exports'].

As per normal Cenvat Rules, Cenvat is available only if duty is payable on final products. Hence, Cenvat credit on inputs used for manufacture of final products which are exported will lapse because final products are exempt from duty. However, as an incentive to export, it has been provided that Cenvat credit will be available on such inputs/input services, which are used in exported final product. The Cenvat credit can be used for clearance of any of the final products/output services. This is applicable to both duty on inputs and service tax on input services - Rule 6(6) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

Duty drawback of excise portion cannot be claimed - If assessee does not reverse Cenvat credit of duties/taxes, he does not get duty drawback of excise portion. However, he can claim duty drawback of customs portion.

Final product exported under advance authorisation - In CCE v. Oswal Agro Mills Ltd. 1997(93) ELT 184 (CEGAT), it was held that Cenvat credit on inputs is available even if final product is exported under DEEC scheme (Advance Authorisation - earlier Advance License), as import of raw materials as replenishment is subsequent to export of goods and those provisions cannot be brought into Cenvat Credit Rules - same view in CCE v. Bhilwara Spinners (2008) 226 ELT 222 (CESTAT SMB), where it was held that refund of Cenvat credit is not available if export is under claim of drawback or rebate. However, if export is under advance authorisation, refund of Cenvat credit on inputs is available. - same view in Bombay Dyeing v. CCE [2015] 315 ELT 309 (CESTAT) * Bombay Dyeing v. CCE [2015] 315 ELT 312 (CESTAT).

Goods exported through merchant exporter - In Evergreen Plywood v. CCE (2001) 138 ELT 229 (CEGAT) - relying on CCE v. Dhayana Electronic (2001) 138 ELT 229 (CEGAT) - it was held that benefit of Cenvat credit is available even when goods are exported through merchant exporter and not directly.

Inputs on which Cenvat availed can be exported under bond without payment of duty or under claim of rebate - In CCE v. RFH Metal Castings 2005 (184) ELT 194 (CESTAT), it has been held that inputs received (on which Cenvat was availed) can be cleared under bond without payment of duty, even if process carried out on inputs is not 'manufacture'. Cenvat credit availed on inputs is not required to be reversed - relying on Rico Auto v. CCE 2003(57) RLT 653 (CEGAT).

In GT Exports v. CCE (2008) 230 ELT 428 (CESTAT), it was held that inputs on which Cenvat credit is availed can be exported as such on payment of duty or under bond. In such case, refund of unutilised Cenvat credit is admissible - relying on Bala Handlooms v. CCE (2008) 223 ELT 100 (CESTAT SMB).

In Bala Handlooms v. CCE (2008) 223 ELT 100 (CESTAT SMB), assessee carried out processing on inputs which was not 'manufacture'. The final product was exported. It was held that assessee is entitled to refund of duty paid on inputs under rule 5 of Cenvat Credit Rules.

Clause (d) in form ARE-2 required a declaration that no drawback has been claimed. In Anandeya Zinc Oxides v. UOI (2016) 55 GST 339 = 68 taxmann.com 238 (Bom HC DB), it was held that if inputs are obtained without payment of duty under rule 19(2) of Central Excise Rules, no drawback is allowable, even if customs portion, in view of specific restriction in drawback notification [Now this decision is not valid].

Rebate even if inputs obtained from North East etc. are used in exported final product - Manufacturers in North East etc. get refund of duty paid by them. However, buyer of such goods is entitled to Cenvat credit. If goods obtained from North East etc. are used in manufacture of final product exported by buyer, rebate can be claimed by the exporter (since refund of duty is given to manufacturer and not the exporter) - MF(DR) Instruction No. 209/11/2005-CX-6 dated 3-4-2007 (8 STT 81 (Stat) = 210 ELT T27).

Rebate even if inputs used in processing without 'manufacture' - Notification No. 21/2004-CE allows rebate when excisable goods are used in the manufacture or processing of export goods. Hence, in A V Industries In re (2011) 269 ELT 122 (GOI), it has been held that rebate is payable even if only goods were tested and re-packed, as it amounts to processing of material for export.

In Sona Koyo Steering v. CCE (2007) 208 ELT 211 (CESTAT), assessee purchased some components, took Cenvat credit and cleared as such on payment of duty. It was held that they could do so even as trader and hence no duty is payable even if the activity is not 'manufacture' (It is advisable to show it as 'amount' and not as 'duty') - followed in AB Stampings v. CCE (2010) 259 ELT 299 (CESTAT SMB)

In Natural Vitamins v. CCE 2005 (179) ELT 326 (CESTAT SMB), it was held that if department collects excise duty on final product, it cannot say that Cenvat is not available as process is not 'manufacture'. Such stand is self-contradictory - same view in CCE v. MP Telelinks v. 2004 (178) ELT 167 (CESTAT) * Markwell Paper Plast v. CCE (2012) 285 ELT 76 (CESTAT) * CCE v. Thus, entire exercise is revenue neutral and demand is not sustainable.

In Rico Auto Industries v. CCE 2003 (157) ELT 170 = 57 RLT 271 (CEGAT), it was held that inputs can be removed 'as such' or 'after processing' under Cenvat Credit Rules. Hence, even if there is no 'manufacture', no further amount is payable - followed in Sona Koyo Steering Systems v. CCE (2007) 5 STR 15 (CESTAT) - view confirmed in CCE v. Delta Corporation (2013) 287 ELT 15 (Guj HC DB).

Mustangs Rubbers (2009) 237 ELT 257 (Ker HC DB). Job work or any process which does not amount to manufacture to be excluded - Job work of test, repairs, reconditioning etc. is not to be included, as this does not amount to 'manufacture' i.e. where new and identifiable product does not emerge. Similarly, if any processing or operation is done which does not amount to manufacture, its value will not be included. - [Same provision for calculating limit of Rs.150 lakhs].

In Pusha Roto Printers v. CCE (2008) 223 ELT 601 (CESTAT), assessee collected some charges for printing. It was held that this is not 'manufacture' and hence its value is not includible.

Goods returned after reprocessing - Goods returned and cleared after processing are not includible as value of goods for clearances can be considered only once and not twice over. - Kusum Kemicals (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2002(144) ELT 346= 51 RLT 651 (CEGAT).

Strips of plastics used within factory - Clearance of strips of plastics used within factory of production for weaving of fabrics or manufacture of sacks or bags made of polymers of ethylene or propylene are exempt. These are not to be included for calculating exemption limit of Rs 400 lakhs [Same provision for calculating limit of Rs150 lakhs]. [This item is omitted w.e.f. 1-4-2008 since strips of plastics intended for weaving of fabrics or sacks are eligible for SSI exemption w.e.f. 1-4-2008].

Inputs brought by assessee and cleared as such not to be considered - A unit can clear inputs as such on payment of duty under rule 3(4) of Cenvat Credit Rules [That time rule 57AB(1)(b) - earlier 57F(1)(ii)]. This turnover is not to be considered for calculating clearances of Rs. 150/400 lakhs - Board circular No. 263/30/88-CX.8 dated 27-10-88 quoted and matter remanded in Essee Metal Containers (P.) Ltd. v. CCE - 1993 (63) ELT 331 (CEGAT). [Though the circular is under old rules, the principle is valid under new rules also, as excise duty is on 'manufacture'. Merely selling bought out components does not amount to 'manufacture'. It is true that under 'Cenvat', inputs or inputs have to be cleared on payment of an 'amount'. However, such 'amount' is not duty. The provision is only for payment of 'amount' on inputs or capital goods cleared and not for any other purpose. It is not 'deemed manufacture'] [Same provision for calculating limit of Rs. 150 lakhs].

Turnover as trader along with own manufactured goods - In Rajdoot Paints v. CCE (2004) 171 ELT 230 (CESTAT), assessee was manufacturing goods under his own brand name. In addition, he was purchasing goods under his brand name and selling them as trader. It was rightly held that value of traded goods cannot be considered for purpose of SSI exemption limit - departmental appeal admitted by SC 180 ELT A136 [Same provision for calculating limit of Rs. 150 lakhs].

In CCE v. S C Patel (2011) 264 ELT 414 (CESTAT), assessee was selling bought out items without bringing them to factory. It was held that this turnover cannot be considered for purpose of SSI exemption limit.

In CCE v. CMS Computers 2005 (182) ELT 20 (SC 3 member bench) also, it was held that value of traded items is not required to be added. In this case, bought out items were supplied to buyer along with own manufactured goods on optional basis.

Activity which is not 'manufacture' is to be excluded - Turnover in relation to activity which is not 'manufacture' is required to be excluded - Karnataka Agro Chemicals v. CCE (2007) 215 ELT 470 (CESTAT).

Final products brought back for inspection - Final products cleared earlier and brought back in next year for inspection is not to be considered in the year in which it was brought back. (It will have been considered in the year in which it was originally cleared) - Manohar Brothers v. CCE 1999(107) ELT 813 = 30 RLT 477 (CEGAT). [Same principle should apply in respect of finished goods brought for repairs under rule 16]. [Same provision for calculating limit of Rs. 150 lakhs].

CCE (2013) 287 ELT 102 (CESTAT). Duty payable on scrap captively consumed if final product exempted - In Burn Standard Co. v. CCE (2008) 231 ELT 265 (CESTAT), assessee was manufacturing railway wagons which were exempt from duty. During manufacture, scrap was generated which was used in manufacture of exempted final product. It was held that duty is payable on scrap captively consumed if final product exempted.

Inputs eligible for Cenvat credit even if intermediate product exempt

45.2-2 CBE&C had clarified vide para 5 of circular No. B4/7/2000-TRU dated 3.4.2000, that Cenvat credit should not be denied if the inputs are used in any intermediate of final product, even if such intermediate product is exempt from payment of duty. The idea is that Cenvat credit is available so long as the inputs are used in or in relation to manufacture of final product, and whether directly or indirectly - view reiterated in Chapter 5 Para 3.9 of CBE&C's CE Manual, 2001 - same view in CCE v. Hindustan Sanitaryware 2002 AIR SCW 3652 = AIR 2002 SC 3162 = 145 ELT 3 (SC), in respect of earlier notification 217/86 - same view in Escorts Ltd. v. CCE (2004) 171 ELT 145 = 2004 AIR SCW 4826 (SC) - followed in Haldyn Glass v. CCE 2005 (187) ELT 263 (CESTAT).

In Hindustan Petroleum Corporation v. CCE 2000 (124) ELT 323 (CEGAT), Naphtha which was manufactured in the factory was used for production of steam and electricity. Steam and electricity were used in manufacture of final product. It was held that Naphtha manufactured within factory is exempt even if steam is exempt from duty and electricity is non-excisable product.

In Sturdy Polymers v. CCE 2004 (164) ELT 442 (CESTAT), assessee was manufacturer of plastic pipes/tubes. During its manufacture, waste and scrap arose. This waste and scrap was converted into granules, which were used in manufacture of pipes/tubes. The pipes/tubes were cleared on payment of duty. The granules were exempt from duty and hence duty was demanded by department on waste and scrap, as it was used in manufacture of 'exempted final product'. It was held that as long as intermediate product (granules in this case) is used for manufacture of dutiable final product, no duty is payable on inputs i.e. waste and scrap. Waste and scrap can be said to have been used indirectly in manufacture of final product and hence exemption under 67/1995-CE will be available - relying on Supreme Industries v. CCE 2004 (148) ELT 484 (CEGAT) - affirmed by SC - 153 ELT A91.

However, in Hindustan Petroleum Corporation v. CCE (2013) 287 ELT 102 (CESTAT), assessee was using Naptha for generation of electricity which was used for allied activities like road lightening, administrative office and canteen. It was held that Cenvat credit of duty paid on such Naptha is not available.

Final product should not be exempt from duty - This exemption is not available if final product is exempt from duty or is chargeable to Nil rate of duty. In other words, if no duty is payable on final products, duty will be payable on intermediate products.

Capital goods manufactured and used within factory

45.2-3 As per notification No. 67/1995-CE dated 16-3-1995, capital goods (as defined in Cenvat Credit Rules) manufactured in a factory and used within the factory of production are exempt from excise duty.

Further, as per explanation 2 to rule 2(g) of Cenvat Credit Rules, inputs include goods used in manufacture of capital goods which are further used in the factory of manufacturer. Thus, if capital goods are manufactured and used within the factory, Cenvat credit can be availed of goods which are used to manufacture such capital goods. Moreover, no duty will be payable on such capital goods.

In CCE v. Jindal Steel 2006 (201) ELT 598 (CESTAT), it was held that since 'capital goods' include parts and components of capital goods in any tariff heading, the parts and components manufactured within factory are exempt, whatever may be its tariff heading.

CCE (2009) 238 ELT 106 (CESTAT), it was held that exempted goods can be exported under bond and in such case, Cenvat credit is available inputs used in manufacture of such exempted products, in view of rule 6(5)(vi) of Cenvat Credit Rules - same view in Sandoz v. Bond and CT-1 by merchant exporter

18.3-1 Merchant exporter is required to execute a bond so that goods can be cleared by the supplier-manufacturer without payment of duty.

The bond can be executed by merchant-exporter in form B-1. Merchant exporter registered with recognised Export Promotion Council and Star Export Houses do not have to furnish any security/surety while executing bond, unless they have come to adverse notice of department. - CBE&C circular No. 613/4/2001-CX dated 31-1-2002, confirmed in CBE&C circular No. 711/27/2003-CX dated 30-4-2003. - - - If bond is executed by merchant exporter, he will obtain certificates in form CT-1 from Superintendent of Central Excise.

The exporter shall ensure that debit in bond does not exceed the credit available in the bond any time. Goods can be cleared by manufacturer on the strength of this certificate, without payment of duty. Forms of bond, letter of undertaking and CT-1 certificate have been given in Notification No. 42/2001-CE(NT). If export is through merchant exporter, ARE-1 form should be signed both by manufacturer as well as merchant exporter.

What about those who did not reverse in GSTR-3B in case of inverted duty structure on textile products w.e.f. 1-8-2018? - The clarification above applies to registered persons who have already reversed the ITC required to be lapsed in terms of the said notification through return in FORM GSTR-3B. What about those registered persons who are yet to perform this reversal? Clarification - All those registered persons required to make the reversal in terms of the said notification and who have not yet done so, may reverse the said amount through FORM GST DRC-03 instead of through FORM GSTR-3B - Sr. No. 2 of para 57 of CBI&C Circular No. 125/44/2019-GST dated 18-11-2019.

9.21-1 Consequences if credit to be lapsed on textile products reversed after August 2018?

What shall be the consequence if any registered person reverses the amount of credit to be lapsed, in terms the said notification, through the return in FORM GSTR-3B for any month subsequent to August, 2018 or through FORM GST DRC-03 subsequent to the due date of filing of the return in FORM GSTR-3B for the month of August, 2018?

Clarification - (a) As the registered person has reversed the amount of credit to be lapsed in the return in FORM GSTR-3B for a month subsequent to the month of August, 2018 or through FORM GST DRC-03 subsequent to the due date of filing of the return in FORM GSTR-3B for the month of August, 2018, he shall be liable to pay interest under section 50(1) of the CGST Act on the amount which has been reversed belatedly. Such interest shall be calculated starting from the due date of filing of return in FORM GSTR-3B for the month of August, 2018 till the date of reversal of said amount through FORM GSTR-3B or through FORM GST DRC-03, as the case may be. (b) The registered person who has reversed the amount of credit to be lapsed in the return in FORM GSTR-3B for any month subsequent to August, 2018 or through FORM GST DRC-03 subsequent to the due date of filing of the return in FORM GSTR-3B for the month of August, 2018 would remain eligible to claim refund of unutilized ITC on account of accumulation due to inverted tax structure w.e.f. 01.08.2018. Drawback Rules, 2017 - Section 75(2) of Customs Act (and Section 37 of Central Excise Act in case of products covered under Central Excise even after 1-7-2017) allows Central Government to frame rules for purpose of the Act. Under these powers, 'Customs and Central Excise Duties Drawback Rules, 2017' have been notified w.e.f. 1-10-2017. No RCMC required for post export remission schemes like duty drawback, RoDTEP, RoSCTL- Schemes such as Duty Drawback, Rebate of State and Central Taxes and Levies (RoSCTL), and Remission of Duties and Taxes on Export Products (RoDTEP) fall under the category of remission-based schemes. These schemes are aimed at remitting duties or taxes on exported goods. For these remission-based schemes, the requirement of an RCMC (Registration-Cum-Membership Certificate) does not apply. Exporters can claim benefits under these schemes without obtaining an RCMC - DGFT trade notice No. 19/2024-25 dated 4-10-2024.

58.1-1 Drawback of customs duty paid on input goods

As per rule 2(a) of Customs and Central Excise Duties Drawback Rules, 2017, Drawback, in relation to any goods manufactured in India and exported, means the rebate of duty excluding IGST and Compensation Cess, chargeable on any imported materials or excisable materials used or taxable services used as input services in manufacture of such goods [The words in italics inserted in 2017 Rules]

Rebate of safeguard duty paid on inputs if final product is exported - If inputs on which safeguard duty has been paid are actually used for manufacture of final product which is exported, the exporter can claim rebate of safeguard duty paid on inputs. This is because the All India duty drawback rates do not include incidence of safeguard duty - MF(DR) circular No. 23/2015-Cus dated 29-9-2015.

Countervailing duty on subsidized article not considered in duty drawback rate - Countervailing duty on subsidized article levied under section 9 of Customs Tariff Act is not considered in All Industry duty drawback rate. However, its drawback is available. Hence, inputs on which these duties are paid are used in manufacture of exported goods, the duty is eligible for duty drawback under brand rate. If the imported goods are exported as such, its refund is permissible under section 74 of Customs Act - MF(DR) circular No. 49/2017-Cus dated 12-12-2017.

Meaning of 'manufacture' - 'Manufacture' includes processing of or any other operation carried out on such goods, and the term 'manufacturer' shall be construed accordingly [rule 2(e) of Customs and Central Excise Duties Drawback Rules, 2017].

The definition is very wide. Simple processing will be eligible for 'drawback'.

What is 'export' for purpose of duty drawback - 'Export' means (a) taking out of India to a place outside India or (b) taking out from a place in Domestic Tariff Area (DTA) to a Special Economic Zone (SEZ) and (c) including loading of provisions or store or equipment for use on board a vessel or aircraft proceeding to a foreign port. [Rule 2(c) Customs and Central Excise Duties Drawback Rules, 2017].

Thus, duty drawback is available not only on physical exports but also in case of goods supplied to SEZ or to store or equipment supplied to aircraft/vessel going abroad.

Processing also eligible for Drawback - Drawback is allowable if any manufacture, process or any operation is carried out in India [section 75(1) of Customs Act]. Thus, drawback is available not only on manufacture, but also on processing and job work, where goods may not change its identity and no 'manufacture' has taken place.

58.1-2 Drawback - When not eligible

Section 75 of Customs Act, 1962 provide some disallowances or cases when drawback allowed can be recovered. Further, section 76(2) of Customs Act, 1962 authorises Central Government to issue notifications prohibiting drawback if the goods are likely to be smuggled back to India after export. Drawback Rules, 2017 also provide for some disallowances. These are summarised below :

If sale proceeds of export goods are not received within time stipulated by RBI

If no customs is paid on the inputs

If imported inputs were obtained under Advance Authorisation without payment of duty

If importer avails DFIA

Goods manufactured under Customs Bond where inputs were obtained without payment of duty

Goods manufactured by EOU or a unit in Special Economic Zone (as they obtain inputs without payment of duty)

In case of negative value addition - i.e. selling price of exported goods is less than value of imported goods i.e. foreign exchange spent on import of raw material is more than FOB Value of exports.

Jute batching oil used in manufacture of jute yarn, twist, twine etc.

Packing materials used in relation to export of jute yarn, jute fabrics and jute manufacture.
